messages.body_plain:
Flat second derivative of the log density?  The second
derivative w.r.t. y of log normal(y | 0, 1) is constant.

We'll need Michael's help for real geometry questions,
so may need to put this discussion in a different thread.

And thanks for posting the model;  it's great to see this
kind of careful numerical coding for real problems.

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2016, at 7:55 AM, Daniel Rosenbloom <daniel.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Thanks for clarifying. Binary search is plenty fast -- I get 70k samples per second using it, with a pretty large table (22000 rows). I'm attaching my pystan code, so that you can see how we are doing the interpolation. The interpolation is linear in x (for x<10) or in log(x) (for x>10); this was chosen since the distribution scales as LL=-2*log(x) for large x. Left and right tail behavior is also given.
>
> The lookup table (landtable.py) is for the Landau distribution, computed using Mathematica, which has the distribution built-in (the standard form of the distribution is LandauDistribution[0,Pi/2] in Mathematica). Note that while there is an analytic approximation to this distribution (Moyal approximation, described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_distribution), it is very bad outside a small interval, and it misses the long tail behavior.
>
> Is it OK to have flat second derivative? This linear approach samples quite accurately, and I'm getting no Metropolis rejection warnings.
>
> Thanks again!
> Daniel
>
> On Thursday, March 3, 2016 at 7:32:03 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We're taking the nanny software approach on this one
> and not implementing it on purpose because it's dangerous.
> In general, it can break the gradients and therefore break
> all of our gradient-based algorithms.
>
> Is there a particular form of interpolation you need
> that we might be able to build in and guarantee that
> the gradients work?  I know there was one built into BUGS.
>
> Binary search is the best you'll be able to do now.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Mar 2, 2016, at 4:52 PM, Daniel Rosenbloom <daniel.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Nathan--
> >
> > I wonder if you, or any others following this thread, figured out a faster way to cast reals to ints. I have an analogous problem that I want to solve by linear interpolation (my likelihood function is slow to compute, and so I pre-computed a lookup table).
> >
> > It appears that I can successfully do inference with my interpolated likelihood, with either optimize or sampling (acceptance probs > 0.9, so it seemed to use the gradient information correctly), using the hack that Bob suggests. Does anyone know of a more direct hack to typecast without searching through a list, to speed things up? (Failing that, I could try binary search, or cubic interpolation on a smaller lookup table.)
> >
> >
> > Marcus pointed out that the second derivative is always zero -- would this end up posing any problems?
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> >
> > On Friday, November 8, 2013 at 2:13:31 PM UTC-5, Marcus wrote:
> > Actually, the gradient is probably fine, note that he said he was doing linear interpolation.  My guess is Nathan is doing something like:
> >
> > xm <- x[floor(c)];
> > xp <- x[ceil(c)];
> > x <- (c - floor(c))*xp + (ceil(c) - c)*xm;
> >
> > In which case the derivative of x with respect to c is reasonably fine.  The second derivative would be wrong (always = 0) but that's another issue.
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Marcus
> >
> >
> >
> > On Fri, Nov 8, 2013 at 10:17 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > For my particular case, I think the floor calculation should not have a significant effect on the gradient calculation.  The index is just used to look up a value from a table which is applied as a small correction to the model value being compared to the data in the likelihood.  I use the floor loop to find the right index in the table, but then I linearly interpolate between the table values, so I think the gradient should still be smooth.  Also, the correction is just a local variable in the model section, so no sampled parameters are being converted to integers.
> >
> > Your correction may very well be smooth, but calculating it this way lose the gradient information of the correction so even if the posterior is calculated correction its gradient won't.  In the end the Metropolis/slice procedure will correct for any error,
> > but whenever the correction becomes important then the error will induce small acceptance probabilities and poor sampling.  That's the biggest concern.
> >

messages.body_plain:
Stan gripes if you don't formulate your model in typical
generative terms.

You'll have to post the rest of your Stan program for us
to see what's going on;  the real problem in your fragment
is that you never define y[n].

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2016, at 5:29 AM, Jacqueline Scholl <jacqueli...@psy.ox.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> I see, so I have now:
> data{
> dat [N];}
>
> model{
> real y[N];
>
> for (n in 1:N)
> y[n] ~ normal(RPE,sigma)
> dat[n]~ bernoulli(f(y));  //with the function f doing a softmax transform of y as typical for a learning/decision model
> }
>
> but now stan says 'Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
> compile: If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.' (for the line where I sample y[n])
>
> I think the problem is that I'm trying to say that there is noise for the learning process (y[n]~...) and the decision (dat[n]~...) ?
> Sorry that I'm a bit slow at understanding this..
>
> On Mon, Mar 7, 2016 at 5:38 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> You can make a variable out of prediction error.  I'll keep going
> back to the simple regression case, which shows the difference:
>
> This is:
>
>   y[n] = x[n] * beta + epsilon[n]
>   epsilon ~ normal(0, 1)
>
>   transformed parameters {
>     vector[N] epsilon;
>     for (n in 1:N)
>       epsilon[n] <- y[n] - x[n] * beta;
>   }
>   model {
>     epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);
>
> Here's the way to do it without epsilon being saved:
>
>   model {
>     vector[N] epsilon;
>     for (n in 1:N)
>       epsilon[n] <- y[n] - x[n] * beta;
>
>     epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);
>
> And here's the way to do it without an explicit epsilon:
>
>   model {
>     y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * beta, sigma);
>
> It works out to the same density either way.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
> > On Mar 6, 2016, at 10:50 AM, Jacqueline Scholl <jacqueli...@psy.ox.ac.uk> wrote:
> >
> > yes, that's pretty much what I'm trying to do;
> >
> > I'm trying to code a variant of a reinforcement learning  model. In this kind of model, there is usually no noise in the learning steps, but only 'noise' when the learnt information gets transformed into a binary choice between e.g. two options the participant selects between based on the learnt information.
> >
> > The standard learning model is something like this:
> > (for each participant and trial t)
> > PredictionError[t]<- Outcome[t]-Prediction[t]; // Outcome would here be say 1 or 0 for getting a reward or not getting one and prediction is how likely the participant/ model thinks the option is going to have a reward
> > Prediction[t+1] <- Prediction[t] + LearningRate[p]*PredictionError[t]; // The Prediction error is used to update the prediction (where the learning rate determines how much the prediction error is weighted
> > RealChoice[t]~bernoulli(f(Predictions[t]); // the predictions for the two option to determine which choice participants are likely to make, and then compare that to the Real choice.
> >
> > What I want to capture now is that there might also be some noise in the learning process itself (for example, my neural data suggests to me that a drug improves the representation of the prediction error in one group). How can I capture this noise?
> > I've tried to add it to the prediction error:
> > PredictionErrorTemp[t] <- Outcome[t]-Prediction[t]; //as before
> > PredictionError[t] ~ normal(PredictionErrorTemp[t],noise[p]); // where noise[s] says how much each participant is representation is noisy.
> > rest as before.
> >
> > The problem now is that I have so far tried to sample PredictionError (or rather the 'Matt trick transform' of it) as a parameter because if I write the code as an _lp function, I can't use it in the generated quantities block. But having this as a parameter (i.e. having as many values as participants x trials) does not seem right either.
> >
> > On Fri, Mar 4, 2016 at 11:45 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > I'd need to see more of what you're trying to do.  Can you
> > write the density down in math terms without worrying about
> > coding in Stan?
> >
> > The idea is that you want:
> >
> >   y[t + 1] ~ normal(f(y[t],theta), noise);
> >
> > where f( ) is some update function to predict the new observation
> > at time t+1 based on the previous observation at t and some parameters theta.
> > Then the function isn't exact and gets some noise.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> > > On Mar 4, 2016, at 4:50 AM, Jacqueline Scholl <jacqueli...@psy.ox.ac.uk> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Bob,
> > >
> > > thanks for your help.
> > > So basically, if I understand you right, you're suggesting:
> > > PredictErrorOld <- Oucome-Prediction
> > > PredictErrorNew ~ normal(PredictErrorOld,sigma)
> > > and then sigma (with an individual value for each person, constraint by a group normal) is a measure of the noise as in standard deviation of the distribution.
> > >
> > > Silly question now, would I code PredictErrorNew as a parameter? Because then the problem is that Stan is fitting this on a trial-by-trial basis (which is maybe why it doesn't converge even after 10,000 iterations). When I tried to just have PredictErrorNew as a variable in the function block, I can't call the function (with '_lp' in the end) from the generated quantities block.
> > >
> > > I'm wondering whether it's maybe a problem with the steps that happen with the PredictErrorNew quantity after I make it:
> > > - Use it to update the predicted reward value (this is a learning model)
> > > - Use the predicted reward value to compute the choice probability
> > > - Link that to the real choice with RealChoice ~ bernoulli(PredictedChoice) [this one is only in the model block, not in the generated quantities block, where I instead use the PredictedChoice to compute the log likelihood]
> > >
> > > [I think that with the 'Matt trick', this may transform to my original:
> > > PredictErrorNew_raw <-normal(0,1)  (what I called 'NOISE')
> > > PredictErrorNew <- PredictErrorOld + sigma*PredictErrorNew_raw (where .._raw is 'NOISE' and sigma is 'InterF1')
> > > ]
> > >
> > > On Thu, Mar 3, 2016 at 8:31 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > On Mar 3, 2016, at 1:05 PM, jacquie...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > >
> > > > I've been thinking that maybe it would actually be more accurate to model this interference as adding some noise to the representation of the prediction error (Outcome[s,t,o]-Prediction[s,t,o]).
> > > >
> > > > I've tried to do this as:
> > > >  Prediction[s,t+1,o] <- alpha[s]*(Outcome[s,t,o]-Prediction[s,t,o]+NOISE*InterF1[s]);
> > > >
> > >
> > > > But the problem with this is that I'm not sure how to code 'NOISE'
> > >
> > > You want to think about modeling the noise probabilistically,
> > > then the formulation becomes easy.  Think about the usual formulation
> > > of regression:
> > >
> > >   y = beta * x + epsilon
> > >   epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma)
> > >
> > > To write this out in Stan, you have:
> > >
> > >   y ~ normal(beta * x, sigma);
> > >
> > > There's no explicit representation of epsilon.  Now you
> > > could equivalently, but much more confusingly, write:
> > >
> > >   real epsilon;
> > >   epsilon <- y - beta * x;
> > >   epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);
> > >
> > > You just need to do the same thing for your problem (only
> > > you need to scale epsilon).
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > - I have tried:
> > > >  for (s in 1:nsub){
> > > >     for (t in 1:ntrials){
> > > >       for (o in 1:2){
> > > > NOISE[s,t,o] ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >       }}}
> > > > but if I then have 'NOISE' in the parameter block (as otherwise, stan tells me that I can't use my model in the generated quantities block by calling a function), the model then fits some value for NOISE on each trial. This seems wrong?
> > > >
> > > > On Monday, February 29, 2016 at 3:05:57 PM UTC, jacquie...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Dear all,
> > > >
> > > > I was hoping I could get some help with checking that the following logic is ok: I want to test whether two groups differ across two parameters of my learning model (like an ANOVA across these parameters). The parameters measure how much their learning is interfered by two different external factors (that's why I called them 'InterF1' and 'InterF2' here). The code is attached. The main part of interest is in the transformed data block where I'm trying to sample each person's InterF1, InterF2:
> > > >
> > > > transformed parameters{
> > > >   for (s in 1:15){ // Drug group
> > > >     InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
> > > >     InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
> > > >   for (s in 16:nsub){ // Placebo group
> > > >     InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
> > > >     InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > The model runs very slowly, compared to a model where I just sample InterF1 and InterF2 directly (from e.g. for drug group: InterF1[drug] ~ normal(mu_InterF1drug, sd_InterF1). But the number of samples for the mu_InterfGroupDiff is very high (~ number of samples drawn), so maybe this is not too bad. Is there anyway to code this better?
> > > >
> > > > I'm also not sure whether if I wanted to model the standard deviation also as different between the groups, I could just replace for example sd_InterF1 with something like sd_InterF1Drug and sd_InterF1Placebo?
> > > >
> > > > The last part I'm not quite sure about is how I can limit the parameters - I would expect InterF1 and InterF2 to be between -1 and +1. This is also ok for the group level parameters that I can limit as I want. But if I try to limit InterF1, the model produces problems because the sums can fall outside this interval.
> > > >
> > > > Many thanks
> > > > Jacquie
> > > >
> > > > Full example code:
> > > > parameters{
> > > >   // group level
> > > >   real mu_alpha_pr;
> > > >   real mu_beta_pr;
> > > >   real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfGeneral;   // how much a person is interfered on average across the two measures
> > > >   real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfGroupDiff; // group difference between drug and placebo
> > > >   real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfType;      // how much Interference factor 1 and Interference factor 2 differ for each person
> > > >
> > > >   real <lower=0> sd_alpha;
> > > >   real <lower=0> sd_beta;
> > > >   real <lower=0> sd_InterF1;
> > > >   real <lower=0> sd_InterF2;
> > > >
> > > >   // Individual subjects
> > > >   real alpha_pr[nsub];
> > > >   real beta_pr[nsub];
> > > >   real InterF1_pr[nsub];
> > > >   real InterF2_pr[nsub];
> > > > }
> > > > transformed parameters{
> > > >   real mu_alpha;
> > > >   real mu_beta;
> > > >
> > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1>  alpha;
> > > >   real<lower=0,upper=10> beta;
> > > >   real<lower=-5,upper=5> InterF1;
> > > >   real<lower=-5,upper=5> InterF2;
> > > >
> > > >   mu_alpha    <- Phi(mu_alpha_pr);
> > > >   mu_beta     <- Phi(mu_beta_pr)*10;
> > > >
> > > >   for (s in 1:15){ // Drug group
> > > >     alpha[s]      <- Phi(alpha_pr[s]);
> > > >     beta[s]       <- Phi(beta_pr[s])*10;
> > > >     InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
> > > >     InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
> > > >   for (s in 16:nsub){ // Placebo group
> > > >     alpha[s]      <- Phi(alpha_pr[s]);
> > > >     beta[s]       <- Phi(beta_pr[s])*10;
> > > >     InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
> > > >     InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > model{
> > > >   // Draw parameters
> > > >   mu_alpha_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >   mu_beta_pr  ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >   mu_InterfGeneral   ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >   mu_InterfGroupDiff ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >   mu_InterfType      ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >
> > > >   sd_alpha   ~ normal(0,1000);
> > > >   sd_beta    ~ normal(0,1000);
> > > >   sd_InterF1 ~ normal(0,1000);
> > > >   sd_InterF2 ~ normal(0,1000);
> > > >
> > > >   InterF1_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >   InterF2_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >
> > > >   // Do the learning (shortened)
> > > >   for (s in 1:nsub){
> > > >     for (t in 1:ntrials)
> > > >       for (o in 1:2){
> > > >         Prediction[s,t+1,o] <- (alpha[s]- InterF1[s]*Dat1 - InterF2[s]*Dat2) * (Prediction[s,t,o]-Outcome[s,t,o]);
> > > >       }
> > > >       DecisionPred[s,t] <- 1.0/(1.0+exp(beta[s]*(Predictions[s,t,2]-Predictions[s,t,1])))
> > > >     }
> > > >   }
> > > > }

And when I say "define" I mean define.  You declare it
as a real N-array, but then you use it in the ~ statement
before it's defined.  The ~ doesn't do a random draw; it's
just shorthand to increment the log density.

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2016, at 1:58 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Monday, March 7, 2016 at 1:05:31 PM UTC-5, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> Is there a simple way to produce (presumably in the generated quantities section?) the partial correlation between pairs of variables that are otherwise modelled as having a multivariate normal distribution?
>
> There are many ways of defining a partial correlation. Some include
> 	• The correlation between i and j given all other variables. This is given by inverting the covariance matrix, rescaling it to a correlation matrix, and negating the off-diagonal elements
> 	• The correlation between i and j given all variables (if any) before i where i < j. These are given by the transformation from a correlation matrix to unconstrained parameters if you do a Fisher transform of the unconstrained parameters. You can do this in R with the unconstrained_pars function.
> 	• The correlation between i and j given all variables (if any) between i and j where i < j. This is not available in Stan but there is code for it in the clusterGeneration R package.
> 	• The correlation between i and j given all variables (if any) after j where i < j. These partial correlations do not have a name as far as I know of and no code either.
> Ben

If I understand you correctly, you want to compute
the CDF of the marginal posterior for a specified parameter.

There's no way to do that from within a Stan program.
You can empirically estimate it using the posterior draws after
the program finishes.

messages.body_plain:
I'd be inclined to take a less extreme hyperprior than beta(0.5, 0.5),
but it probably isn't too sensitive (you could check).

This specification of a beta prior in terms of mean and a kind
of precision is discussed in the manual and I also talk about it
in the case study I just added on repeated binary trials (which in
turn is based on the case study in chapter 5 of Gelman et al.'s
Bayesian Data Analysis book).  In this model, it's hard to control
the tendency of multi to drift off to infinity if the data is consistent
with complete pooling (all the p2 are the same).

So what I did to change the model in the case study is switch to
a logit-scale rather than trying to fiddle with beta distributions.

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies.html

I've been meaning to announce the case studies, but so far there
are only three of mine.  I still need to get some more examples out
there (I believe there's one in the mail queue).

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2016, at 12:54 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Your post made me realize that my priors were misspecified as well.
>
> I wanted to shrink mixture assignments toward an overall distribution of probabilities (beta), but the prior to that beta was directly another beta, which is incorrect.
>
> That is, the hyper prior distribution was a beta(.5,.5) or something, and a realization of that distribution was entered as the beta prior parameter for the mixture assignment.
> This is totally incorrect --- The prior distribution was getting <lower=0,upper=1>, when it should be getting a scaled version of that.  The mean of the prior beta was correct, but the width was totally wrong.
>
> Before:
>
> p2 ~ beta(P2,1-P2);
> P2 ~ beta(.5,.5)
>
> This is totally incorrect.
> Now it is:
> p2 ~ beta(P2*multi,(1 - P2)*multi); (conceptually speaking)
> P2 ~ beta(.5,.5);
>
> The multi (multiplier) changes the scale of the p2 distribution.  It didn't help with mixing, but it did improve inference a bit.
>
> On Sunday, March 6, 2016 at 11:45:06 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Suppose I have a normal(2, 1) distribution.  If I don't
> truncate, the mean is 2.  If I truncate setting lower=1,
> the mean is 2.3.
>
> > library(rstan)
> > prog <- "parameters { real<lower=1> y; } model { y ~ normal(2, 1); }"
> > fit <- stan(model_code=prog)
> > print(fit)
> ...
>       mean ...
> y     2.29 ...
>
>
> So the original posterior mean is 2, but by truncating at lower=1,
> it moves the posterior mean up to 2.3.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> > On Mar 5, 2016, at 6:57 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > The reason I was using the <1 priors was to favor categorization (p2 = 0 or 1 being more probable than .4-.6), which is a trick I used in jags to guide the sampler a bit.
> >
> > Could you elaborate on your point that it'll make a difference if the posterior has parameters < 1?
> >
> > On Saturday, March 5, 2016 at 2:01:05 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Yup.  Theoretically the ones less than 1 are very different, but
> > in practice as long as you see both positive and negative instances,
> > it's not going to make a huge difference.  It will make a difference
> > though if the posterior has parameters < 1.
> >
> > And yes, a log normal can help keep things away from zero, but
> > it can also cause computational issues if the data really wants
> > to push things out into the tail.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Mar 4, 2016, at 8:07 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Currently, N=200, with N_1 = 100, N_2 = 100.
> > >
> > > I've tried a few beta priors, all fairly uninformative:
> > > (.2,.2)
> > > .5,.5
> > > 1,1
> > > 2,2
> > >
> > > Doesn't seem to make a difference.

> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Mar 4, 2016, at 6:54 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Noted. Eek, glad I made the transition then.
> > > >
> > > > As for divergences, most of the mixtures I've been fitting have a *huge* number of divergent transitions, sometimes equal to the number of post-warmup iterations.
> > > > If it's occurring near boundaries, I'm guessing the issue is that some people load *very* highly on one model vs another model, and the prior is already inverted to favor that, so the likelihood and the prior are both favoring extreme drops near boundaries (0 or 1).
> > > >
> > > > I'll tweak the priors a bit to not favor such assignments and see whether it fixes the issue. In Jags, I typically used mixture weights of, e.g., dbeta(.5,.5) to favor assigning individuals to one or the other. Stan may not need that as much, because it doesn't have to swap between entire models.
> > > >
> > > > On Friday, March 4, 2016 at 5:27:05 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > Nope.  Here's from page 8 of the JAGS manual (v3.3.0):
> > > >
> > > >   If initial values are not supplied by the user, then
> > > >   each parameter chooses its own initial value based on
> > > >   the values of its parents. The initial value is chosen
> > > >   to be a “typical value” from the prior distribution.
> > > >   The exact meaning of “typical value” depends on the
> > > >   distribution of the stochastic node, but is usually the
> > > >   mean, median, or mode.
> > > >
> > > >   If you rely on automatic initial value generation and
> > > >   are running multiple parallel chains, then the initial
> > > >   values will be the same in all chains. You may not want
> > > >   this behaviour, especially if you are using the Gelman
> > > >   and Rubin convergence diagnostic, which assumes that
> > > >   the initial values are over-dispersed with respect
> > > >   to the posterior distribution. In this case, you are
> > > >   advised to set the starting values manually using the
> > > >   ”parameters in” statement.
> > > >
> > > > So the "stability" you're seeing is probably a combination of
> > > > using the same inits in each chain and Gibbs poor mixing,
> > > > especially with discrete parameters.
> > > >
> > > > The divergent transitions arise when there's a numerical
> > > > error (underflow, overflow, divide by zero, etc.), and it
> > > > almost always indicates areas of the posterior with extreme
> > > > curvature.
> > > >
> > > > What are the messages coming back from the divergences?  It
> > > > indicates another situation where you're probably getting bias
> > > > from missing part of the parameter space.
> > > >
> > > > This can happen if your data's consistent with parameters at
> > > > constraint boundaries, like scales (std devs) of zero.
> > > >
> > > > And it's not the high-density modes that we want to explore,
> > > > it's the typical set (high probability mass volume) of the posterior,
> > > > which can be far away from the modes (as it is in a high-dimensional
> > > > multivariate normal --- almost none of the mass is close to the mode above
> > > > 50 or 100 dimensions).
> > > >
> > > > - Bob
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > > On Mar 4, 2016, at 11:25 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > I never really messed with the inits of jags; from what I could tell, jags randomly generates inits, but I don't really know how they do it.
> > > > >
> > > > > And right -- I'm glad stan better explores the parameter space, even if it does result in multimodal posteriors.
> > > > > That sort of thing is expected, I think, with highly complex models. There can be several high probability solutions to a complex model.
> > > > >
> > > > > I do have a question though. Most of the time when I run a mixture model in stan, I see fairly severe n_divergent warnings at the end.
> > > > > I know that those are undesirable, and I know that to 'get rid of them' one should set adapt_delta to a higher value, but what exactly *is* a divergent transition? I couldn't find it in the manual, and google didn't help much either.
> > > > > Again, despite the divergences, the inference seems to be correct (in my weird mixture-DIF with items of varying DIF probability model, it recovers the DIF items well and the recovered ability scores correlate ~ .8 with the true ability scores), but I have a TON of divergences.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thursday, March 3, 2016 at 6:29:03 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > A simple example would be good.
> > > > >
> > > > > Are you using diffuse random inits in JAGS?  As far as I know,
> > > > > you need to do that yourself (or I may be confusing it with BUGS).
> > > > >
> > > > > The diffuse initialization will help diagnose any underlying
> > > > > multimodality in your model.
> > > > >
> > > > > The fact that Stan actually explores your posterior should
> > > > > be considered a good thing!  You can't do proper Bayesian inference
> > > > > on only a subset of the posterior (though you can do approximate
> > > > > Bayes that way and maybe get a good enough answer to an applied
> > > > > problem).
> > > > >
> > > > > - Bob
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > > On Mar 3, 2016, at 5:16 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I can probably dig some up. I have a ton of jags (and now stan) files where I've played with mixture modeling.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I typically generate the data myself (so I know the parameter values), fit the model, then determine how well the model assigned individuals to clusters (and cluster parameters).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I'm not sure I could say jags "works better", it just works "more consistently", in that the chains typically find the same spot of parameter space and it converges quickly.
> > > > > > Stan is better at finding various solutions, and so it yields multimodal posteriors. This isn't a bad thing, it's just less consistent. I'm not opposed to this, and usually the inferences aren't really affected by it very much.
> > > > > > Both of them generally estimate cluster memberships well (after accounting for any between-chain label switching, which still occasionally happens despite some order constraints).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The meta-mixture model I posted on earlier just flops in both of them. Jags never leaves the starting model, and Stan basically finds a unique solution per-chain, so it's not even 'multi-modal', so much as there are as many solutions as there are chains; sometimes the posterior is practically flat as a result.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I haven't quantitatively compared stan and jags in their inferential accuracies for mixture models. In time, I probably will and I can determine which sampler works better in certain conditions. My guess is both will perform well, but stan will continue to find annoying points in the parameter space that doesn't change inference much but does take 16 hours (as per today).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thursday, March 3, 2016 at 4:00:05 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > > Do you have an example where JAGS works better than
> > > > > > Stan for mixture models?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > - Bob
> > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Mar 3, 2016, at 4:36 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I'm sure you're correct --- It's part of the reason I'm using Stan.
> > > > > > > Even if jags gives more consistent results for mixture models in particular, it's largely because it fails to adequately explore the parameter space.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > That said -- The model wasn't inferentially incorrect. The parameters recovered were generally correct (given that I know the true parameters).
> > > > > > > The issue with this model in Stan isn't that it's finding multiple solutions (that, I'm ok with. Multimodality is expected when several adequate solutions exist). My issue with it is that it's hitting areas that are difficult *to sample* and is causing the sampler to run for 16 hours until completion.  To some degree, if I know the non-difficult areas yield valid inferences, I'd rather just skip the problematic areas in some way.
> > > > > > > That is, the pathology of the model seems to affect the sampling performance moreso than the /inference/, which is all I really care about.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thursday, March 3, 2016 at 3:27:23 PM UTC-6, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > > > > I am highly confident that JAGS is missing these pathological regions
> > > > > > > entirely and actually giving biased estimates.  It’s something we see
> > > > > > > over and over again.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Mar 3, 2016, at 9:22 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >> Like I said, it works in jags, and by the nature of conditional sampling, the chains aren't hitting these weird warmup issues or problematic spots.

messages.body_plain:
Hm, interesting. I ran into the "multiplier -> infinity" issue and constrained the multiplier from 1 to N (or 1 to J, depending on the distribution).

So if instead of using p2<lower=0,upper=1>[N] ~ beta(P2*P2_multi,(1 - P2)*P2_multi), P2_multi<lower=1,upper=N>
I could use logit2[N].

My question then:
beta:probability :: _____:logit

On Monday, March 7, 2016 at 2:40:09 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'd be inclined to take a less extreme hyperprior than beta(0.5, 0.5),
> but it probably isn't too sensitive (you could check).
>
> This specification of a beta prior in terms of mean and a kind
> of precision is discussed in the manual and I also talk about it
> in the case study I just added on repeated binary trials (which in
> turn is based on the case study in chapter 5 of Gelman et al.'s
> Bayesian Data Analysis book).  In this model, it's hard to control
> the tendency of multi to drift off to infinity if the data is consistent
> with complete pooling (all the p2 are the same).
>
> So what I did to change the model in the case study is switch to
> a logit-scale rather than trying to fiddle with beta distributions.
>
> http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies.html
>
> I've been meaning to announce the case studies, but so far there
> are only three of mine.  I still need to get some more examples out
> there (I believe there's one in the mail queue).
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Mar 7, 2016, at 12:54 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Your post made me realize that my priors were misspecified as well.
> >
> > I wanted to shrink mixture assignments toward an overall distribution of probabilities (beta), but the prior to that beta was directly another beta, which is incorrect.
> >
> > That is, the hyper prior distribution was a beta(.5,.5) or something, and a realization of that distribution was entered as the beta prior parameter for the mixture assignment.
> > This is totally incorrect --- The prior distribution was getting <lower=0,upper=1>, when it should be getting a scaled version of that.  The mean of the prior beta was correct, but the width was totally wrong.
> >
> > Before:
> >
> > p2 ~ beta(P2,1-P2);
> > P2 ~ beta(.5,.5)
> >
> > This is totally incorrect.
> > Now it is:
> > p2 ~ beta(P2*multi,(1 - P2)*multi); (conceptually speaking)
> > P2 ~ beta(.5,.5);
> >
> > The multi (multiplier) changes the scale of the p2 distribution.  It didn't help with mixing, but it did improve inference a bit.
> >
> > On Sunday, March 6, 2016 at 11:45:06 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Suppose I have a normal(2, 1) distribution.  If I don't
> > truncate, the mean is 2.  If I truncate setting lower=1,
> > the mean is 2.3.
> >
> > > library(rstan)
> > > prog <- "parameters { real<lower=1> y; } model { y ~ normal(2, 1); }"
> > > fit <- stan(model_code=prog)
> > > print(fit)
> > ...
> >       mean ...
> > y     2.29 ...
> >
> >
> > So the original posterior mean is 2, but by truncating at lower=1,
> > it moves the posterior mean up to 2.3.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> > > On Mar 5, 2016, at 6:57 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > The reason I was using the <1 priors was to favor categorization (p2 = 0 or 1 being more probable than .4-.6), which is a trick I used in jags to guide the sampler a bit.
> > >
> > > Could you elaborate on your point that it'll make a difference if the posterior has parameters < 1?
> > >
> > > On Saturday, March 5, 2016 at 2:01:05 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > Yup.  Theoretically the ones less than 1 are very different, but
> > > in practice as long as you see both positive and negative instances,
> > > it's not going to make a huge difference.  It will make a difference
> > > though if the posterior has parameters < 1.
> > >
> > > And yes, a log normal can help keep things away from zero, but
> > > it can also cause computational issues if the data really wants
> > > to push things out into the tail.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Mar 4, 2016, at 8:07 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Currently, N=200, with N_1 = 100, N_2 = 100.
> > > >
> > > > I've tried a few beta priors, all fairly uninformative:
> > > > (.2,.2)
> > > > .5,.5
> > > > 1,1
> > > > 2,2
> > > >
> > > > Doesn't seem to make a difference.
> > > >
> > > > On Friday, March 4, 2016 at 7:00:03 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > The beta priors aren't particularly strong, though.  What's
> > > > the data size that's going with those priors?
> > > >
> > > > - Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] sort_asc problems
messages.body_plain:
If you're sorting arrays of dummy values and setting special
edge conditions, there's probably a better way to do what you're
trying to do.

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2016, at 10:41 AM, Jacqueline Scholl <jacqueli...@psy.ox.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> Hi Daniel,
> thanks for the quick reply, this is a great suggestion. The NANs are just there from initialising an array and not filling these values, so putting them as infinity (which I didn't even know existed!) should solve the sorting.
> Thanks!!
>
> On Mon, Mar 7, 2016 at 3:38 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> Hi Jacquie,
>
> 1. I don't think we ever intended for these functions to allow NaN. I believe this is an error in our implementation. I've created an issue for it: https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/253
> 2. NaN doesn't behave like a number: If x is a real number, both (x < NaN) and (NaN < x) are false. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NaN
> 3. It's inconsistent due to the underlying implementation relying on std::sort() in C++: http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/sort.
>
> Without the full program, it's hard to tell what you're doing with the NaNs, but you could replace those values with negative_infinity().
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
>
> On Mon, Mar 7, 2016 at 10:12 AM, <jacquie...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I've been trying to use sort_asc on part of a 2D array. Alright, I like your idea.

I'll try using logit units rather than probabilities.

It seems like the logistic distribution is what I'll want to use.

So, for shrinking logits, I'll want to estimate a logistic distribution of some mean and scale.
An 'uninformed' logistic distribution seems to be logistic(0,1) --- By that, I mean uniformly distributed probabilities, converted to logit, is approximately distributed logistic(0,1).

Would a good prior for the logistic distribution mean itself be a logistic distribution?
I'm not sure what the logistic scale prior should be; The larger the scale, the more it is like beta(<1,<1). The smaller, the more it is like beta(>1,>1).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,
Thanks very much for your answer. Yes, you are right for any distribution curve, that would be cdf. My aim, however, is to be able to compute area under any curve (and not necessarily a probability distribution). For instance, you may consider an area under a GP curve.

Now that it's not possible to do it with Stan, is there anyway to use some of the R functions inside stan? Of course, one way is to generate points off of a GP in Stan and tp export them from Stan and to use them inside an AUC function in R. Is there any better way to do it?

Thanks very much,
-Sepehr

messages.body_plain:
Usually normal;  Stan doesn't require (or even use) conjugacy.
See the example in the case study.

The typical motivation for making things a logit is either
(a) to do maximum likelihood in an unconstrained space, or
(b) to add other predictors or to generalize to a hierarchical
or multilevel model.

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2016, at 3:53 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hm, interesting. I ran into the "multiplier -> infinity" issue and constrained the multiplier from 1 to N (or 1 to J, depending on the distribution).
>
> So if instead of using p2<lower=0,upper=1>[N] ~ beta(P2*P2_multi,(1 - P2)*P2_multi), P2_multi<lower=1,upper=N>
> I could use logit2[N].
>
> My question then:
> beta:probability :: _____:logit
>
>
> On Monday, March 7, 2016 at 2:40:09 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'd be inclined to take a less extreme hyperprior than beta(0.5, 0.5),
> but it probably isn't too sensitive (you could check).
>
> This specification of a beta prior in terms of mean and a kind
> of precision is discussed in the manual and I also talk about it
> in the case study I just added on repeated binary trials (which in
> turn is based on the case study in chapter 5 of Gelman et al.'s
> Bayesian Data Analysis book).  In this model, it's hard to control
> the tendency of multi to drift off to infinity if the data is consistent
> with complete pooling (all the p2 are the same).
>
> So what I did to change the model in the case study is switch to
> a logit-scale rather than trying to fiddle with beta distributions.
>
> http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies.html
>
> I've been meaning to announce the case studies, but so far there
> are only three of mine.  I still need to get some more examples out
> there (I believe there's one in the mail queue).
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Mar 7, 2016, at 12:54 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Your post made me realize that my priors were misspecified as well.
> >
> > I wanted to shrink mixture assignments toward an overall distribution of probabilities (beta), but the prior to that beta was directly another beta, which is incorrect.
> >
> > That is, the hyper prior distribution was a beta(.5,.5) or something, and a realization of that distribution was entered as the beta prior parameter for the mixture assignment.
> > This is totally incorrect --- The prior distribution was getting <lower=0,upper=1>, when it should be getting a scaled version of that.  The mean of the prior beta was correct, but the width was totally wrong.
> >
> > Before:
> >
> > p2 ~ beta(P2,1-P2);
> > P2 ~ beta(.5,.5)
> >
> > This is totally incorrect.
> > Now it is:
> > p2 ~ beta(P2*multi,(1 - P2)*multi); (conceptually speaking)
> > P2 ~ beta(.5,.5);
> >
> > The multi (multiplier) changes the scale of the p2 distribution.  It didn't help with mixing, but it did improve inference a bit.
> >
> > On Sunday, March 6, 2016 at 11:45:06 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Suppose I have a normal(2, 1) distribution.  If I don't
> > truncate, the mean is 2.  If I truncate setting lower=1,
> > the mean is 2.3.
> >
> > > library(rstan)
> > > prog <- "parameters { real<lower=1> y; } model { y ~ normal(2, 1); }"
> > > fit <- stan(model_code=prog)
> > > print(fit)
> > ...
> >       mean ...
> > y     2.29 ...
> >
> >
> > So the original posterior mean is 2, but by truncating at lower=1,
> > it moves the posterior mean up to 2.3.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> > > On Mar 5, 2016, at 6:57 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > The reason I was using the <1 priors was to favor categorization (p2 = 0 or 1 being more probable than .4-.6), which is a trick I used in jags to guide the sampler a bit.
> > >
> > > Could you elaborate on your point that it'll make a difference if the posterior has parameters < 1?
> > >
> > > On Saturday, March 5, 2016 at 2:01:05 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > Yup.  Theoretically the ones less than 1 are very different, but
> > > in practice as long as you see both positive and negative instances,
> > > it's not going to make a huge difference.  It will make a difference
> > > though if the posterior has parameters < 1.
> > >
> > > And yes, a log normal can help keep things away from zero, but
> > > it can also cause computational issues if the data really wants
> > > to push things out into the tail.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Mar 4, 2016, at 8:07 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Currently, N=200, with N_1 = 100, N_2 = 100.
> > > >
> > > > I've tried a few beta priors, all fairly uninformative:

> > > > .5,.5

> > > >
> > > > Doesn't seem to make a difference.

> > > > On Friday, March 4, 2016 at 7:00:03 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > The beta priors aren't particularly strong, though.  What's

> > > >

> > > > > On Friday, March 4, 2016 at 5:27:05 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > Nope.  Here's from page 8 of the JAGS manual (v3.3.0):
> > > > >
> > > > >   If initial values are not supplied by the user, then
> > > > >   each parameter chooses its own initial value based on
> > > > >   the values of its parents. The initial value is chosen
> > > > >   to be a “typical value” from the prior distribution.
> > > > >   The exact meaning of “typical value” depends on the
> > > > >   distribution of the stochastic node, but is usually the
> > > > >   mean, median, or mode.
> > > > >
> > > > >   If you rely on automatic initial value generation and

> > > > >   values will be the same in all chains. You may not want
> > > > >   this behaviour, especially if you are using the Gelman

> > > > >

> > > > > indicates another situation where you're probably getting bias
> > > > > from missing part of the parameter space.
> > > > >
> > > > > This can happen if your data's consistent with parameters at
> > > > > constraint boundaries, like scales (std devs) of zero.
> > > > >
> > > > > And it's not the high-density modes that we want to explore,
> > > > > it's the typical set (high probability mass volume) of the posterior,

messages.subject: Copula on observed variable and latent variable
messages.subject_clean: Copula on observed variable and latent variable
messages.body_plain:
Consider observed data y1 and y2. y1 is measured on a continuous scale and y2 is measured on a binary scale. A latent variable z is assumed to generate y2 as: y2 = I(z > 0). Furthermore, a copula model dependency between y1 and z. This model could be written hierarchically (with some abuse of notation) as:

y2        =  I(z > 0)
(y1, z)  ~  C(F_y1( |w), F_z( |w) | phi)
w, phi   ~ priors

where w is the vector of marginal parameters for y1 and z, F_y1 and F_z are respective marginal cdfs for y1 and z, phi is the copula parameter.

How could this be modelled in Stan? I have written a custom probability function to sample y1 and z from the bivariate likelihood produced by the copula. What I don't know how to do is to account for (generate?) the latent variable(s) z, and how to specify the relationship between y2 and z.

Thank you,
Ved Deshpande

On Mon, Mar 7, 2016 at 2:58 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Monday, March 7, 2016 at 1:05:31 PM UTC-5, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > Is there a simple way to produce (presumably in the generated quantities section?) the partial correlation between pairs of variables that are otherwise modelled as having a multivariate normal distribution?
>
> There are many ways of defining a partial correlation. Some include
> The correlation between i and j given all other variables. This is given by inverting the covariance matrix, rescaling it to a correlation matrix, and negating the off-diagonal elements
> The correlation between i and j given all variables (if any) before i where i < j. These are given by the transformation from a correlation matrix to unconstrained parameters if you do a Fisher transform of the unconstrained parameters. You can do this in R with the unconstrained_pars function.
> The correlation between i and j given all variables (if any) between i and j where i < j. This is not available in Stan but there is code for it in the clusterGeneration R package.
> The correlation between i and j given all variables (if any) after j where i < j. These partial correlations do not have a name as far as I know of and no code either.
>
> Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Bayesian football model in rstan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Bayesian football model in rstan
messages.body_plain:
Because you center the parameters:

  att[nteams] <- -sum(att_free);
  def[nteams] <- -sum(def_free);

the intercept can't get absorbed into the parameters here:

  for (i in 1:ngames) {
    theta_home[i] <- exp(home + att[team_home[i]] + def[team_away[i]]);
    theta_away[i] <- exp(att[team_away[i]] + def[team_home[i]]);
  }

For theta_home, the parameter home will act as an intercept.  If you
really wanted an intercept, it'd look like this:

  log_theta_home[i] <- alpha + home + att[team_home[i]] + def[team_away[i]]);
  log_theta_away[i] <- alpha + att[team_away[i]] + def[team_home[i]]);

Then alpha is the intercept either way (it may need to be negative on one
side to make sense --- you'll have to check), and home is an additional offset
for away games.

That's basically like setting up def as centered and att as being centered
around alpha (or vice-versa).

- Bob

messages.subject: WAIC and LOO giving very different estimates of elpd
messages.subject_clean: WAIC and LOO giving very different estimates of elpd
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a problem where LOO and WAIC are giving very different estimates of the expected log pointwise predictive density (elpd). In particular, I get estimates of elpd from LOO-CV that have an absolute value of about an order of magnitude of smaller that that from WAIC; both in terms of point estimates, and the standard errors. I am used to a little difference in these estimates, but not an order of magnitude.

I do get a warning message from the loo package when I estimate LOO-CV on the log-likelihood matrix, that says the following:

Warning messages:
1: 332 (14.1%) Pareto k estimates between 0.5 and 1
2: 241 (10.3%) Pareto k estimates greater than 1

I have got these type of messages before, and usually I have ignored them because the latter percentage is small, (and usually the first is small as well.)

My question is, which of these metrics should I trust? I am guessing that I should use WAIC, because it involves less approximation, but I wanted to check.

Best,

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ved,

you could model y2 as binary logit or as step {0,1} probability. I'm not aware, how the discontinuity is handled by STAN.
It mostly leads, in optimization, to NP-hard optimization problems.
Thus for the first y2 could be:

y2 <- inv_logit(z)
z ~ normal(0,5);

If you model y2 as a step function your distribution becomes a PMF in which you need to take the differences in C.

Andre

I hope it is OK to post a job opening here. Stan users and Bayesian statisticians would be very welcome!

The University of Potsdam, Structural Unit Cognitive Sciences is seeking to fill the following position by June 1st, 2016:

Junior Research Group Leader “Applied Statistics in Cognitive Sciences” (m/f)
Requisition No.: 104/2016

The position is for 40 hours of work per week (100%). The salary is determined by the collective bargaining agreement for public employees in Germany (TV-L E 13). This is a temporary position limited to a term of 3 years in accordance with Section 2 Para 1 of the Academic Fixed-Term Contract Law (WissZeitVG).

The junior research group is part of the university's structural unit on cognitive sciences. In addition to the position of the group leader, funding includes a budget for two PhD students (20 hours per week), for travelling and other expenses.

The successful candidate will lead a new, independent research group on applied statistics in cognitive sciences. Areas of interest within cognitive sciences include experimental psycholinguistics, cognitive psychology, experimental linguistics, human movement and sport sciences, and other topics. The candidate must have a proven track record of high-quality international publications on applications of statistical methodology, ideally in several of the above mentioned application and research areas. The successful candidate should have teaching experience, and experience in writing research grant proposals and in obtaining third-party funding.

The candidate is expected to participate in related interdisciplinary research activities (e.g., experimental psycholinguistics, cognitive psychology, experimental linguistics, human movement and sport sciences) within the Faculty of Human Sciences at the University of Potsdam. These are, for example, (i) experimental design design and planning of appropriate data analyses for research in cognitive sciences, (ii) development of new methods for customized designs, (iii) application of newly developed statistical methods (e.g., linear mixed models and generalized additive mixed models), (iv) improving reproducible research via open access repositories for computer code and experimental data.

The group leader is expected to contribute to advanced-level teaching activities (one weekly 90 minute class per semester), in particular, to the new English-language MSc programs in Cognitive Science/Embodied Cognition and/or in Cognitive Systems.

Applications should include a CV, a publication list, a third-party funding record, a teaching record, a brief research statement outlining the candidate's research plans for the next three years, and the names and email addresses of at least three senior scientists willing to provide letters of reference.

At least one third of the working time is reserved for academic work. The University strives  to achieve a balanced gender ratio in all occupational groups. The University of Potsdam provides support for dual career couples and families. Handicapped applicants will be given preference in case of equal suitability. People with an immigrant background are specifically encouraged to apply.

The university is located in the historical city of Potsdam, and its Golm campus, where Cognitive Sciences is based, is reachable by a direct and fast (30 minutes) train connection from Berlin, a vibrant and international city that offers an unbeatable quality of life.

Applicants should send their application materials, by April 5th, 2016 at the latest, either by mail to the University of Potsdam, Structural Unit on Cognitive Sciences, Building 14, Karl-Liebknecht-Straße 24-25, 14476 Potsdam, Germany, or via email to csch...@uni-potsdam.de with the subject line: Requisition No.: 104/2016.”

In order to return your application documents, we request that you include a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Potsdam, 08.03.2016

messages.subject: Re: message: increase adapt_delta
messages.subject_clean: message: increase adapt_delta
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stéphane,
Responses below:

On Tuesday, 8 March 2016 18:30:30 UTC+11, Stéphane Laurent wrote:
> Hello,
> In this blog post <http://stla.github.io/stlapblog/posts/MixedRepeatModel.html> I show how to fit a certain model by several ways, including nlme::lme in R and JAGS.  I wanted to add the STAN way but I get some warnings and I would like to understand.
>
> Warning messages:
> 1: There were 6417 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta above 0.8 may help.
> 2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
>
>
> My code is given below. The model is explained in the blog post. It is true that I get less "divergent transitions" when I increase adapt_delta . What does it mean ?

n_divergent counts the number of iterations within a given sample that have diverged and any non-zero value suggests that the samples may be biased in which case the step size needs to be decreased. adapt_delta is the target acceptance probability. By default it is set at 0.8. Try increasing it to 0.99 or 0.999. You'll likely need to increase the max_treedepth as well (see below)

> Even when I increase it to 0.98 I still get "divergent transitions". I did several attempts and I also got a warning suggesting to increase max_treedepth.

max_treedepth specifies the maximum number of leapfrogs NUTS will take before to hit a U-turn. If it hits this limit then NUTS prematurely terminates and becomes a random walk. Making your sampling less efficient... and potentially (bias??) any posterior estimates.
By default rstan has this set at 10. You could increase this by adding `control=list(adapt_delta=0.99, stepsize = 0.01, max_treedepth =15). Often if you are increasing adapt_delta you'll likely need to also increase max_treedepth. You may also want to lower the initial step size as this might help with warmup. How many divergent iterations do you get at 0.98?

> And I don't know what does that mean to "Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems".

I think this warning is pretty self evident. Use rsptan's pairs() function. e.g. pairs(model). Basically it allows a user to visualise potential problems with posteriors (e.g. bimodal, hitting up against some constraint etc). It also tells you where the divergent iterations are occurring.
Straight from the help (?pairs.stanfit):
By default, the lower (upper) triangle of the plot contains draws with below (above) median acceptance probability. Also, if condition is not"n_divergent__", red points will be superimposed onto the smoothed density plots indicating which (if any) iterations encountered a divergent transition. Otherwise, yellow points indicate a transition that hit the maximum treedepth rather than terminated its evolution normally.
Here is one of my questions with an example of a pairs plot.
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Convergence$20issues/stan-users/gcXWm1-yM8A/tsySS7IBMs4J

> The estimates of the between variances sigma_b[1,2] and look unstable: they are sensible to the choice of the prior. The estimates of the other parameters look quite good (similar to those obtained with lme or JAGS, and close to the true values used for simulating the data).
> The data are simulated. I get less "divergent transitions" when I use a larger number of groups (the "sample size" is rather small on my example : only three groups to estimate the between components).
> Should I use more informative priors on the between variances ? Is it usual to get such warnings with small sample sizes ?
> I would welcome any comments.

Is there a reason you are using gamma priors on the sigma? I think Andrew tends to recommend people avoid these and instead you should consider using other priors such as the half cauchy. http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf

I haven't really used multi_normal_cholesky's so I can't be sure whether you could use a non-centered parameterisation here. Maybe one of the others might help here.

Not sure this will help much but stan normally does a pretty good job with initialising parameters without you specifying the initials. You might want to see how well stan goes without setting them.

Lastly, it's rare for a stan model to take 20,000 iterations to converge. That might be over kill. Try something like 4000.

>
>
> library(rstan)
> rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
> options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
>
>
> # simulated data ----------------------------------------------------------
> I <-  3 # number of groups
> J <-  4 # number of replicates per group
> set.seed(444)
> ### simulation of overall means ###
> Mu.t1 <- 20 # overall mean at timepoint 1
> Mu.t2 <- 5  # overall mean at timepoint 2
> Mu <- c(Mu.t1, Mu.t2)
> names(Mu) <- c("t1", "t2")
> sigmab.t1 <- 8 # between standard deviation at timepoint 1
> sigmab.t2 <- 1 # between standard deviation at timepoint 1
> rho <- 0.2 # correlation between the two timepoints
> Sigma <- rbind(
>   c(sigmab.t1^2, rho*sigmab.t1*sigmab.t2),
>   c(rho*sigmab.t1*sigmab.t2, sigmab.t2^2)
> )
> mu <- mvtnorm::rmvnorm(I, Mu, Sigma) # group means
> ### simulation within-groups ###
> sigmaw.t1 <- 2
> sigmaw.t2 <- 0.5
> y.t1 <- c(sapply(mu[,"t1"], function(m) rnorm(J, m, sigmaw.t1)))
> y.t2 <- c(sapply(mu[,"t2"], function(m) rnorm(J, m, sigmaw.t2)))
> ### constructs the dataset ####
> Timepoint <- rep(c("t1", "t2"), each=I*J)
> Group <- paste0("grp", rep(gl(I,J), times=2))
> Repeat <- rep(1:J, times=2*I)
> dat <- data.frame(
>   Timepoint=Timepoint,
>   Group=Group,
>   Repeat=Repeat,
>   y=c(y.t1,y.t2)
> )
>
>
> # STAN --------------------------------------------------------------------
> dat <- transform(dat, timepoint=as.integer(Timepoint), group=as.integer(Group))
>
>
> stancode <- 'data {
>   int<lower=1> N; // number of observations
>   real y[N]; // observations
>   int<lower=1> ngroups; // number of groups
>   int<lower=1> group[N]; // group indices
>   int<lower=1> timepoint[N]; // timepoint indices
> }
> parameters {
>   vector[2] Mu;
>   vector[2] mu[ngroups]; // group means
>   cholesky_factor_corr[2] L;
>   vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_b;
>   vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_w;
> }
> model {
>   sigma_w ~ gamma(1, 0.001);
>   for(k in 1:N){
>     y[k] ~ normal(mu[group[k], timepoint[k]], sigma_w[timepoint[k]]);
>   }
>   sigma_b ~ gamma(1, 0.01);
>   L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1);
>   Mu ~ normal(0, 25);
>   for(j in 1:ngroups){
>     mu[j] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, diag_pre_multiply(sigma_b, L));
>   }
> }
> generated quantities {
>   matrix[2,2] Omega;
>   matrix[2,2] Sigma;
>   real rho_b;
>   Omega <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L);
>   Sigma <- quad_form_diag(Omega, sigma_b);
>   rho_b <- Sigma[1,2]/(sigma_b[1]*sigma_b[2]);
> }'
>
>
> ### compile Stan model
> stanmodel <- stan_model(model_code = stancode, model_name="stanmodel")
>
>
> ### Stan data
> standata <- list(y=dat$y, N=nrow(dat), ngroups=nlevels(dat$Group),
>                  timepoint=dat$timepoint, group=dat$group)
>
>
> ### Stan initial values
> estimates <- function(dat, perturb=FALSE){
>   if(perturb) dat$y <- dat$y + rnorm(length(dat$y), 0, 1)
>   mu <-  matrix(aggregate(y~timepoint:group, data=dat, FUN=mean)$y, ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
>   Mu <- colMeans(mu)
>   sigma_b <- sqrt(diag(var(mu)))
>   L <- t(chol(cor(mu)))
>   sigmaw1 <- mean(aggregate(y~Group, data=subset(dat, Timepoint=="t1"), FUN=sd)$y)
>   sigmaw2 <- mean(aggregate(y~Group, data=subset(dat, Timepoint=="t2"), FUN=sd)$y)
>   return(list(mu=mu, Mu=Mu, L=L, sigma_b=sigma_b, sigma_w = c(sigmaw1, sigmaw2)))
> }
> inits <- function(chain_id){
>   values <- estimates(dat, perturb = chain_id > 1)
>   return(values)
> }
>
>
> ### run Stan
> samples <- sampling(stanmodel, data = standata, init=inits,
>                     iter = 20000, warmup = 10000, chains = 4,
>                     control=list(adapt_delta=0.8))
>
>
> ### outputs
> library(coda)
> codasamples <- do.call(mcmc.list,
>                        plyr::alply(rstan::extract(samples, permuted=FALSE,
>                                         pars = c("Mu", "sigma_b", "sigma_w", "rho_b")), 2, mcmc))
> summary(codasamples)
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
The difference in speed between a good cpu and a really good cpu is going to be much much less than the difference between a sloppily written model and a carefully parameterized model. So with that amount of money a box with a multi socket motherboard, decent multi core cpu's and over 64 128gb RAM lets you run a dozen chains of different algorithms and still analyze the last round of results.

A lot of modeling problems require completely independent parallel computation (multiple chains, multiple algorithms, multiple data sets), so multiple cores with enough RAM is where you really can make your workflow easier. Also if you're going to spend that amount of money on a desktop find somebody to buy from who can source reliable components, rather than just the best spec as silly stuff like bad RAM can waste much more time than a marginally faster machine will ever save you.

of 1600 MHz DDR3 memory.  Michael and Andrew have slightly newer
ones, as does Rayleigh.

We have the newer mini trash-can server in the office for unit
and integration tests and longer-running jobs.  And then we (and by
that I mean people with more patience for config than me) just
run on the linux cluster at Columbia.

- Bob

On Thursday, March 10, 2016 at 10:21:08 AM UTC-5, Liang Chen wrote:
>
> That makes sense thank you. So should I define the co-variance matrix v in the transformed parameters, as I am giving a Jeffery prior for v in the model, "increment_log_prob(-2*log(determinant(v)));”

Well,

det(v) = det(chol_v * chol_v') = det(chol_v) * det(chol_v') = det(chol_v)^2

so

increment_log_prob(-2 * log(determinant(v)));

becomes

increment_log_prob(-4 * sum(log(diag_vector(chol_v))));

But in case Andy is reading this, I'm not saying Jeffreys' prior makes the most sense here. I'm just saying you don't need v to evaluate it.

Ben

On Thursday, March 10, 2016 at 12:33:17 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> Stan produces a number of warnings for human consumption; some of these are in the progress output (e.g., numerical problems), and for RStan, some of these are given by warnings() (e.g., divergent transitions). Is there any way in RStan to access these as objects that R code can examine? Are they stored in the stanfit object anywhere?

They aren't stored in the stanfit object. There is a random file in tempdir() that numerical problems are written to, but they are not broken down by chain. The warnings() are generated based on things that are stored, namely the matrices produced by get_sampler_params().

Ben

Krzysztof is absolutely right that fast and reliable memory is

than CPU.  And that includes cache on the CPU.

So with that amount of money a box with a multi socket motherboard, decent multi core cpu's and over 64 128gb RAM lets you run a dozen chains of different algorithms and still analyze the last round of results.
>
> A lot of modeling problems require completely independent parallel computation (multiple chains, multiple algorithms, multiple data sets), so multiple cores with enough RAM is where you really can make your workflow easier. messages.subject: model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
messages.subject_clean: model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

in my understanding, WAIC and (PSIS) LOO are metrics for model selection.

However, it happens that PSIS-LOO can also be used as a model diagnostics since if the measured LOO tail exponents are large it means that there are possibly influential observations and that the model is not robust (so it might be overfitting those); see also my previous post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/EOF6fhd9EWM/AkmbXePaAwAJ> (and answers) on this mailing list.
So PSIS-LOO could be an informative tool in itself even if we are not comparing models.

Is this usage of PSIS-LOO appropriate, or is it somewhat dodgy? e.g., could I mention it in a paper as suggestive evidence for issues in a model?
(and are there references for specifically this usage -- perhaps this <http://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.04544v3.pdf>?)

Secondly -- this is more speculative.
I understand that there are theoretical advantages in performing continuous inference in a "large" model as opposed to discrete model selection.
(In the "large" model, specific hypotheses are identified by sub-regions in parameter space.)
However, how do I prevent overfitting / increase generalizability -- that is, how do I check my priors -- if I have a single "large model" and I don't want to go back to discrete model selection?

Best,
Luigi

messages.subject: ODE solver: initial or solution times that depend on parameters
messages.subject_clean: ODE solver: initial or solution times that depend on parameters
messages.body_plain:
I'm hitting a road block to implementing PK models that include lag times or infusions that end at times that are model parameters. The lag times and times at which input rates change result in discontinuities in the ODEs. This results in a situation where I want to stop and restart the ODE solver at those times to get the solver to correctly deal with the discontinuity. Because those times depend on parameters I cannot use the current solvers because they require that the initial and solution times be data.

I am usually not interested in the solution at the parameter-dependent lag or rate change times. As a result there is no reason to calculate gradients w.r.t. those times. They are just nuisance "parameters" needed to make the ODE solver more correctly calculate the solutions at times relevant to observations.

Is there any way to coerce those parameter-dependent time values to be treated as data other than hacking the C++ code to force coercion from var to double?

More generally we may want to reconsider the current limitation on the initial or solution times in the ODE solvers.

Thanks,
Bill

In addition to the reasons Krzysztof mentions, the uniform priors are almost

mass near the boundaries.

For efficiency, it's best to compute the entire vector of mu values
(as a local) then call normal once with vectorization.  It cuts down on
the number of interpreted autodiff calls internally.

Also, you don't have much data, which means the priors are even more
important.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficiently draw Monte Carlo Samples from Posterior Predictive [ADVI]
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Efficiently draw Monte Carlo Samples from Posterior Predictive [ADVI]
messages.body_plain:
You'll need someone who knows the ADVI code and linear algebra
better than me to help at a deeper level.

In NUTS/HMC, the generated quantities are run once per iteration,
not at the end.  So I don't know how you get the ADVI estimate in
2 hours then hang after that.  But then I don't know how ADVI is
working w.r.t. generated quantities.

Might you be running into problems with memory swapping or
file I/O with the size?  And do you really need 1000 draws?

- Bob

> On Mar 10, 2016, at 8:06 PM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Stanners,  I'm using vb() in rstan to estimate a GP model similar to that described in the manual for NT = 2500 observations with P = 2 predictors under varying length scales in a squared exponential covariance formula.   The stan script, below, builds an MCMC model for the parameters of the covariance formula.  My interest is to extract the latent (de-noised) function, which i sample from the posterior predictive distribution in the generated quantities block.  The advi estimate is returned in about 2 hours, but it has not yet completed generating 1000 samples after a day.   The long time period is not due to returning samples of the parameters (since I have separately run that and validated such) but due to the monte carlo draws from the posterior predictive for the latent function.  Since the generated quantities block draws monte carlo samples, only, i'm assuming there are no gradients to compute.   I'd appreciate any tips on how I might re-configure the script in the generated quantities block to speed up the generated monte carlo samples.
>
> /*
>   y[c] ~ N_{T}(u[c], sigma_y[c]),  where c = 1,..,NT are domain-time case. sigma_y[c] are known
>   // squared exponential covariance function for NT x NT covariance matrix, Sigma
>   Sigma[i,j] = 1/eta * sum_{c=1}^{NT}sum_{c'=1}^{NT}
>                             sum_{p=1}^{P} exp(-1/rho[p](x[c,p] - x[c',p])^{2})
>   u[1] ,..., u[NT] ~ * N_{NT}(0, Sigma),
>   eta     ~ Gamma(1,1) - precision parameter of squared exponential covariance function
>   rho[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1) - predictor indexed length-scale parameters
>
>   We may marginalize over the u to achieve
>   y[c] ~ N_{T}(0, Sigma + diag(sigma2_y))
>
>   Marginalizing over u adds the known response variances, sigma2_y, to the diagonals
>   which stabilizes the cholesky computation for Sigma (which is very high-dimensional).
>   We use the properties of the Gaussian wrapper in which the nonparametric GP is parameterized
>   to draw u as a post-processing step using sampled values of c(rho,eta)
>
> */
>
> data{
>   int<lower=1> NT; // number of domain-months
>   int<lower=1> P; // number of predictors
>   vector[NT] y; // vectorized response variable, with T faster than N
>   matrix[NT,P] x; // Set of NT, 1 x P predictors
>   vector<lower=0>[NT] sigma2_y; // known domain variances
>   real<lower=0> jitter; // stabilizing constant to add to diagonals of GP cov, Sigma */
> } /* end data block */
>
>
> transformed data{
>   vector[NT] zros_NT;
>   zros_NT <- rep_vector(0,NT); /* vector of zeros for sampling Tx1 fixed effects, beta */
> } /* end transformed data block */
>
> parameters{
>   // parameters for squared exponential covariance function
>   real<lower=0> eta; /* rational quadratic precision parameter */
>   real<lower=0> rho[P]; /* length-scale parameters, indexed by predictor, x[,p] */
> } /* end parameters block */
>
> transformed parameters{
>   matrix[NT,NT] Sigma; /* GP covariance matrix for NT x 1, u */
>   matrix[NT,NT] K; /* GP covariance matrix for u */
>   matrix[NT,NT] L; /* cholesky_decompose(Sigma) */
>
>   { /* local block */
>     real covformula_ijp;
>     real s_ij;
>      // off-diagonal
>     for( i in 1:(NT-1) )
>     {
>       for( j in (i+1):NT )
>       {
>         s_ij <- 0;
>         for( p in 1:P )
>         {
>           covformula_ijp      <- inv(rho[p])* pow(x[i,p] - x[j,p],2);
>           s_ij                <- s_ij + covformula_ijp ;
>         }/* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
>         s_ij       <-  exp( -s_ij ) ;
>         s_ij       <-  inv(eta) * s_ij;
>         K[i,j]     <- s_ij;
>         K[j,i]     <- s_ij;
>       } /* end loop j over columns to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
>     } /* end loop i over rows to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
>
>     // diagonal
>     for( k in 1:NT )
>     {
>       for( p in 1:P )
>       {
>         K[k,k]     <- inv(eta) + jitter;
>       } /* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
>     } /* end loop k over diagonal entries of Sigma */
>   } /* end local block for building Sigma */
>
>   /* add model noise on the diagonal to achieve the marginal distribution */
>   /* of y */
>   Sigma     <- K + diag_matrix( sigma2_y );
>   L         <- cholesky_decompose( Sigma );
>
> } /* end transformed parameters block */
>
>
> model{
>
>   // priors for mean and covariance cluster location
>   eta       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
>   rho       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
>
>
>   // observed response likelihood
>   y         ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zros_NT,L);
>
>
>
> } /* end model{} block */
>
> generated quantities{
>   matrix[NT,NT] K_transpose_div_Sigma; /* K'Sigma^-1 */
>   matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
>   matrix[NT,NT] L_u;
>   vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
>   vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
>   /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
>   real<lower=0> TSE;
>   real<lower=0> MSE;
>   /* posterior predictive quantities */
>   K_transpose_div_Sigma  <- K' / Sigma;
>   mu_u                   <- K_transpose_div_Sigma * y;
>   Tau                    <- K - K_transpose_div_Sigma * K;
>   L_u                    <- cholesky_decompose( Tau );
>   u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
>   TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
>   MSE <- TSE/(NT);
>
>
> } /* end generated quantities block */
>
>
> I also used a variation on the above script for generated quantities that leverages the cholesky decomposition of Sigma that is already computed, but there was no speed improvement.
>
> generated quantities{
>   matrix[NT,NT] div_L_K; /* L^-1 * K */
>   matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
>   matrix[NT,NT] L_u; /* cholesky of Tau */
>   vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
>   vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
>   /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
>   real<lower=0> TSE;
>   real<lower=0> MSE;
>   /* posterior predictive quantities */
>   div_L_K                <- mdivide_left_tri_low(L,K);
>   mu_u                   <- div_L_K' * mdivide_left_tri_low(L,y);
>   Tau                    <- K - div_L_K' * div_L_K;
>   // for( i in 1:(NT-1))
>   // {
>   //   for( j in (i+1):NT)
>   //   {
>   //     Tau[i,j]  <- Tau[j,i];
>   //   }
>   // }
>   L_u <- cholesky_decompose(Tau);
>   u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
>   TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
>   MSE <- TSE/(NT);
>
>
> } /* end generated quantities block */
>
>
> Thanks very much your help and comments.
>
> Terrance
>
> --
> Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
messages.body_plain:
All predictive measure are, and mathematically have to be, relative measures
of fit.  They provide no absolute measure of fit (because to do that you would
need to know the true model). The use of these methods in isolation, particularly
in posterior predictive checks, is always in reference to some default model (i.e.,
“this fit is so bad another model _has_ to be better”) but such comparisons can’t
be quantified in any meaningful way.  So it’s easy to use these measures to
identity suspicious behavior and use that to motivate model improvements, but
they do not quantify any guarantee of your model being correct.

On Mar 11, 2016, at 5:46 PM, Luigi Acerbi <luigi....@gmail.com> wrote:

> OK, but suppose that I have a single "large" model and PSIS-LOO does not detect any major issue.
> This means that all the LOO posteriors are "close enough" to the full posterior, which seems to be a good sign (i.e., at least the model is not overfitting to single observations).
> To me, this seems informative in itself (of course then I can go and do predictive checks, but that's another point).
>
> The question is, what do I report to provide partial evidence of (lack of) overfitting?
> For a standard model selection, I would have some simpler and more complex models to compare against, and that's how the LOO-CV would play out.
> But if you have a single model, it seems to me that PSIS-LOO would still allow you to say something.
> First of all, is that acknowledged (any reference?); and second, what would be a good metric? (e.g., the maximum of the Pareto-fitted exponents, the largest IS weight, or something else based on the PSIS-LOO analysis)
>
>
> On Friday, 11 March 2016 09:22:15 UTC-5, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > Sure you could use it to identify issues but it's better not to stop there.  Try to plot the problematic observation to illustrate which model feature causes the issue.  You can get surprisingly specific answers that way about which aspect of a model to improve.
>

messages.body_plain:
I think you want to treat this as a general linear model, in other words

theta_{i} ~ normal(mu, tau); // hierarchical model
sigma_{i} <- exp( theta_{i}); // map to constrained scale assuming log link function

I’ve built similarly models that do this for the negative binomial dispersion
parameter and it has worked reasonably well.

messages.body_plain:
Yes it’s true that diagnostics such as PPC’s are technically comparing against a true model. But I think the argument still holds—that PPC’s (or “model diagnostics” in general) are useful in light of not having another candidate model in mind. This is how Rubin (1981, 1984) phrases this.

Following this, I think Luigi’s question is also valid. That is, can PSIS-LOO be used as a model diagnostic in which we are assessing the goodness-of-fit without another candidate model in mind.

Dustin
