messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob, I appreciate your response.   The linear algebra is pretty efficient; in fact, I was going to suggest it for the manual since the efficient (NUTS) sampling procedure is to sample using the cholesky.   So i just use that and the nice functions mdivide_left_tri_low().  But i digress.  I think maybe ADVI also generates quantities once per iteration.   The cholesky of the high-dimensional covariance matrix is already computed for sampling, so it would seem to be relatively quick to generate a monte carlo draw.    If this is the case, I don't know why the model converges after 2 hours and then hangs indefinitely for generating samples.   To your point about hitting memory limits, I've reduced the number of samples to 200, but still the same problem.  I'll try 100, next.   Lastly, one subtle point that i would really appreciate to have clarified is whether - under ADVI and also NUTS - there is any benefit or cost taking the cholesky of a covariance matrix used to generate a quantity from some distribution.  Unlike under sampling, I would think it doesn't matter for generated quantities.

Thank you,

Terrance.

On Fri, Mar 11, 2016 at 5:14 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> You'll need someone who knows the ADVI code and linear algebra
> better than me to help at a deeper level.
>
> In NUTS/HMC, the generated quantities are run once per iteration,
> not at the end.  So I don't know how you get the ADVI estimate in
> 2 hours then hang after that.  But then I don't know how ADVI is
> working w.r.t. generated quantities.
>
> Might you be running into problems with memory swapping or
> file I/O with the size?  And do you really need 1000 draws?
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Mar 10, 2016, at 8:06 PM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Stanners,  I'm using vb() in rstan to estimate a GP model similar to that described in the manual for NT = 2500 observations with P = 2 predictors under varying length scales in a squared exponential covariance formula.   The stan script, below, builds an MCMC model for the parameters of the covariance formula.  My interest is to extract the latent (de-noised) function, which i sample from the posterior predictive distribution in the generated quantities block.  The advi estimate is returned in about 2 hours, but it has not yet completed generating 1000 samples after a day.   The long time period is not due to returning samples of the parameters (since I have separately run that and validated such) but due to the monte carlo draws from the posterior predictive for the latent function.  Since the generated quantities block draws monte carlo samples, only, i'm assuming there are no gradients to compute.   I'd appreciate any tips on how I might re-configure the script in the generated quantities block to speed up the generated monte carlo samples.
> >
> > /*
> >   y[c] ~ N_{T}(u[c], sigma_y[c]),  where c = 1,..,NT are domain-time case. sigma_y[c] are known
> >   // squared exponential covariance function for NT x NT covariance matrix, Sigma
> >   Sigma[i,j] = 1/eta * sum_{c=1}^{NT}sum_{c'=1}^{NT}
> >                             sum_{p=1}^{P} exp(-1/rho[p](x[c,p] - x[c',p])^{2})
> >   u[1] ,..., u[NT] ~ * N_{NT}(0, Sigma),
> >   eta     ~ Gamma(1,1) - precision parameter of squared exponential covariance function
> >   rho[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1) - predictor indexed length-scale parameters
> >
> >   We may marginalize over the u to achieve
> >   y[c] ~ N_{T}(0, Sigma + diag(sigma2_y))
> >
> >   Marginalizing over u adds the known response variances, sigma2_y, to the diagonals
> >   which stabilizes the cholesky computation for Sigma (which is very high-dimensional).
> >   We use the properties of the Gaussian wrapper in which the nonparametric GP is parameterized
> >   to draw u as a post-processing step using sampled values of c(rho,eta)
> >
> > */
> >
> > data{
> >   int<lower=1> NT; // number of domain-months
> >   int<lower=1> P; // number of predictors
> >   vector[NT] y; // vectorized response variable, with T faster than N
> >   matrix[NT,P] x; // Set of NT, 1 x P predictors
> >   vector<lower=0>[NT] sigma2_y; // known domain variances
> >   real<lower=0> jitter; // stabilizing constant to add to diagonals of GP cov, Sigma */
> > } /* end data block */
> >
> >
> > transformed data{
> >   vector[NT] zros_NT;
> >   zros_NT <- rep_vector(0,NT); /* vector of zeros for sampling Tx1 fixed effects, beta */
> > } /* end transformed data block */
> >
> > parameters{
> >   // parameters for squared exponential covariance function
> >   real<lower=0> eta; /* rational quadratic precision parameter */
> >   real<lower=0> rho[P]; /* length-scale parameters, indexed by predictor, x[,p] */
> > } /* end parameters block */
> >
> > transformed parameters{
> >   matrix[NT,NT] Sigma; /* GP covariance matrix for NT x 1, u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] K; /* GP covariance matrix for u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] L; /* cholesky_decompose(Sigma) */
> >
> >   { /* local block */
> >     real covformula_ijp;
> >     real s_ij;
> >      // off-diagonal
> >     for( i in 1:(NT-1) )
> >     {
> >       for( j in (i+1):NT )
> >       {
> >         s_ij <- 0;
> >         for( p in 1:P )
> >         {
> >           covformula_ijp      <- inv(rho[p])* pow(x[i,p] - x[j,p],2);
> >           s_ij                <- s_ij + covformula_ijp ;
> >         }/* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
> >         s_ij       <-  exp( -s_ij ) ;
> >         s_ij       <-  inv(eta) * s_ij;
> >         K[i,j]     <- s_ij;
> >         K[j,i]     <- s_ij;
> >       } /* end loop j over columns to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
> >     } /* end loop i over rows to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
> >
> >     // diagonal
> >     for( k in 1:NT )
> >     {
> >       for( p in 1:P )
> >       {
> >         K[k,k]     <- inv(eta) + jitter;
> >       } /* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
> >     } /* end loop k over diagonal entries of Sigma */
> >   } /* end local block for building Sigma */
> >
> >   /* add model noise on the diagonal to achieve the marginal distribution */
> >   /* of y */
> >   Sigma     <- K + diag_matrix( sigma2_y );
> >   L         <- cholesky_decompose( Sigma );
> >
> > } /* end transformed parameters block */
> >
> >
> > model{
> >
> >   // priors for mean and covariance cluster location
> >   eta       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
> >   rho       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
> >
> >
> >   // observed response likelihood
> >   y         ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zros_NT,L);
> >
> >
> >
> > } /* end model{} block */
> >
> > generated quantities{
> >   matrix[NT,NT] K_transpose_div_Sigma; /* K'Sigma^-1 */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] L_u;
> >   vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
> >   vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
> >   /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
> >   real<lower=0> TSE;
> >   real<lower=0> MSE;
> >   /* posterior predictive quantities */
> >   K_transpose_div_Sigma  <- K' / Sigma;
> >   mu_u                   <- K_transpose_div_Sigma * y;
> >   Tau                    <- K - K_transpose_div_Sigma * K;
> >   L_u                    <- cholesky_decompose( Tau );
> >   u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
> >   TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
> >   MSE <- TSE/(NT);
> >
> >
> > } /* end generated quantities block */
> >
> >
> > I also used a variation on the above script for generated quantities that leverages the cholesky decomposition of Sigma that is already computed, but there was no speed improvement.
> >
> > generated quantities{
> >   matrix[NT,NT] div_L_K; /* L^-1 * K */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] L_u; /* cholesky of Tau */
> >   vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
> >   vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
> >   /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
> >   real<lower=0> TSE;
> >   real<lower=0> MSE;
> >   /* posterior predictive quantities */
> >   div_L_K                <- mdivide_left_tri_low(L,K);
> >   mu_u                   <- div_L_K' * mdivide_left_tri_low(L,y);
> >   Tau                    <- K - div_L_K' * div_L_K;
> >   // for( i in 1:(NT-1))
> >   // {
> >   //   for( j in (i+1):NT)
> >   //   {
> >   //     Tau[i,j]  <- Tau[j,i];
> >   //   }
> >   // }
> >   L_u <- cholesky_decompose(Tau);
> >   u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
> >   TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
> >   MSE <- TSE/(NT);
> >
> >
> > } /* end generated quantities block */
> >
> >
> > Thanks very much your help and comments.
> >
> > Terrance
> >
> > --
> > Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.body_plain:
Hello. The case study I have in the works is actually for the partial credit model, not the graded response model.

The Stan model that Hans Hansen suggested above looks about right to me, except that there may be problems if the items have differing numbers of response categories. If there are differing numbers of response categories, the items with fewer response categories will have extra kappa parameters that are unused. I have found that having unused paramters lead to convergence problems. I think there is a solution to this problem, but programming it would take some time and creativity.

On the other hand, if the items have the same number of response categories, Hans' model should work.

messages.body_plain:
If you can do a Cholesky factorization once, it's much
better than doing it N times.  But if you only do it once,
then no worries.

But I just realized the reason ADVI may be hanging after
getting the posterior mean is that I think it then does
multivariate normal draws around the variational approximation
and converts back to the constrained space.  That's probably
where the time's going, not into generated quantities.

You could always try running iterations in Stan with
fixed parameters just to run generated quantities (then you
have to feed it the parameter values as inits or just
use the random inits).

- Bob

> On Mar 11, 2016, at 6:25 PM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob, I appreciate your response.   The linear algebra is pretty efficient; in fact, I was going to suggest it for the manual since the efficient (NUTS) sampling procedure is to sample using the cholesky.   So i just use that and the nice functions mdivide_left_tri_low().  But i digress.  I think maybe ADVI also generates quantities once per iteration.   The cholesky of the high-dimensional covariance matrix is already computed for sampling, so it would seem to be relatively quick to generate a monte carlo draw.    If this is the case, I don't know why the model converges after 2 hours and then hangs indefinitely for generating samples.   To your point about hitting memory limits, I've reduced the number of samples to 200, but still the same problem.  I'll try 100, next.   Lastly, one subtle point that i would really appreciate to have clarified is whether - under ADVI and also NUTS - there is any benefit or cost taking the cholesky of a covariance matrix used to generate a quantity from some distribution.  Unlike under sampling, I would think it doesn't matter for generated quantities.
>
> Thank you,
>
> Terrance.
>
> On Fri, Mar 11, 2016 at 5:14 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> You'll need someone who knows the ADVI code and linear algebra
> better than me to help at a deeper level.
>
> In NUTS/HMC, the generated quantities are run once per iteration,
> not at the end.  So I don't know how you get the ADVI estimate in
> 2 hours then hang after that.  But then I don't know how ADVI is
> working w.r.t. generated quantities.
>
> Might you be running into problems with memory swapping or
> file I/O with the size?  And do you really need 1000 draws?
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Mar 10, 2016, at 8:06 PM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Stanners,  I'm using vb() in rstan to estimate a GP model similar to that described in the manual for NT = 2500 observations with P = 2 predictors under varying length scales in a squared exponential covariance formula.   The stan script, below, builds an MCMC model for the parameters of the covariance formula.  My interest is to extract the latent (de-noised) function, which i sample from the posterior predictive distribution in the generated quantities block.  The advi estimate is returned in about 2 hours, but it has not yet completed generating 1000 samples after a day.   The long time period is not due to returning samples of the parameters (since I have separately run that and validated such) but due to the monte carlo draws from the posterior predictive for the latent function.  Since the generated quantities block draws monte carlo samples, only, i'm assuming there are no gradients to compute.   I'd appreciate any tips on how I might re-configure the script in the generated quantities block to speed up the generated monte carlo samples.
> >
> > /*
> >   y[c] ~ N_{T}(u[c], sigma_y[c]),  where c = 1,..,NT are domain-time case. sigma_y[c] are known
> >   // squared exponential covariance function for NT x NT covariance matrix, Sigma
> >   Sigma[i,j] = 1/eta * sum_{c=1}^{NT}sum_{c'=1}^{NT}
> >                             sum_{p=1}^{P} exp(-1/rho[p](x[c,p] - x[c',p])^{2})
> >   u[1] ,..., u[NT] ~ * N_{NT}(0, Sigma),
> >   eta     ~ Gamma(1,1) - precision parameter of squared exponential covariance function
> >   rho[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1) - predictor indexed length-scale parameters
> >
> >   We may marginalize over the u to achieve
> >   y[c] ~ N_{T}(0, Sigma + diag(sigma2_y))
> >
> >   Marginalizing over u adds the known response variances, sigma2_y, to the diagonals
> >   which stabilizes the cholesky computation for Sigma (which is very high-dimensional).
> >   We use the properties of the Gaussian wrapper in which the nonparametric GP is parameterized
> >   to draw u as a post-processing step using sampled values of c(rho,eta)
> >
> > */
> >
> > data{
> >   int<lower=1> NT; // number of domain-months
> >   int<lower=1> P; // number of predictors
> >   vector[NT] y; // vectorized response variable, with T faster than N
> >   matrix[NT,P] x; // Set of NT, 1 x P predictors
> >   vector<lower=0>[NT] sigma2_y; // known domain variances
> >   real<lower=0> jitter; // stabilizing constant to add to diagonals of GP cov, Sigma */
> > } /* end data block */
> >
> >
> > transformed data{
> >   vector[NT] zros_NT;
> >   zros_NT <- rep_vector(0,NT); /* vector of zeros for sampling Tx1 fixed effects, beta */
> > } /* end transformed data block */
> >
> > parameters{
> >   // parameters for squared exponential covariance function
> >   real<lower=0> eta; /* rational quadratic precision parameter */
> >   real<lower=0> rho[P]; /* length-scale parameters, indexed by predictor, x[,p] */
> > } /* end parameters block */
> >
> > transformed parameters{
> >   matrix[NT,NT] Sigma; /* GP covariance matrix for NT x 1, u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] K; /* GP covariance matrix for u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] L; /* cholesky_decompose(Sigma) */
> >
> >   { /* local block */
> >     real covformula_ijp;
> >     real s_ij;
> >      // off-diagonal
> >     for( i in 1:(NT-1) )
> >     {
> >       for( j in (i+1):NT )
> >       {
> >         s_ij <- 0;
> >         for( p in 1:P )
> >         {
> >           covformula_ijp      <- inv(rho[p])* pow(x[i,p] - x[j,p],2);
> >           s_ij                <- s_ij + covformula_ijp ;
> >         }/* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
> >         s_ij       <-  exp( -s_ij ) ;
> >         s_ij       <-  inv(eta) * s_ij;
> >         K[i,j]     <- s_ij;
> >         K[j,i]     <- s_ij;
> >       } /* end loop j over columns to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
> >     } /* end loop i over rows to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
> >
> >     // diagonal
> >     for( k in 1:NT )
> >     {
> >       for( p in 1:P )
> >       {
> >         K[k,k]     <- inv(eta) + jitter;
> >       } /* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
> >     } /* end loop k over diagonal entries of Sigma */
> >   } /* end local block for building Sigma */
> >
> >   /* add model noise on the diagonal to achieve the marginal distribution */
> >   /* of y */
> >   Sigma     <- K + diag_matrix( sigma2_y );
> >   L         <- cholesky_decompose( Sigma );
> >
> > } /* end transformed parameters block */
> >
> >
> > model{
> >
> >   // priors for mean and covariance cluster location
> >   eta       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
> >   rho       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
> >
> >
> >   // observed response likelihood
> >   y         ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zros_NT,L);
> >
> >
> >
> > } /* end model{} block */
> >
> > generated quantities{
> >   matrix[NT,NT] K_transpose_div_Sigma; /* K'Sigma^-1 */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] L_u;
> >   vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
> >   vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
> >   /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
> >   real<lower=0> TSE;
> >   real<lower=0> MSE;
> >   /* posterior predictive quantities */
> >   K_transpose_div_Sigma  <- K' / Sigma;
> >   mu_u                   <- K_transpose_div_Sigma * y;
> >   Tau                    <- K - K_transpose_div_Sigma * K;
> >   L_u                    <- cholesky_decompose( Tau );
> >   u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
> >   TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
> >   MSE <- TSE/(NT);
> >
> >
> > } /* end generated quantities block */
> >
> >
> > I also used a variation on the above script for generated quantities that leverages the cholesky decomposition of Sigma that is already computed, but there was no speed improvement.
> >
> > generated quantities{
> >   matrix[NT,NT] div_L_K; /* L^-1 * K */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] L_u; /* cholesky of Tau */
> >   vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
> >   vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
> >   /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
> >   real<lower=0> TSE;
> >   real<lower=0> MSE;
> >   /* posterior predictive quantities */
> >   div_L_K                <- mdivide_left_tri_low(L,K);
> >   mu_u                   <- div_L_K' * mdivide_left_tri_low(L,y);
> >   Tau                    <- K - div_L_K' * div_L_K;
> >   // for( i in 1:(NT-1))
> >   // {
> >   //   for( j in (i+1):NT)
> >   //   {
> >   //     Tau[i,j]  <- Tau[j,i];
> >   //   }
> >   // }
> >   L_u <- cholesky_decompose(Tau);
> >   u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
> >   TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
> >   MSE <- TSE/(NT);
> >
> >
> > } /* end generated quantities block */
> >
> >
> > Thanks very much your help and comments.
> >
> > Terrance

messages.subject_clean: multiple missing data(x) in MVN/GP
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am wondering if anyone has some expereince in handling multple missing data (x) with STAN in a MV/GP context.

For a very simple model is as follow

x ~ MVN (0, Sigma)

Let's assume I have the following x:

[  0.01, NA,   NA,
  -0.02, NA,   NA,
   0.05, NA,   0.02,
     NA, 0.03, -0.01 ]

Note that for row 1 and row 2, we have 2 missing values per "observation"

[ 0.01, NA, NA]
[-0.02, NA, NA]

If i just follow the manual and declare them as paramters (vector[6] x_miss) and create a new matrix as:

x_new <-
[ 0.01, x_miss[1], x_miss[2],
 -0.02, x_miss[3], x_miss[4],
  0.05, x_miss[5], 0.02,
x_miss[6], 0.03, -0.01]

x_new ~ multi_normal(0, Sigma)

Q1: Following the menu, x_miss is not given any prior. If the columns are indeed somehow correlated, would this create any issue?

Q2: If i have some prior information about the mean and variance (but not the correlation) on the missing data, is it possible to encode this?

Q3: Extending this to a GP with MV input (x) that has multiple missing values, can I handle the declaration if I have no prior information on the missing value (Q1) and some prior information (Q2).

Many thanks,

Andy

Which estimate from Stan are you talking about?  The optimization
result?  Those should be the same, at least up to several digits,
assuming you've coded the model properly.

>
> The 1.05 was something I set recently. Previously I had constrained it to be between -1 and 1, but I was worried that it would be problematical computationally if the actual value was near 1. However, physical constraints require that the values be between -1 and 1.

Then you absolutely need to constrain it to be between -1 and 1 if
that's required.  Otherwise, Stan's HMC will devolve into a random
walk for values near -1 or 1.  Either way, if there is a lot of mass
near -1 or 1, the sampling can be difficult if you're talking about HMC.

>
> I had trouble making all those transformed parameters local variables because the final result of the model, Gmeasured and GmeasuredImag are the results of much of the transformations. As a result, I was very unsure of how to do that. If you have any advice, that would be very helpful.

Functions and/or locally scoped blocks.  If you do this

  real final_result;
  {
     real temp;
     .... compute ...
     final_result <- ...
  }

then temp is a local variable and not included in the results.

> Again, vectoring was something that I was having trouble getting to work and was something that I intended to get eventually.

It can make up to an order of magnitude difference in speed
(or more in multivariate cases) due to shared computations
across the items.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Stan also supports MLE calculations, by the way.  It's
just called "optimizing" as it finds the posterior mode
(which is the MLE if the prior is uniform).

The problems near boundaries are just due to numerical
stability of the transforms.  For instance, we log constrain
positive values, but this only gives us an effective
range of (-320, +320) or so in the unconstrained space,
beyond which we overflow or underflow.  So we either have
to take small steps, or deal with a lot of rejection because
Stan's HMC is only using the gradient (first-order derivatives)
with multiple steps to simulate the Hamiltonian, which has more
curvature (higher-order derivatives).

We need to get all this written up in a user-facing way.

- Bob

Variables always get uniform priors on their support.  With upper
and lower bound constraints, that's a proper prior.

We're just saying that you probably don't want an interval-constrained
parameter unless the constraint is due to a physical constraint.

As to which prior to use, you almost always have some idea of
which values are more probable than others.  Or as someone just
wrote on Andrew's blog, it's the rare situation where you think
it's just as likely a value is in (0, 1) as in (1e10, 1e10+1).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If there's a problem with too large values for a parameter alpha,
it's often possible to parameterize as 1 / alpha. For example, we
typically use scale for parameterizing a normal, not precision, with
a prior with support at zero like a half-Cauchy.

- Bob

> 2015-10-22 10:35 GMT-07:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:
> This

> > int ngis[n_obs];
>
> declares a local variable which is never defined before it used
> here:
>
> >     ngis[s] ~ poisson(lambda[s])T[1,];
>
> Stan doesn't work this way --- the ~ doesn't do a random number
> generation.  Nor does it define a graphical model the way BUGS does.
> It just increments the log density with the value of the probability
> function at the argument.  If the arguments are undefined, so is the
> result.
>
> One thing Stan can't do is latent Poisson variables.  So if everything
> hinges on that, then you won't be able to use Stan.  Usually these
> models go the other way around, though, with a continuous mixture.
>
> So it looks like the Tweedie distribution is going to be beyond
> Stan's ability to model as is;  here's what the Wikipedia says:
>
>   In probability and statistics, the Tweedie distributions are a family of probability
>   distributions which include the purely continuous normal and gamma distributions,
>   the purely discrete scaled Poisson distribution, and the class of mixed compound
>   Poisson–gamma distributions which have positive mass at zero, but are otherwise continuous.
>
> The only way it'd be possible is if ngis could be analytically marginalized out.

messages.subject: Re: model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
messages.subject_clean: model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
messages.body_plain:
There is a lot of literature about using
 - LOO log predictive densities aka conditional predictive ordinates (CPO) to detect influential observations
 - and LOO cdfs aka probability integral transform (PIT) and to check calibration.
(some other test quantities have been also proposed)
These can be informative even if not comparing models.

PSIS-LOO computes in addition Pareto shape parameter estimates khats. These will tell, for example, whether CPOs and PITs can be trusted. khat values may sometimes indicate also influential observations, but there are also sensible models where khats can be large. For example, Gaussian process models tend to be difficult for importance sampling LOO even with PSIS and thus khats are often large, even if models are robust and not "overfitting" (overfitting is not well defined term).

Aki

On Friday, March 11, 2016 at 4:05:35 PM UTC+2, Luigi Acerbi wrote:

> in my understanding, WAIC and (PSIS) LOO are metrics for model selection.

> So PSIS-LOO could be an informative tool in itself even if we are not comparing models.

> However, how do I prevent overfitting / increase generalizability -- that is, how do I check my priors -- if I have a single "large model" and I don't want to go back to discrete model selection?

messages.subject_clean: Two new psycholinguistics papers using Stan
messages.body_plain:
@article{LogacevVasishthQJEP2016,
title = {Understanding underspecification: {A} comparison of two computational implementations},
year = {2016},
journal = {Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology},
author = {Pavel Loga{\v c}ev and Shravan Vasishth},
volume={69},
number={5},
pages={996–1012},
doi={http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/17470218.2015.1134602},
pdf = {http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/pdfs/LogacevVasishthQJEP2016.pdf},
abstract={Swets et al. (2008) present evidence that the so-called ambiguity advantage (Traxler et al., 1998), which has been explained in terms of the Unrestricted Race Model, can equally well be explained by assuming underspecification in ambiguous conditions driven by task-demands. Specifically, if comprehension questions require that ambiguities be resolved, the parser tends to make an attachment: when questions are about superficial aspects of the target sentence, readers tend to pursue an underspecification strategy. It is reasonable to assume that individual differences in strategy will play a significant role in the application of such strategies, so that studying average behavior may not be informative. In order to study the predictions of the good-enough processing theory, we implemented two versions of underspecification: the partial specification model (PSM), which is an implementation of the Swets et al. proposal, and a more parsimonious version, the non-specification model (NSM). We evaluate the relative fit of these two kinds of underspecification to Swets et al.’s data; as a baseline, we also fit three models that assume no underspecification. We find that a model without unspecification provides a somewhat better fit than both underspecification models, while the NSM model provides a better fit than the PSM. We interpret the results as lack of unambiguous evidence in favor of underspecification; however, given that there is considerable existing evidence for good-enough processing in the literature, it is reasonable to assume that some underspecification might occur. Under this assumption, the results can be interpreted as tentative ev- idence for NSM over PSM. More generally, our work provides a method for choosing between models of real-time processes in sentence comprehension that make qualitative predictions about the relationship between several dependent variables. We believe that sentence processing research will greatly benefit from a wider use of such methods.}
}

@article{SafaviEtAlFrontiers2016,
Author = {Molood Sadat Safavi and Samar Husain and Shravan Vasishth},
journal = {Frontiers in Psychology},
Title = {Dependency resolution difficulty increases with distance in Persian separable complex predicates: Implications for expectation and memory-based accounts},
pdf = {http://journal.frontiersin.org/article/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00403/full},
code={http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/code/SafaviEtAl2016DataCode.zip},
year = {2016},
volume = {7},
issue = {403},
doi = {10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00403},
    abstract = {Delaying the appearance of a verb in a noun-verb dependency tends to increase processing difficulty at the verb; one explanation for this locality effect is decay and/or interference of the noun in working memory. Surprisal, an expectation-based account, predicts that delaying the appearance of a verb either renders it no more predictable or more predictable, leading respectively to a prediction of no effect of distance or a facilitation.  Recently, Husain et al (2014) suggested that when the exact identity of the upcoming verb is predictable (strong predictability), increasing argument-verb distance leads to facilitation effects, which is consistent with surprisal; but when the exact identity of the upcoming verb is not predictable (weak predictability), locality effects are seen. We investigated Husain et al.'s proposal using Persian complex predicates (CPs), which consist of a non-verbal element---a noun in the current study---and a verb. In CPs, once the noun has been read, the exact identity of the verb is highly predictable (strong predictability); this was confirmed using a sentence completion study. In two self-paced reading (SPR) and two eye-tracking (ET) experiments, we delayed the appearance of the verb by interposing a relative clause (Expt. 1 and 3) or a long PP (Expt. 2 and 4).
We also included a simple Noun-Verb predicate configuration with the same distance manipulation; here, the exact identity of the verb was not predictable (weak predictability). Thus, the design crossed Predictability Strength and Distance.  We found that, consistent with surprisal, the verb in the strong predictability conditions was read faster than in the weak predictability conditions. Furthermore, greater verb-argument distance led to slower reading times;  strong predictability did not neutralize or attenuate the locality effects. As regards the effect of distance on dependency resolution difficulty, these four experiments  present evidence in favor of  working memory accounts of argument-verb dependency resolution, and against the surprisal-based expectation account of Levy (2008). However, another expectation-based measure, entropy, which was computed using the offline sentence completion data, predicts reading times in Experiment 1. We suggest that forgetting due to memory overload leads to greater entropy at the verb.}
    }

messages.subject: ODE solver: initial or solution times that depend on parameters
messages.subject_clean: ODE solver: initial or solution times that depend on parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bill!

lag times are a pain!

As you write, lag times influence the parameter values of the PK system quite a bit. Hence, the gradients wrt to the lag times are needed to my understanding; casting them away in C++ would be dangerous, I think.

So what you can do (this is in the archives of stan users), is to pass the tlag into the rhs of the ODE as a parameter. The rhs function then needs to handle the dosing event itself. Restarting the integrator at an unknown time is not possible, but you can just let the integrator handle the dosing discontinuity by himself. I know this is not ideal for the integrator, but the only solution I am aware of.

What I would attempt to do is to first fit a transit cmt Model first on some data which is informative about the tlag and then simply fix the lag and rerun with the full data. This is a hack, yes, but it should work. The transit cmt model can be written in Stan fully analytic, since you have all those nice gamma functions available.

I hope that helps. In case others have better ideas, I am very interested to hear these.

Best,
Sebastian

First, I'd listen to whatever Aki has to say.

But to answer the simple Stan question, no it won't
lead to rejected proposals.

If you have

  real<lower=0> b
  ...
  b ~ normal(1, 1);

then what you get is the normal(1, 1) truncated below at 0.
The normalizing term for the truncation is a constant, so
we don't need it.  The constraint will automatically do a log
transform to where the real sampling is happening in the
unconstrained space.

- Bob

messages.subject: Positivity and centering constraints in stan
messages.subject_clean: Positivity and centering constraints in stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan-users!

When coding the SCAM model from Pia and Wood in Stan, I run into a problem.
Knowledge of this model is not required. $X_s$ is a smoothing spline base,
stored as a NxK matrix. $\beta_s$ is an ordered vector of K coefficients
(to simplify). The expected value of the regression is $X_s \beta_s$.

Now the problem comes if I want to center the smoothing spline and model the
intercept explicitly. Conceptually, what needs to be done is
1) Center the smoothing spline so its mean is always zero (using the QR
decomposition of $X_s^T 1$), yielding $X_c$ a Nx(K-1) matrix of a centered
smoothing spline base.
2) Build the full design matrix X from a column vector of ones and the $X_c$
matrix. The expectation is then $X\beta$. $\beta$ can be decomposed in the
intercept $\beta_1$ and a vector $\beta_c$ (which corresponds to the K-1
last components of the vector obtained by representing $\beta_s$ in a base whose
first component is the constraint).

My problem arises because I have two constraints, applied in different
bases. The first one is the ordering constraint in $\beta_s$, the second one is the
centering constraint of the spline base. Two options came to my mind,
none of which made it to the end.

A. In the parameters block define `ordered[K] beta_s` and `real beta_1`.
In the transformed parameters block, compute `vector[K] beta` and other
quantities.  It seems to me that doing so can cause the optimizer to have problems
because there is one coefficient of beta_s whose value is arbitrary, as its variation
will be absorbed by the others due to the subsequent centering constraint.

B. In the paramters block, define `vector[K] beta`. That will fix the

messages.body_plain:
Thanks all for the answers -- I'll have a look at the literature on diagnostics with LOO.

On Saturday, 12 March 2016 15:21:59 UTC-5, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> There is a lot of literature about using
>  - LOO log predictive densities aka conditional predictive ordinates (CPO) to detect influential observations
>  - and LOO cdfs aka probability integral transform (PIT) and to check calibration.
> (some other test quantities have been also proposed)
> These can be informative even if not comparing models.
>
> PSIS-LOO computes in addition Pareto shape parameter estimates khats. These will tell, for example, whether CPOs and PITs can be trusted. khat values may sometimes indicate also influential observations, but there are also sensible models where khats can be large. For example, Gaussian process models tend to be difficult for importance sampling LOO even with PSIS and thus khats are often large, even if models are robust and not "overfitting" (overfitting is not well defined term).
>
> Aki
>
> On Friday, March 11, 2016 at 4:05:35 PM UTC+2, Luigi Acerbi wrote:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > in my understanding, WAIC and (PSIS) LOO are metrics for model selection.
> >
> > However, it happens that PSIS-LOO can also be used as a model diagnostics since if the measured LOO tail exponents are large it means that there are possibly influential observations and that the model is not robust (so it might be overfitting those); see also my previous post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/EOF6fhd9EWM/AkmbXePaAwAJ> (and answers) on this mailing list.

messages.subject_clean: ODE solver: initial or solution times that depend on parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sebastian,

Thanks for the ideas.

To be clear I'm not proposing to neglect the gradient w.r.t. the lag times. Lag times would still be passed to the solver as part of the parameter array. I just want to incorporate additional initial and solution times that depend on such lag times, so the solver doesn't need to struggle with the discontinuities. In the vast majority of cases, that will not affect the true solution of the ODEs at times relevant to the likelihood. As a result the gradient with respect to the initial and solution times passed to integrate_ode would not be required even when they depend on model parameters.

Thanks,
Bill

On Sunday, March 13, 2016 at 12:50:57 PM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi Bill!
>
> lag times are a pain!
>
> As you write, lag times influence the parameter values of the PK system quite a bit. Hence, the gradients wrt to the lag times are needed to my understanding; casting them away in C++ would be dangerous, I think.
>
> So what you can do (this is in the archives of stan users), is to pass the tlag into the rhs of the ODE as a parameter. The rhs function then needs to handle the dosing event itself. Restarting the integrator at an unknown time is not possible, but you can just let the integrator handle the dosing discontinuity by himself. I know this is not ideal for the integrator, but the only solution I am aware of.
>
> What I would attempt to do is to first fit a transit cmt Model first on some data which is informative about the tlag and then simply fix the lag and rerun with the full data. This is a hack, yes, but it should work. The transit cmt model can be written in Stan fully analytic, since you have all those nice gamma functions available.
>
> I hope that helps. In case others have better ideas, I am very interested to hear these.
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>

Sorry for the long delay. Other important things came up. Also, I had time to think about the model and go over that paper again. When I finally tried to model it based on what is on page 411, it (mostly) worked.

I had not realized that the data I was using to test this version had one standard point far out of range, which threw off the curve (well it was making sense given that data, but not given the rest of the data, e.g. the highest standard concentration was estimated at 10^4 instead of ~20). Making the model multilevel has solved the issue (although obviously not for a single plate).

For example, the data (std in blue, unknowns in red, lines link serial dilutions of the same sample): (plate 12 was the one that threw me for a loop, everything but the top 2 dilutions is lower)

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-OG7cYqJtKvI/VucijR_HAHI/AAAAAAAAAB4/zlgNBzmhud86oQZOJGIhycoOKPzuO66VA/s1600/Data.png>

The regressions with 95% HDI on the calculated concentrations (std in red):

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-l6lfPUV5cH4/Vuci8jv-UMI/AAAAAAAAAB8/RVgXFVpFhRwH3EgZretSVTyzyM0iSlnIg/s1600/Regressions%2Band%2Bpredictions.png>

Overall, the model estimates the individual points (each replicate of each dilution of each sample) with a, imho, remarkable accuracy. The output is consistent with the previous results and makes sense given the background.

I am still having issues with divergent transitions, hitting the max_treedepth, and major autocorrelation. From the little I understand about HMC, there are probably things in there that can be reparameterised to improve efficiency.

Newest model and code (with the same data I was using) are attached.  **This model took about 1.75 hours to sample on a i7-6700K overclocked at 4.6 GHz with 32 Gb of RAM.

>

> On Tuesday, February 16, 2016 at 6:52:42 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> > I think I am starting to figure out what the main issue is with this model. Normally, the curve parameters are dependent on the standard, i.e. P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope | x_std, OD_std), and the unknown concentrations are dependent on the curve parameters, i.e. P(theta | Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, OD_unkn). In the current model, since everything is calculated at once we have P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, theta | x_std, OD_std, OD_unkn) which implies that the curve parameters are also optimized as a function of the unknowns, this makes no logical or physical sense.
>
> I disagree that it makes no logical or physical sense.  The "unknowns" are run repeatedly so they have a known dilution and a known reading.  The fact the dilution level is known _should_ contribute because the reading should go down with the dilution in a sensible way, following the estimated curve.  I get that in practice this model is not working out as written but I wouldn't blame it on logical/physical inconsistency.  In BUGS people avoid this kind of problem using a function called (I think...) "cut", but Stan does not do that.  It's possible that dealing with this issue takes this project from "applying a model described in a paper" to "extending the paper" and if you don't want to do that using generated quantities is the right way  to go.
>
> > Also, since there are 72 wells of unknowns (18 samples, 2 dilutions each, in duplicate) and 24 wells of standard per plate, the unknown overwhelm the standards.
>
> Yes, I think the most likely issue is that a level of noise is not being taken into account---e.g.-the variation inherent in the enzyme that leads wells to develop at different speeds.
>
> > As I said earlier, one solution is to use inverse calculation in the generated quantities block. However that has two problems: 1) Artificial limits have to be placed on some parameters (so that Bottom < OD < Bottom + Span), even though OD readings above the top of the curve are possible due to measurement and enzymatic noise (this is an ELISA <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELISA> assay);
>
> These limits are not so much artificial as physical if you include the appropriate noise.  The true OD for a very low concentration sample can't be lower than the true instrument output with a negative control, but those things are all measured and recorded as averages.  The best data to go into a model like this would be a series of measurements (not averaged) or the sufficient statistics (mean measurement, measurement noise) and the equations for the curve would only be written for the "true" values not the measured values.  I think this is all possible in Stan just maybe more work that you want to put in at the moment.
>
> > 2) In biological assays, in my experience, interpolated values do not quite scale across dilutions, i.e. simply multiplying to reverse the dilution can yield surprisingly different values, that is the strength (in theory) of the approach used in the paper, it can weigh different dilutions depending on the precision they yield.
>
> That's the aspect of the model I find most interesting as well but it might take more work on the model itself to get the benefits---especially since you mentioned divergent iterations in the previous post.  It's a good signal that part of the parameter space is difficult for the sampler to deal with.
>
> > Is there a way to make the curve parameters independent of the unknowns' OD while keeping the multilevel unknown estimation? That issue did not seem to be a problem in the paper.

> This is what the "cut" function does in BUGS, there is no parallel in Stan.

I have been using Stan to estimate 2 parameter IRT models with roll call data from the House and Senate.  I recently decided to estimate a common space model by relying on the overlap of legislators that served in both legislatures (so called "bridges").  I also thought why not use House and Senate votes on versions of the same bill as "bridges."  This latter restriction seems intuitive to me but I am wondering if there is a way to test it.  Would estimating the model with and without imposing that the roll call locations are the same and then using WAIC be appropriate in this case?

Any thoughts are much appreciated.

messages.subject: psychophysical modelling in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: psychophysical modelling in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to understand if Stan is suitable for the class of models I usually work with in computational psychophysics.

The typical model has the structure (mmh MathJax support?):

$\log p(X | S, θ) = \sum_i \log p(x_i | s_i, θ)
                          = \sum_i \log \int p(x_i | y_i, θ) p (y_i | s_i, θ) dy_i$

where:
S is an array of known stimulus values s_i (a stimulus is usually a real scalar or 2-d real vector);
X is an array of recorded responses x_i (a response is usually a scalar, either integer or real-valued);
Y is an array of latent internal measurements y_i (an internal measurement is a real scalar or 2-d real vector) -- we are not interested in these;
the cardinality of S, X, Y is of the order of 10^3 trials;
θ is a low-to-medium dimensional parameter vector (2 to 20 parameters);
for simplicity, let's assume here that p(y_i | s_i, θ) is normal;
for simplicity, let's also assume that p(x_i | y_i, θ) = N(x_i | f(y_i, θ), σ^2(y_i, θ)), where, crucially, for many models f(y_i, θ) can be only computed via numerical integration (e.g., trapezoidal rule) of some expression involving y_i and θ.
In Matlab, I can efficiently marginalize Y away (via massively vectorized numerical integration and several computational tricks) to compute p(X | S, θ).
So far, I have been using slice sampling with moderate success, or simple MLE/MAP. However, I'd like to start using HMC -- but computing chain derivatives of parameters of dozens of different models with nested integrations quickly loses its fun.

Would Stan be able to work efficiently with this class of models?
Essentially, would it be able to handle the numerical integrations (both in terms of efficiency and autodiff?).

Thanks for your help!
Luigi

PS: Note that one numerical integration is always necessary (to obtain f(y_i, θ)).
The second integration -- to marginalize the y_i's away -- is perhaps not technically needed as I could sample from the joint posterior p(θ, Y | S, X) and then simply ignore the Y.
But this introduces a thousand or so auxiliary variables to sample from, so it's probably not the fastest thing to do -- I would probably stick to integrating each y_i away numerically (unless there are some magical gains in mixing properties).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] psychophysical modelling in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] psychophysical modelling in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
We don't yet have a definite integrator built in yet, so
there's no way at the moment to easily implemment that
model in Stan.

But we do have a prototype that Marco Inacio built that
works with known upper/lower bounds that does the right
thing in differentiating under the integral, i.e.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiation_under_the_integral_sign

That Wikipedia page also shows how to extend it to unknown
bounds (that is, how to calculate derivatives through it).

But rather than calculating that marginalization over y_i
by integrating, could you just take y to be a latent parameter
so that MCMC can do the marginalization for you?

- Bob

> So far, I have been using slice sampling with moderate success, or simple MLE/MAP. However, I'd like to start using HMC -- but computing chain derivatives of parameters of dozens of different models with nested integrations quickly loses its fun.
>
> Would Stan be able to work efficiently with this class of models?
> Essentially, would it be able to handle the numerical integrations (both in terms of efficiency and autodiff?).
>
> Thanks for your help!
> Luigi
>
> PS: Note that one numerical integration is always necessary (to obtain f(y_i, θ)).
> The second integration -- to marginalize the y_i's away -- is perhaps not technically needed as I could sample from the joint posterior p(θ, Y | S, X) and then simply ignore the Y.
> But this introduces a thousand or so auxiliary variables to sample from, so it's probably not the fastest thing to do -- I would probably stick to integrating each y_i away numerically (unless there are some magical gains in mixing properties).
>

Thanks!  May I suggest replacing this:

   for(k in 1:m[i]) {
      if(k == 1) {
        kappa[pos_kappa[i]] <- mu[i];
      }
      if(k > 1) {
        kappa[pos_kappa[i]+k-1] <- kappa[pos_kappa[i]+k-2] +
          delta[pos_delta[i]+k-2];
      }
    }

with

  if (m[i] > 0)
    kapa[pos_kappa[i]] <- mu[i];
  for (k in 2:m[i])
    kappa[pos_kappa[i]+k-1]
      <- kappa[pos_kappa[i]+k-2] + delta[pos_delta[i]+k-2];

It's almost always a good idea to reduce nesting (from 2-deep to
1-deep here) when possible.   And if you know that m[i] > 0, then
you can drop the conditional (there isn't a constraint to that effect
in the transformed data variable declaration, but there should probably
at least be a lower=0)

I thought these

 segment(kappa, pos_kappa[ii[n]], m[ii[n]]))

would get phased out in favor of the R/MATLAB style, but this
is really unreadable:

  kappa[pos_kappa[ii[n]]:(pos_kappa[ii[n]] + m[ii[n]])]

so would require a different computation for m as end-position
rather than size.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There were some neat adjustments in Wing Wong's dChip software
(for genomic microarrays) for noisy chips (people putting fingers
on them, getting contaminated, etc.).

If you've increased adapt_delta and upped the max depth
and are still having issues, you'll need to reparameterize.
It's probably a good idea anyway if possible.

Looking at the model, you definitely want to make the hierarchical
parts of it non-centered (aka, use the "Matt trick");  there's
a writeup in the language manual.

The other thing you can do is separate the uId[i] == std_loc
cases from the others so that you don't need a loop over N_unkn.

You'll save some time with vectorizing those normals in the loop over
n_unkn.  For instance, if log_x is just the std_loc versions, then you
can convert this

  log_x[i] ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions[i] + log(pred_std), sigma_x[uID[i]] * abs_log_ser_dilutions[i]);

to

  log_x ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions + log(pred_std),
                 sigma_x[uID] .* abs_log_ser_dilution);

Or, you can just build one big vector foo that for each i contains
either log(pred_std) or log_theta[uID[i]] depending on the
std_loc condition.  Then get rid of the original loop and use:

  log_x ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions + foo,
                 sigma_x[uID] .* abs_log_ser_dilutions);

It may seem like extra work to populate foo, but the vectorization of
normal() more than makes up for it.

- Bob

P.S.  Overclocked at 4.6 GHz?  Isn't that thing melting its case?

> On Tuesday, February 16, 2016 at 6:52:42 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> I think I am starting to figure out what the main issue is with this model. Normally, the curve parameters are dependent on the standard, i.e. P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope | x_std, OD_std), and the unknown concentrations are dependent on the curve parameters, i.e. P(theta | Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, OD_unkn). In the current model, since everything is calculated at once we have P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, theta | x_std, OD_std, OD_unkn) which implies that the curve parameters are also optimized as a function of the unknowns, this makes no logical or physical sense.
>
> I disagree that it makes no logical or physical sense.  The "unknowns" are run repeatedly so they have a known dilution and a known reading.  The fact the dilution level is known _should_ contribute because the reading should go down with the dilution in a sensible way, following the estimated curve.  I get that in practice this model is not working out as written but I wouldn't blame it on logical/physical inconsistency.  In BUGS people avoid this kind of problem using a function called (I think...) "cut", but Stan does not do that.  It's possible that dealing with this issue takes this project from "applying a model described in a paper" to "extending the paper" and if you don't want to do that using generated quantities is the right way  to go.
>
> Also, since there are 72 wells of unknowns (18 samples, 2 dilutions each, in duplicate) and 24 wells of standard per plate, the unknown overwhelm the standards.
>
> Yes, I think the most likely issue is that a level of noise is not being taken into account---e.g.-the variation inherent in the enzyme that leads wells to develop at different speeds.
>
> As I said earlier, one solution is to use inverse calculation in the generated quantities block. However that has two problems: 1) Artificial limits have to be placed on some parameters (so that Bottom < OD < Bottom + Span), even though OD readings above the top of the curve are possible due to measurement and enzymatic noise (this is an ELISA assay);
>
> These limits are not so much artificial as physical if you include the appropriate noise.  The true OD for a very low concentration sample can't be lower than the true instrument output with a negative control, but those things are all measured and recorded as averages.  The best data to go into a model like this would be a series of measurements (not averaged) or the sufficient statistics (mean measurement, measurement noise) and the equations for the curve would only be written for the "true" values not the measured values.  I think this is all possible in Stan just maybe more work that you want to put in at the moment.
>
> 2) In biological assays, in my experience, interpolated values do not quite scale across dilutions, i.e. simply multiplying to reverse the dilution can yield surprisingly different values, that is the strength (in theory) of the approach used in the paper, it can weigh different dilutions depending on the precision they yield.
>
> That's the aspect of the model I find most interesting as well but it might take more work on the model itself to get the benefits---especially since you mentioned divergent iterations in the previous post.  It's a good signal that part of the parameter space is difficult for the sampler to deal with.
>
> Is there a way to make the curve parameters independent of the unknowns' OD while keeping the multilevel unknown estimation? That issue did not seem to be a problem in the paper.
>
> This is what the "cut" function does in BUGS, there is no parallel in Stan.
>
> Sorry I can't be more helpful, I don't have time to dig in at the moment.
>
> Krzysztof

The question isn’t whether or not adding a bunch of auxiliary
variables is slower, it’s whether or not numerically integrating
over a 1000 dimensional space is faster than the corresponding
Monte Carlo estimate.  But Monte Carlo integration tends to do
_really_ well in high-dimensions so I think it’s worth trying a
full MCMC solution.  As Bob notes it will depend on the posterior
geometry, but doing everything at once is much easier anyways.

> > > PS: Note that one numerical integration is always necessary (to obtain f(y_i, θ)).
> > > The second integration -- to marginalize the y_i's away -- is perhaps not technically needed as I could sample from the joint posterior p(θ, Y | S, X) and then simply ignore the Y.
> > > But this introduces a thousand or so auxiliary variables to sample from, so it's probably not the fastest thing to do -- I would probably stick to integrating each y_i away numerically (unless there are some magical gains in mixing properties).
>

Thanks for the tips!

I have used non-centered parameterization in other models, but did not realize it would help here.

I will try those changes out tomorrow.

Re 4.6 GHz: It does worry me whenever I look at the temperature but that is from Asus’ OC utility… and it cools down pretty quick.

From: Bob Carpenter
Sent: March 15, 2016 18:09
To: stan-...@googlegroups.com
Cc: krzysztof...@gmail.com
Subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel serial dilution assay

There were some neat adjustments in Wing Wong's dChip software
(for genomic microarrays) for noisy chips (people putting fingers
on them, getting contaminated, etc.).

If you've increased adapt_delta and upped the max depth
and are still having issues, you'll need to reparameterize.
It's probably a good idea anyway if possible.

Looking at the model, you definitely want to make the hierarchical
parts of it non-centered (aka, use the "Matt trick");  there's
a writeup in the language manual.

The other thing you can do is separate the uId[i] == std_loc
cases from the others so that you don't need a loop over N_unkn.

You'll save some time with vectorizing those normals in the loop over
n_unkn.  For instance, if log_x is just the std_loc versions, then you
can convert this

  log_x[i] ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions[i] + log(pred_std), sigma_x[uID[i]] * abs_log_ser_dilutions[i]);

to

  log_x ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions + log(pred_std),
                 sigma_x[uID] .* abs_log_ser_dilution);

Or, you can just build one big vector foo that for each i contains
either log(pred_std) or log_theta[uID[i]] depending on the
std_loc condition.  Then get rid of the original loop and use:

  log_x ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions + foo,
                 sigma_x[uID] .* abs_log_ser_dilutions);

It may seem like extra work to populate foo, but the vectorization of
normal() more than makes up for it.

- Bob

P.S.  Overclocked at 4.6 GHz?  Isn't that thing melting its case?

> On Mar 14, 2016, at 4:56 PM, Jonathan Audet <jona...@hotmail.com> wrote:

> Sorry for the long delay. Other important things came up. Also, I had time to think about the model and go over that paper again. When I finally tried to model it based on what is on page 411, it (mostly) worked.

>

> On Tuesday, February 16, 2016 at 6:52:42 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> I think I am starting to figure out what the main issue is with this model. Normally, the curve parameters are dependent on the standard, i.e. P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope | x_std, OD_std), and the unknown concentrations are dependent on the curve parameters, i.e. P(theta | Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, OD_unkn). In the current model, since everything is calculated at once we have P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, theta | x_std, OD_std, OD_unkn) which implies that the curve parameters are also optimized as a function of the unknowns, this makes no logical or physical sense.
>
> I disagree that it makes no logical or physical sense.  The "unknowns" are run repeatedly so they have a known dilution and a known reading.  The fact the dilution level is known _should_ contribute because the reading should go down with the dilution in a sensible way, following the estimated curve.  I get that in practice this model is not working out as written but I wouldn't blame it on logical/physical inconsistency.  In BUGS people avoid this kind of problem using a function called (I think...) "cut", but Stan does not do that.  It's possible that dealing with this issue takes this project from "applying a model described in a paper" to "extending the paper" and if you don't want to do that using generated quantities is the right way  to go.
>
> Also, since there are 72 wells of unknowns (18 samples, 2 dilutions each, in duplicate) and 24 wells of standard per plate, the unknown overwhelm the standards.
>
> Yes, I think the most likely issue is that a level of noise is not being taken into account---e.g.-the variation inherent in the enzyme that leads wells to develop at different speeds.
>
> As I said earlier, one solution is to use inverse calculation in the generated quantities block. However that has two problems: 1) Artificial limits have to be placed on some parameters (so that Bottom < OD < Bottom + Span), even though OD readings above the top of the curve are possible due to measurement and enzymatic noise (this is an ELISA assay);
>
> These limits are not so much artificial as physical if you include the appropriate noise.  The true OD for a very low concentration sample can't be lower than the true instrument output with a negative control, but those things are all measured and recorded as averages.  The best data to go into a model like this would be a series of measurements (not averaged) or the sufficient statistics (mean measurement, measurement noise) and the equations for the curve would only be written for the "true" values not the measured values.  I think this is all possible in Stan just maybe more work that you want to put in at the moment.
>
> 2) In biological assays, in my experience, interpolated values do not quite scale across dilutions, i.e. simply multiplying to reverse the dilution can yield surprisingly different values, that is the strength (in theory) of the approach used in the paper, it can weigh different dilutions depending on the precision they yield.
>
> That's the aspect of the model I find most interesting as well but it might take more work on the model itself to get the benefits---especially since you mentioned divergent iterations in the previous post.  It's a good signal that part of the parameter space is difficult for the sampler to deal with.
>
> Is there a way to make the curve parameters independent of the unknowns' OD while keeping the multilevel unknown estimation? That issue did not seem to be a problem in the paper.
>
> This is what the "cut" function does in BUGS, there is no parallel in Stan.
>
> Sorry I can't be more helpful, I don't have time to dig in at the moment.
>
> Krzysztof

If you can currently fit the model (even without unknowns) I would run that version and look at the pairs plots of other parameters with tau and see if some are highly or non-linearly correlated with it.

@ Aki: Maybe I was imprecise. The unit normal CDF can be approximated with (according to the Stan user manual)

Phi_approx„(x)… ƒ = logit^{-1}(0.07056 * x^3 ‚ + 1.5976 * x)…

Now, this can be used for a much improved (approximate) version of normal_cdf_log, since it won't under- or overflow so quickly. Robustness via a student_t or any other distributions would be a different approach which I haven't tried back then, but the above works splendid (in particular with ADVI which does not like NaNs so much, at least in the past). All I wanted to say is that putting a note in the manual besides the normal_cdf (where you warn about the numerical issues due to over+underflow) would be helpful for users who wonder how they may get around these numerical challenges.

Sebastian

>
>
> On Wednesday, March 16, 2016 at 12:19:00 PM UTC+2, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > BTW, it would be nice for users to point out in the manual at the normal_cdf doc that you can actually approximate this function in log-space very well using the Phi_approx function approach (log_inv_logit). This gave me much better model runs for left-censored data due to the improved numerical stability.
>
> Using logit is close to using student_t_cdf with degrees of freedom nu=7. Switching from normal to something with thicker tails may also explain the improved stability.
>

>
> Does anyone have code demonstrating how to apply such a procedure to estimate the standard error of the difference in WAIC/LOO between two models fit using Stan? I understand how to calculate a bootstrap, but found the description in Vehtari and Lampinen (2002) difficult to follow.

Yes there is code available.
For Matlab you can use bbmean function in GPstuff <http://research.cs.aalto.fi/pml/software/gpstuff/>
For R look Rasmus Bååth's Bayesian bootstrap code and nice examples here <http://www.sumsar.net/blog/2015/07/easy-bayesian-bootstrap-in-r/> and here <https://github.com/rasmusab/bayesboot>.
For Python see here <https://github.com/ilanfri/StatsML/blob/master/Bayesian_bootstrap.ipynb>
You can probably find something with Google for other languages, too.
Bayesian bootstrap is really simple as it's enough that you are able to sample from Dirichlet distribution, which you can do by sampling from Gamma distribution which you can do if you can sample from uniform distribution.
We probably add Bayesian bootstrap (and demo) to R loo package later.

Aki

On Wednesday, March 16, 2016 at 6:24:50 PM UTC+2, Ben Lambert wrote:
> In the 'generated quantities' part of the Stan program, I capture the log probability from my model, for each of my nk data points in the hold out sample (Yk is the hold out dependent variable):
>
>     for (i in 1:nk){
>         ...
>         lLogLikelihood[i] <- neg_binomial_2_log(Yk[i],aLambda,aKappa);
>     }
>
> I therefore end up with a nSamples x nk matrix of log probabilities. Let's call this mLogProb.
>
> I am following Aki's et al. (2015) paper, 'Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC', to estimate the elpd. In each of the K iterations, I get this matrix mLogProb. My hold out data sets are, in general, of different sizes in each iteration. My question is, how can I use this series (mLogProb_1,mLogProb_2,...,mLog_k) to estimate the elpd? I'm just not quite understanding how I follow the paper here.
> Finally, I'm wanting to calculate a standard error on this elpd. This is given by eqn. (23) in the paper. How can I estimate the standard error in elpd here?

You can combine your matrices to one nSamples x n matrix (e.g. LogProb). Compute log of the expected predictive densities log(mean(exp(LogProb))) or the numerically more accurate version log_sum_exp(LogProb)-log(n), and you get 1xn vector elpd values. Then you can use the same formula for standard error as in leave-one-out cross-validation.

Aki

>
> Best,
>
> Ben

On Tuesday, February 16, 2016 at 5:54:28 PM UTC+1, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> Hi Michael,
>
> Can you update to the just-released update of rstanarm on CRAN (version 2.9.0-3)? We added a Note section to the documentation for posterior_predict that explains how N is handled for binomial models and changed some things internally related to this.
>
> If you don't specify newdata when calling posterior_predict the Ns are the Ns from the original data. If you do specify newdata then you should be required to specify your own Ns and get an error otherwise (the error wasn't being thrown in the first version of rstanarm). In your case, since the LHS of your formula is cbind(K, N-K) you could include in newdata a variable K=0 and a variable N that has the number of trials you want to use. If there are multiple observations in newdata N can be different for each of them. The predicted counts can then easily be divided by the number of trials if you want probabilities.
>
> Relatedly, we don't recommend trying to directly use the posterior distribution of the inverse-logit transformed linear predictor (i.e., the predicted probabilities), but rather to always sample from the posterior predictive distribution of the outcome. If you want you can then get probabilities by division, as mentioned above.

Could you expand on why directly using the posterior of the inv-logit is not recommended?

>
> Also, in case it's helpful, one of the examples in the How to Use the rstanarm Package vignette has been updated in the new version of the package and now shows how to correctly specify the number of trials to use for prediction after binomial models.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> Jonah

For a bernoulli model you can use a function like this, making use of some rstanarm internal functions,

predicted_prob <- function(fit) {
  dat <- rstanarm:::pp_data(fit)
  eta <- rstanarm:::pp_eta(fit, dat)$eta

}

It's not that it's particularly discouraged, we just want to encourage people to work with predicted outcomes, i.e. the full posterior predictive distribution, rather than just (functions of) the linear predictor.

Maybe we should reconsider our decision and provide a convenience function for this in the package.

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
Ved,

(y1,z) should considered to be independent. They are used to define the marginal CDF as input to the Copula.
Lets call this copula C.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copula_(probability_theory)

Have a look at Definition:

In probabilistic <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_theory> terms,  is a d-dimensional copula if C is a joint cumulative distribution function <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumulative_distribution_function> of a d-dimensional random vector on the unit cube <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_cube>  with uniform <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_distribution_(continuous)> marginals <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_distribution>.[1] <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copula_(probability_theory)#cite_note-nelsen-1>

That means, we have to map (y1,z) to [0,1]^2  in our case.

We decided already to map y2 via y2 <- inv_logit(z) which maps z to [0,1],
next we have to map y1 to [0,1].
Thus we need to assume a marginal distribution to y1.

As example, we could  sample y1 as
y1 ~ normal(0,1)
and then we would need a STAN function to calculate the cdf of the
univariate standard normal distribution. Thus y1_cdf <- normal_cdf(y1,0,1);

Or directly sample to y1_cdf ~ uniform(0,1);

And lets assume C is a frank copula:

then u: = y1_cdf and v :=  y2 and
theta ~ normal(0,5);
(If rare case theta == 0, the term becomes NAN and being rejected by
the sampler)
the frank copula above defines a CDF.
For log-likelihood estimation in STAN we need the density c(u,v,theta) of
our copula C(u,v,theta). Wikipedia doesn't provide them, but
you can easily take the derivatives or search the internet.

Last step would be to add
increment_log_prob(log(c(u,v,theta)));

In the discrete case, we cannot take the
derivatives, we have to take the differences.
This result into a copula probability mass function,
which can be found here, eg.

http://www-1.ms.ut.ee/tartu07/presentations/kolev.pdf

Visualise the probability mass function as one or more
plateau(s) or hyperplanes connected together.

Andre

@article{LogacevVasishthQJEP2016,

title = {Understanding underspecification: {A} comparison of two computational implementations},
year = {2016},
journal = {Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology},
author = {Pavel Loga{\v c}ev and Shravan Vasishth},

volume={69},
number={5},
pages={996-1012},
doi={http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/17470218.2015.1134602},
pdf = {http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/pdfs/LogacevVasishthQJEP2016.pdf},
abstract={Swets et al. (2008) present evidence that the so-called ambiguity advantage (Traxler et al., 1998), which has been explained in terms of the Unrestricted Race Model, can equally well be explained by assuming underspecification in ambiguous conditions driven by task-demands. Specifically, if comprehension questions require that ambiguities be resolved, the parser tends to make an attachment: when questions are about superficial aspects of the target sentence, readers tend to pursue an underspecification strategy. It is reasonable to assume that individual differences in strategy will play a significant role in the application of such strategies, so that studying average behavior may not be informative. In order to study the predictions of the good-enough processing theory, we implemented two versions of underspecification: the partial specification model (PSM), which is an implementation of the Swets et al. proposal, and a more parsimonious version, the non-specification model (NSM). We evaluate the relative fit of these two kinds of underspecification to Swets et al.’s data; as a baseline, we also fit three models that assume no underspecification. We find that a model without unspecification pro- vides a somewhat better fit than both underspecification models, while the NSM model provides a better fit than the PSM. We interpret the results as lack of unambiguous evidence in favor of underspecification; however, given that there is considerable existing evidence for good-enough processing in the literature, it is reasonable to assume that some underspecification might occur. Under this assumption, the results can be interpreted as tentative ev- idence for NSM over PSM. More generally, our work provides a method for choosing between models of real-time processes in sentence comprehension that make qualitative predictions about the relationship between several dependent variables. We believe that sentence processing research will greatly benefit from a wider use of such methods.}
}

@article{NicenboimEtAlFrontiers2016Capacity,
  author = {Bruno Nicenboim and Pavel Loga{\v c}ev and Carolina Gattei and Shravan Vasishth},
  title = {When high-capacity readers slow down and low-capacity readers speed up: {W}orking memory differences in unbounded dependencies},
  year = {2016},

  volume={7},
  number={280},

  journal = {Frontiers in Psychology},

  note ={Special Issue on Encoding and Navigating Linguistic Representations in Memory},
  abstract={We examined the effects of argument-head distance in SVO and SOV languages (Spanish and German), while taking into account readers’ working memory capacity and controlling for expectation (Levy, 2008) and other factors. We predicted only locality effects, that is, a slow-down produced by increased dependency distance (Gibson, 2000; Lewis & Vasishth, 2005). Furthermore, we expected stronger locality effects for readers with low working memory capacity. Contrary to our predictions, low-capacity readers showed faster reading with increased distance, while high-capacity readers showed locality effects. We suggest that while the locality effects are compatible with memory-based explanations, the speedup of low-capacity readers can be explained by an increased probability of retrieval failure. We present a computational model based on ACT-R built under the previous assumptions, which is able to give a qualitative account for the present data and can be tested in future research. Our results suggest that in some cases, interpreting longer RTs as indexing increased processing difficulty and shorter RTs as facilitation may be too simplistic: The same increase in processing difficulty may lead to slowdowns in high-capacity readers and speedups in low-capacity ones. Ignoring individual level capacity differences when investigating locality effects may lead to misleading conclusions.},
  doi={10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00280},
  issn={1664-1078},
  pdf = {http://journal.frontiersin.org/article/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00280/abstract}
  }

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm looking for guidance on legitimate interpretations of the elpd. Briefly: can the elpd difference between two models be interpreted as the log odds ratio of the posterior model probabilities?

Example:

Model 1 elpd_loo = -50
Model 2 elpd_loo = -48

abs difference: 2

>From these results, could one state that Model 2 "describes the data" (in the sense of expected prediction error) about 7 times better than model 1 (i.e. exp(2)), on average? Similarly, if one converted the elpd difference to base 2 (2 / log(2) = 2.89), could one say that the average expected information gain of Model 2 relative to Model 1 is 2.89 bits?

I am seeking ways to describe the results of loo such that they could be more easily understood or communicated to non-mathematical audiences. Apologies if my interpretations are way off base (I am a member of that non-mathematical audience).

> NOTE: it only re-compiles if I do not assign the output to a name, i.e. foo.out<-fecr_stan(...) does not re-compile while fecr_stan(...) does.

That is correct. If a stanfit or stanmodel object is assigned to a symbol (that can easily be found), then calling the same Stan program does not recompile the model and instead fishes the compiled model out of the existing stanfit or stanmodel object. Otherwise, it has to recompile because loading the same dynamic shared object off of the disk crashes R.

Ben

messages.subject: Comparing parameters from different regression models?
messages.subject_clean: Comparing parameters from different regression models?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I used two ways to estimate regression weights:
a) a hierarchical model with post stratification
b) an ordinary/non-hierarchical regression

Now I would like to compare the regression weights
obtained by these two methods.

Currently I am using a Bayesian bootstrap to do this,
but I am unsure if I am doing this right or if I should
use a different method altogether.

My specific questions are:

1) Which method would you recommend?
2) For the Bayesian bootstrap: Should I  for each
    bootstrap sample
- first calculate the weighted mean/median for each
  parameter and then calculated the ratio
  (or difference) or
- first select random samples from the
  posteriors, then calculate the element wise
  ratio, and finally calculate the mean/median
  of that ratio
- something entirely different?

I'd appreciate any pointer to relevant literature, my
own literature search has been without success
so far.

Best - Guido

PS:
At first I just took a large random sample
(with replacement) from each posterior and simply
calculated the element wise ratio to get a posterior
distribution of ratios. However, these posteriors are
not easy to deal with, because when parameter values
get close to zero ratios become very large.

You could state like this, but then you are ignoring the uncertainty in the estimates. This approach has been proposed informally as pseudo Bayes factor, but there are no papers showing formally or experimentally that this would be a good way to report results. I recommend using the approach described in section 5.2 of "Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC" http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544, which is also implemented in compare function in loo package.

Aki
