messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Guidance on interpreting loo's elpd
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Guidance on interpreting loo's elpd
messages.body_plain:
Remember that LOO, cross-valiadtion, WAIC and all of the like
are just estimators of some number that quantifies the _relative_
compatibility of the model with the data.

That number is tricky to interpret as information gain or loss because
it’s really a difference of two different Kullback-Leibler divergences.
And it’s definitely not a probability so shouldn’t be interpreted as
such.

Really this is just a way to rank models relative to each other.

On Mar 17, 2016, at 5:48 PM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:

> On Thursday, March 17, 2016 at 11:46:08 AM UTC+2, Tom Wallis wrote:
> > I'm looking for guidance on legitimate interpretations of the elpd. Briefly: can the elpd difference between two models be interpreted as the log odds ratio of the posterior model probabilities?
> >
> > Example:
> >
> > Model 1 elpd_loo = -50
> > Model 2 elpd_loo = -48
> >
> > abs difference: 2
> >
> > From these results, could one state that Model 2 "describes the data" (in the sense of expected prediction error) about 7 times better than model 1 (i.e. exp(2)), on average? Similarly, if one converted the elpd difference to base 2 (2 / log(2) = 2.89), could one say that the average expected information gain of Model 2 relative to Model 1 is 2.89 bits?
>
> You could state like this, but then you are ignoring the uncertainty in the estimates. This approach has been proposed informally as pseudo Bayes factor, but there are no papers showing formally or experimentally that this would be a good way to report results. I recommend using the approach described in section 5.2 of "Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC" http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544, which is also implemented in compare function in loo package.
>
> Aki
>
> >
> > I am seeking ways to describe the results of loo such that they could be more easily understood or communicated to non-mathematical audiences. Apologies if my interpretations are way off base (I am a member of that non-mathematical audience).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: K Fold Cross Validation - its explicit calculation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: K Fold Cross Validation - its explicit calculation
messages.body_plain:
You can always divide by sample size.

It's a standard move in information theory from cross-entropy
to cross-entropy rate (just KL-divergence plus a constant divided
by sample size);  Shannon used it in his original paper in
the 1940s to estimate bounds for the entropy rate of characters
in English, and it's still the standard measure for compression.
As far as I can tell, information theory is just probability theory
done on the log_2 scale.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Consequences of putting multiple models in model block
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Consequences of putting multiple models in model block
messages.body_plain:
Nothing wrong in principle, but the algorithms tend to be
faster done separately because of coupling all the systems
step-by-step in HMC.

One thing you can try to do is pull out functionality into
functions, but don't (yet) have a way to set up a library of
functions to include (but it's on my to-do list for this year).

More on code inline.

- Bob

> On Mar 16, 2016, at 6:20 PM, Quinn Lathrop <quinn....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> In working with simulations, I often have competing models fit to the same data. Each model is kept in a different .stan file, but they often contain very similar syntax. My question here is, what are the consequences of putting multiple models within the same model block? More simply, is there any situation where this is a reasonable approach?
>
> I have found this helpful in communicating the differences in models and in understanding how to implement those models in stan. So the question is, is this a valid use of stan? Or should I never write model code like this ever again?
>

> ...

> data {
>   int<lower=0> n_obs; //number of obs cases
>   int<lower=0> n_mis; //number of missing cases
>   vector[2] xy_obs[n_obs]; //xy for observed cases
>   real x_mis[n_mis]; //x for cases with missing y
> }
>
> parameters {
>   // Complete Case Parameters
>   vector[2] mu_1;
>   cov_matrix[2] sigma_1;
>
>   // Available Data Parameters
>   vector[2] mu_2;
>   cov_matrix[2] sigma_2;
>   real y_mis[n_mis];
> }

You really want to parameterize this in terms of Cholesky
factors.  We strongly recommend scaling a Cholesky factor for a
correlation matrix (with an LKJ prior), but if you really want
the improper uniform on covariance matrices, it's
much more arithmetically stable and efficient to use the Cholesky
forms (of both variables and densities).

> transformed parameters{
>   vector[2] xy_mis[n_mis]; //xy for cases with missing y
>
>                      // I could not figure out how to vectorize this loop
>                      // seems simple. Any tips?
>   for(i in 1:n_mis){
>     xy_mis[i,1] <- x_mis[i]; //x_mis is obsvered
>     xy_mis[i,2] <- y_mis[i]; //y_mis is parameter
>   }
> }

You can do this:

  x[, 1] <- x_mis;
  x[, 2] <- y_mis;

> // This model block has pedagogical qualities

I'd avoid this kind of comment, too --- comments overall make
code *less* readable if the code is reasonable.

> model {
>
>     //Complete Case Model
>     xy_obs ~ multi_normal(mu_1, sigma_1);
>
>     //Available Data Model
>     xy_obs ~ multi_normal(mu_2, sigma_2);
>     xy_mis ~ multi_normal(mu_2, sigma_2);

Even more efficient if you append_put xy_mis together into
a single array of vectors.  But in this case, I don't think
the xy_mis ~ ... line will affect the estimates of mu_2 and
sigma_2;  instead, you could probably generate the predictions
for missing y in generated quantities more efficiently (with
help from someone better than me at conditioning a multivariate
normal).  But what you have will also work.

- Bob

If you have same number of posterior samples for each you can just concatenate them. If you have

nSamples x n1
nSamples x n2
nSamples x n3

then the combined matrix is

nSamples x (n1+n2+n3)

where n=n1+n2+n3 is the total number of observations

and then you proceed as if you would have been doing LOO (and in this case you don't need to divide by sample size as Bob suggests).

Aki

Although it's not technically passing an arg to the init
function, you can do it implicitly by having vaiables in the
but you do get scoping out of definitions in R, so you can
have an init function

> f <- function(c) list(rho=runif(K,-1,1))

which won't even run out of the box

> f(2)
Error in runif(K, -1, 1) : object 'K' not found

and then set the variable in it (can't do that in C++)!

> K <- 3

and then eval to get rho to be a 3-vector

> f(2)
$rho
[1] 0.9084397 0.8430041 0.4831463

and then change K:

> K <- 4

and eval again:

> f(2)
$rho
[1] -0.79284105 -0.14985411 -0.05549911  0.65483971

So as long as you can get in and set the parameter, the init
function f can depend on it.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Is there anyone on this list that has experimented with pymc3, and can attest as to whether it's ready for prime time?

https://github.com/pymc-devs/pymc3

Apparently pymc3 implements NUTS via Theano's automatic differentiation engine. Using Theano means that theoretically you could even sample from models using the GPU; I'm curious if this actually works/provides a decent speed-up for big models.

(I ran into this by thinking, hey, if there were an autodiff engine built on Python, that would be a nice way to implement NUTS. And Googled it. And discovered, hey, cool, there is one, and somebody has implemented NUTS that way.)

Even if it's not ready, I can see pymc3's approach as having some big advantages over Stan's over the long term, and I imagine wouldn't be too hard to write a Stan-to-pymc3 cross-compiler so you could reuse existing models/continue to use the Stan language.

Ed

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I don’t know of people specifically who take advantage of pymc3’s GPU support for NUTS but certainly it is being done. There are implementations of HMC in TensorFlow (not NUTS) that share the same benefits; for research purposes I’m also playing with HMC code written in these computational graph frameworks, as I needed to try MCMC as a baseline method for some big data sets and it could not done fast enough in Stan.

When I last checked, pymc3 is slower on CPUs than Stan, and it does an adaptation phase that isn’t as optimized as the one in Stan. My high-level understanding of the library is that it’s slower in terms of getting behind new ideas and their implementation (e.g., they’re still working on ADVI), but they do have added advantages due to the backend using computational graphs for symbolic diffs and enabling GPUs.

A cross-compiler would be cool but also difficult. If it underlies Stan’s call to functions such as log prob and grad log prob, then these would need to enable GPU support as well (after all that’s where the bottleneck in computation goes). So if someone develops one, then we should use it in native Stan too!

Dustin

I had the same question in doing my recent case study (which
has some related code).  The average of logs isn't the
same as the log of the averages, so you want to do the average
on the linear scale.  But you also want to avoid losing too
much arithmetic precision.  So we calculate it as

  log_sum_exp(lps) - log(N)

  = log (exp(lps[1]) + ... + exp(lps[N]) / N)

So if the inputs are on the log scale, it does the linear
scale average (by exponentiating first), and then goes back
to the log scale.

It's just the sum(ps) / N on the log scale.  So that if

  lps = log(ps)

then

  log_sum_exp(lps) - log(N)  =  log(sum(ps) / N)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifiability in multinomial logistic models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Identifiability in multinomial logistic models
messages.body_plain:
There are two possible interpretations of "the subjects don't all interact":

1. There are subjects s1 and s2 that never appear together in a case i.

2. Creating a graph where the subjects are nodes, with an edge between s1 and s2 whenever s1 and s2 appear together in a case, this graph is not fully connected: there is at least one pair of subjects with no path connecting them.

#1 isn't a problem by itself, but #2 could be a problem.

Strictly speaking, even with a fully connected graph you have likelihood non-identifiability, but the large number of subjects plus your prior on the effects should greatly reduce the posterior correlation. If the graph is not connected but each connected component has a large number of subjects in it, the situation is similar. The problem case would be if there exists one or more connected component with a small number of subjects in it; that would be a small group of subjects that never get compared, even indirectly, to a larger group of subjects.

I have some blog posts that don't directly address your problem, but which you might find useful in thinking about these kinds of issues. See

    http://bayesium.com/full-dummy-coding-for-nominal-variables/

and maybe

    http://bayesium.com/a-symmetric-effects-prior/

and

    http://bayesium.com/implementing-the-symmetric-effects-prior/

(Think of "subject" as a nominal input variable with 500 levels.)

Hi Bob,
Maybe I've missed something in the original question.
But I can't see why stan cannot calculate AUC, especially if you can in JAGS using the example below:

library(R2jags)

set.seed(1)
J <- 2
n <- 5000
X <- cbind(1, matrix(runif(n*J, -1, 1), ncol=2))
b <- 1:3
p <- plogis(X %*% b)
y <- rbinom(n, 1, p)

M <- function() {
  for(i in 1:n) {
    y[i] ~ dbern(p[i])
    logit(p[i]) <- inprod(X[i, ], b)
  }
  for(j in 1:(J+1)) {
    b[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
  }
  for (t in 1:length(thr)) {
    sens[t] <- sum((p > thr[t]) && (y==1))/n1
    spec[t] <- sum((p < thr[t]) && (y==0))/n0
    fpr[t] <- 1 - spec[t]
    fnr[t] <- 1 - sens[t]
  }
  auc <- sum((sens[2:length(sens)]+sens[1:(length(sens)-1)])/2 *
    -(fpr[2:length(fpr)] - fpr[1:(length(fpr)-1)]))
}

j <- jags(list(X=X, y=y, n=n, J=J, n1=sum(y), n0=sum(!y), thr=seq(0, 1, 0.05)),
          NULL, c('b', 'sens', 'spec', 'fpr', 'fnr', 'auc'), M, 3, 1000)

Though having said this, it isn't immediately clear how this would be efficiently coded in stan.

Let’s be clear — what you’re proposing is an _estimate_ of the AUC, and an
estimate with potentially large error.  The problem with these kinds of naive
estimates is that they completely undermine the theoretical guarantees of
MCMC as the error biases the Markov chains away from true target distribution.

If you can guarantee that the error in the AUC estimate is around machine
precision then you’re okay, but that is highly unlikely with such a simple
quadrature procedure here.  At least not unless you pay a huge computational
burden with really tiny intervals.

messages.body_plain:
I've never found AUC very useful for anything other than
bakeoffs based on AUC and its relatives (like TREC for
information retrieval).  In real applications, there's usually
a decision problem involving operating points to maximize
expected value, with costs for false positives and negatives,
and benefits for true positives and true negatives.  That is,
rarely is a classifier intended to be used at all specificy
or sensitivity levels.

messages.body_plain:
I'd recommend replacing the Wishart with a scaled LKJ
prior.  See Ben's paper:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

What we really need is a Cholesky-parameterized (inverse)
Wishart with the Jacobian baked in, the way Ben set up
the LKJ priors.  The full derivation of the Jacobians required
is in the manual chapter on the underlying transforms (near
the end of the manual).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The Dirichlet is conjugate and you're using labeled data,
so the posteriors for alpha and beta will also be Dirichlet
and can be computed directly in the generated quantities block.

An intermediate step would be to collect sufficient stats
and convert the looped categorical into multinomials.  That
will be a whole lot faster, but still not as fast as just
calculating the analytic posterior and drawing a sample from
that directly.

There's a discussion of doing both of these thing in the language
manual chapter on optimizing Stan code.

- Bob

The model is being fit on what the machine learning people
call "log loss", so I'd use that as a direct measure of
probabilistic accuracy.  It's nice to see the received
operating curve (either precision-recall or specificity-sensitivity),
but I don't know of any siutation other than evaluating classifiers
for their own sake where it's relevant.  When you want to actually
use a classifier for an application, you usually care about
the sensitivity-specificity tradeoff at a particular application
point.  Or about whether your model's calibrated in that it makes
the right predictions at the rate its probabilities say it does.

- Bob

Luckily it's pretty straightforward. If y (observed) and yhat (predicted) are N-vectors then you could do something like this in R:

-1 / length(y) * sum(y * log(yhat) + (1 - y) * log(1 - yhat))

You could also do it in generated quantities in a Stan program, but you might have y declared as an integer array and yhat as a real array or vector, in which
case you'd probably have to do it in a loop.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] issues with inference on lengthscale parameter of gaussian process in stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] issues with inference on lengthscale parameter of gaussian process in stan
messages.body_plain:
I’m going to have to complicate things by disagreeing with Andy and Seth a nontrivial amount.

As most people have noted, GPs are horrendously non-identified.  This is in fact a fundamental
property of these objects!  It turns out that the functions supported by any two distinct set of
hyperparameters (even those varying by an epsilon amount) are completely different; in other
words you’ll never see the same function sampled from a GP with two different sets of
hyperparameters.

Hence by taking only a single set of hyperparameters you are ignoring a giant space of functions
that could interpolate between your data just as well as those supported by your distinguished
hyperparameters but in different ways.  This in term manifests as _drastic_ underestimates
of your predictive uncertainty away from the data.

If you care only about predictive performance near your data then you might be okay, but
if you really want to know what’s going on between your data then you really do have to
marginalize over the hyperparameters.  Empirical Bayes has the same problem of misrepresenting
the posterior uncertainty.  WON’T SOMEBODY THINK OF THE UNCERTAINTY? <insert
Helen Lovejoy>.

Also, as Seth, Mike, and Aki note, spending some time to think about the relevant length scales
can help you build some really informative priors to clean things up.  As in Seth’s example, if
you can put together some good priors then you might be able to do a full marginalization in
practice.

On Mar 21, 2016, at 7:58 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Rachael. Just to clarify what you have in mind--your fake data simulation creates 2000 draws from a GP, but you're interested in the standard case that you're modeling, which is just inference based on a single draw, right? (If you could use all 2000 draws that would certainly help with identification, but I'm guessing that's not the case.)
>
> As Aki says, the noise variance (sd = 3) is overwhelming the signal variance (sd = 1).  But another issue is that with the covariance parameterized as exp(-.1 d^2), the lengthscale is 2.23 in the parameterization I like, which is exp(-.5 d^2 / l^2). But the data you're observing is on a regular grid in the interval [0,1], and thus the lengthscale is way too long to recover.
>
> I switched it to noise variance of 0.1 and lengthscale 0.2 and prior on lengthscale and now it does a fine job recovering the parameters.
>
> Broadly my thinking, which Andrew mentioned, is that informative priors on the hyperparameters make a lot of sense, and fixing those hyperparameters is just a very informative prior which can be reasonable in many cases. (As a practical matter, it can also help with finding bugs!) Another thing that I think is very helpful as you're testing out / debugging models is to estimate the hyperparameters from the data ("empirical Bayes") which as you note has a long history, and not just in frequentist settings. In Stan, I've had success finding learning parameters using optimizing(...), an example of which I also included in the attached.
>
> In terms of scalability in a hierarchical setting, you might also get some ideas from our paper, which has Stan code at the end: http://sethrf.com/files/fast-hierarchical-GPs.pdf
> Seth
>
> On Mon, Mar 21, 2016 at 9:52 AM, Rachael Meager <rachael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thanks Mike, the x-axis data is already from 0-1 but I will try out the rest of it and see if it helps.
> >
> > On Monday, 21 March 2016 12:58:05 UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > > Not sure this will make much difference, but I like to:
> > >
> > > (1) first rescale the x-axis data to range from 0-1
> > >
> > > (2) reparameterize in terms of inv_rho_sq (ie. `Sigma[i,j] <-  exp(-pow(x[i] - x[j],2)/inv_rho_sq)`) so that values toward zero reflect more linear data
> > >
> > > (3) use a cauchy(0,1) prior (inc. using the tan trick, pg 214 manual v2.9.0) so that the peak prior reflects a linear prior, and half of the mass of the prior reflects length scales that are less than the range of the data
> > >
> > >
> > > --
> > > Mike Lawrence
> > > Graduate Student
> > > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > > Dalhousie University
> > >
> > > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> > >
> > > On Mon, Mar 21, 2016 at 1:34 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > > > Hi, just a quick thought which Seth F and I have been bouncing around recently . . . you could try just setting the length scale parameter to a fixed value.  There are a few reasons for this.  Most obviously it should make computing go faster.  At the same time, in any particular application such as yours, I think there is a lot of prior information so you should be able to choose a reasonable value for this parameter.
> > > >
> > > > To put it another way:  from a Bayesian perspective, the right thing to do is to use an informative prior.  But in this case the prior info might be much stronger than the data anyway, so why not just treat this parameter as data?  Alternatively, a strong prior (for example, lognormal centered at the prior estimate with a small sd) should also work well.  In that case, just make sure to run Stan with reasonable inits.
> > > >

> > > > > Right now, I'm simulating Gaussian Processes in rstan and trying to fit models for inference about the covariance functions. I find that this sometimes produces relatively poor inference on the covariance kernel's lengthscale parameter ("rho_sq"), and am wondering if I'm making some obvious mistake that I just don't have the experience to spot. I've attached my R file and the session log file, including the execution of sessionInfo().
> > > > >
> > > > > To generate data, I'm using the stan simulation model in the manual in section 15.2 (on page 160, in version 2.9.0). First I construct an "x" vector of 100 points on [0,1], then draw from a GP on the space, like this:
> > > > >
> > > > > data {
> > > > > int<lower=1> N;
> > > > > real x[N];
> > > > > }
> > > > > transformed data {
> > > > > vector[N] mu;
> > > > > cov_matrix[N] Sigma;
> > > > > for (i in 1:N)
> > > > > mu[i] <- 0;
> > > > > for (i in 1:N)
> > > > > for (j in 1:N)
> > > > > Sigma[i,j] <- exp(-0.1*pow(x[i] - x[j],2))
> > > > > + if_else(i==j, 3, 0.0);
> > > > > }
> > > > > parameters {
> > > > > vector[N] y;
> > > > > }
> > > > > model {
> > > > > y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > >

The mean of the rho_sq posterior jumps around because of the heavy right tail and this is quite sensitive to the dispersion in the priors (compare output of models 1, 2, in the attached file). I tried to get rid of the heavy tail using uniform priors but that does worse inference overall (see output of model 3). messages.subject: Visualising the results for estimated ELPD and its standard error
messages.subject_clean: Visualising the results for estimated ELPD and its standard error
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I want to show the results for estimated ELPD across a number of models, which has been estimated using K-fold cross validation on a hierarchical model.

I have used the method in Vehtari et al. (2015) 'Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC', to estimate the ELPD, and its standard error across a number of models. I would now like to make a graph of these results for a publication. However, I realise that really this measure is meant only to be used for pairwise comparisons; if model A's ELPD is higher than model B's, accounting for the standard error of their difference, then we prefer the former.

As such, does it make sense to graph these results at all? The issue I am having is illustrated in the attached pdf. This shows the point estimates of the ELPD for each of 7 models, along with the standard errors. When viewed this way, it looks like I shouldn't prefer the exponential model over the gompertz-Makeham one, since there is considerably overlap in their standard errors.

However, when I explicitly estimate the standard error of their difference, as:

se = sqrt(N sum_i var(lpd_i^exponential - lpd_i^gompertz-makeham)

I find that there is a difference between them in terms of score. As such, I am unclear whether it makes any sense to graph these results at all, and perhaps I just need to mention this in the text. Does a graph of these model scores make any sense, or should I just shelve it?

If there are other ways to visualise these scores, that I have not considered, then also it'd be good to hear them!

Best,

Ben

significance of the difference based on the overlap between the grey band and
the interval of each particular model.  But that might not be a universally well-liked
visualization.

My guess is David has both a while loop and an inverse! ;)

David, can you just comment out the generated quantities block and report back whether there are significant time savings? Also, I guess you're using RStan? I think at some point when I had large covariance matrices (in transformed parameters, not generated quantities, but still...) there was indeed significant i/o overhead, even to the point that I could imagine that just one call to the generated quantities block would be slow what with allocating memory for a 6000x6000 matrix and getting that passed from Stan into R...

Seth

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] issues with inference on lengthscale parameter of gaussian process in stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] issues with inference on lengthscale parameter of gaussian process in stan
messages.body_plain:
Mike:

I don’t see how you’re really disagreeing with me!  You write, “spending some time to think about the relevant length scales can help you build some really informative priors to clean things up.”  An informative prior is great.  A delta function prior (that is, treating the lengthscale parameter as known) can be a useful approximation and speed up computation, then the researcher can replace this by a strongly informative prior later.  It’s the usual “pick your battles” strategy.  GP with a reasonable fixed lengthscale will do the smoothing that is needed so the researcher can focus on the more important aspects of the model.

When we’re looking for a generic lowess replacement, it’s another story, we’d like the model to “learn” the lenghscale, requiring only a minimal amount of prior information.  But for specific applications, more and more I’ve been leaning toward running hier models with fixed hyperparameters, or with strong priors on the hyperparams.

A

> On Mar 21, 2016, at 5:21 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I’m going to have to complicate things by disagreeing with Andy and Seth a nontrivial amount.
>
> As most people have noted, GPs are horrendously non-identified.  This is in fact a fundamental
> property of these objects!  It turns out that the functions supported by any two distinct set of
> hyperparameters (even those varying by an epsilon amount) are completely different; in other
> words you’ll never see the same function sampled from a GP with two different sets of
> hyperparameters.
>
> Hence by taking only a single set of hyperparameters you are ignoring a giant space of functions
> that could interpolate between your data just as well as those supported by your distinguished
> hyperparameters but in different ways.  This in term manifests as _drastic_ underestimates
> of your predictive uncertainty away from the data.
>
> If you care only about predictive performance near your data then you might be okay, but
> if you really want to know what’s going on between your data then you really do have to
> marginalize over the hyperparameters.  Empirical Bayes has the same problem of misrepresenting
> the posterior uncertainty.  WON’T SOMEBODY THINK OF THE UNCERTAINTY? <insert
> Helen Lovejoy>.
>
> Also, as Seth, Mike, and Aki note, spending some time to think about the relevant length scales
> can help you build some really informative priors to clean things up.  As in Seth’s example, if
> you can put together some good priors then you might be able to do a full marginalization in
> practice.
>
>
> On Mar 21, 2016, at 7:58 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Hi Rachael. Just to clarify what you have in mind--your fake data simulation creates 2000 draws from a GP, but you're interested in the standard case that you're modeling, which is just inference based on a single draw, right? (If you could use all 2000 draws that would certainly help with identification, but I'm guessing that's not the case.)
> >
> > As Aki says, the noise variance (sd = 3) is overwhelming the signal variance (sd = 1).  But another issue is that with the covariance parameterized as exp(-.1 d^2), the lengthscale is 2.23 in the parameterization I like, which is exp(-.5 d^2 / l^2). But the data you're observing is on a regular grid in the interval [0,1], and thus the lengthscale is way too long to recover.
> >
> > I switched it to noise variance of 0.1 and lengthscale 0.2 and prior on lengthscale and now it does a fine job recovering the parameters.
> >
> > Broadly my thinking, which Andrew mentioned, is that informative priors on the hyperparameters make a lot of sense, and fixing those hyperparameters is just a very informative prior which can be reasonable in many cases. (As a practical matter, it can also help with finding bugs!) Another thing that I think is very helpful as you're testing out / debugging models is to estimate the hyperparameters from the data ("empirical Bayes") which as you note has a long history, and not just in frequentist settings. In Stan, I've had success finding learning parameters using optimizing(...), an example of which I also included in the attached.
> >
> > In terms of scalability in a hierarchical setting, you might also get some ideas from our paper, which has Stan code at the end: http://sethrf.com/files/fast-hierarchical-GPs.pdf
> > Seth
> >
> > On Mon, Mar 21, 2016 at 9:52 AM, Rachael Meager <rachael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Thanks Mike, the x-axis data is already from 0-1 but I will try out the rest of it and see if it helps.
> > >
> > > On Monday, 21 March 2016 12:58:05 UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > > > Not sure this will make much difference, but I like to:
> > > >
> > > > (1) first rescale the x-axis data to range from 0-1
> > > >
> > > > (2) reparameterize in terms of inv_rho_sq (ie. `Sigma[i,j] <-  exp(-pow(x[i] - x[j],2)/inv_rho_sq)`) so that values toward zero reflect more linear data
> > > >
> > > > (3) use a cauchy(0,1) prior (inc. using the tan trick, pg 214 manual v2.9.0) so that the peak prior reflects a linear prior, and half of the mass of the prior reflects length scales that are less than the range of the data
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > --
> > > > Mike Lawrence
> > > > Graduate Student
> > > > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > > > Dalhousie University
> > > >
> > > > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> > > >
> > > > On Mon, Mar 21, 2016 at 1:34 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > > > > Hi, just a quick thought which Seth F and I have been bouncing around recently . . . you could try just setting the length scale parameter to a fixed value.  There are a few reasons for this.  Most obviously it should make computing go faster.  At the same time, in any particular application such as yours, I think there is a lot of prior information so you should be able to choose a reasonable value for this parameter.
> > > > >
> > > > > To put it another way:  from a Bayesian perspective, the right thing to do is to use an informative prior.  But in this case the prior info might be much stronger than the data anyway, so why not just treat this parameter as data?  Alternatively, a strong prior (for example, lognormal centered at the prior estimate with a small sd) should also work well.  In that case, just make sure to run Stan with reasonable inits.
> > > > >
> > > > > A
> > > > >
> > > > > > On Mar 21, 2016, at 11:38 AM, Rachael Meager <rachael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Hi Folks,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > First, thank you all so much for rstan and for staffing this forum. My research would be approximately 5000 times harder without you and I'm forever grateful .
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Right now, I'm simulating Gaussian Processes in rstan and trying to fit models for inference about the covariance functions. I find that this sometimes produces relatively poor inference on the covariance kernel's lengthscale parameter ("rho_sq"), and am wondering if I'm making some obvious mistake that I just don't have the experience to spot. I've attached my R file and the session log file, including the execution of sessionInfo().
> > > > > >
> > > > > > To generate data, I'm using the stan simulation model in the manual in section 15.2 (on page 160, in version 2.9.0). First I construct an "x" vector of 100 points on [0,1], then draw from a GP on the space, like this:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > data {
> > > > > > int<lower=1> N;
> > > > > > real x[N];
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > transformed data {
> > > > > > vector[N] mu;
> > > > > > cov_matrix[N] Sigma;
> > > > > > for (i in 1:N)
> > > > > > mu[i] <- 0;
> > > > > > for (i in 1:N)
> > > > > > for (j in 1:N)
> > > > > > Sigma[i,j] <- exp(-0.1*pow(x[i] - x[j],2))
> > > > > > + if_else(i==j, 3, 0.0);
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > parameters {
> > > > > > vector[N] y;
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > model {
> > > > > > y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > So you can see I've set eta to 1, rho_sq to 0.1 and sigma to 3. I then fit the following simplified version of the stan model in the manual in section 15.3 to one of the (vector) draws from the GP above. This is model 1 in the R file:
> > > > > > data {
> > > > > > int<lower=1> N;
> > > > > > vector[N] x;
> > > > > > vector[N] y;
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > transformed data {
> > > > > > vector[N] mu;
> > > > > > for (i in 1:N) mu[i] <- 0;
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > parameters {
> > > > > >
> > > > > > real<lower=0> inv_rho_sq;
> > > > > > real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > transformed parameters {
> > > > > > real<lower=0> rho_sq;
> > > > > > rho_sq <- inv(inv_rho_sq);
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > model {
> > > > > > matrix[N,N] Sigma;
> > > > > > // off-diagonal elements
> > > > > > for (i in 1:(N-1)) {
> > > > > > for (j in (i+1):N) {
> > > > > > Sigma[i,j] <-  exp(-rho_sq * pow(x[i] - x[j],2));
> > > > > > Sigma[j,i] <- Sigma[i,j];
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > // diagonal elements
> > > > > > for (k in 1:N)
> > > > > > Sigma[k,k] <- 1 + sigma_sq; // + jitter
> > > > > >
> > > > > > inv_rho_sq ~ cauchy(0,5);
> > > > > > sigma_sq ~ cauchy(0,5);
> > > > > > y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > > This model works pretty well, however, the inference on rho_sq is patchy relative to the inference on sigma_sq. The mean of the rho_sq posterior jumps around because of the heavy right tail and this is quite sensitive to the dispersion in the priors (compare output of models 1, 2, in the attached file). I tried to get rid of the heavy tail using uniform priors but that does worse inference overall (see output of model 3). The inference breaks totally if I do either of these 2 things: (1) try to have improper uniform priors to do MLE (model 4), or (2) try to put a prior on rho_sq instead of inv_rho_sq (model 5).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Obviously you can see I've dispensed with inference on the eta parameter for now, setting it to its correct value of 1. I did this because at first I thought the instances of poor inference were due to a weak identification issue with eta in there, but this model is not performing any better without it. Fortunately, the inference on sigma_sq is always really good, which is the main goal of my project -- but I do want to know what's going on with rho_sq.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Does anyone know if there's a way to avoid the fat right tail on the rho_sq without the pathologies of the uniform? Should I be using normals here instead - and would that be generally helpful or just for this specific rho_sq? And do we know why the posterior gives up when I put a prior on rho_sq directly, or use an improper uniform prior?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > As I said, I'm attaching an R file that does this all together. I usually save the stan models separately as per the manual's suggestion, but I figured it would be more convenient for you guys to have it in 1 place. I'm also attaching the log file from running this R script on the unix server I have access to at MIT.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I hope this is clear, let me know if I should provide further information or clarification. Thanks in advance for any input or suggestions you have!
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Cheers
> > > > > > Rachael

> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > transformed data {
> > > > > > > vector[N] mu;
> > > > > > > cov_matrix[N] Sigma;
> > > > > > > for (i in 1:N)
> > > > > > > mu[i] <- 0;
> > > > > > > for (i in 1:N)
> > > > > > > for (j in 1:N)
> > > > > > > Sigma[i,j] <- exp(-0.1*pow(x[i] - x[j],2))
> > > > > > > + if_else(i==j, 3, 0.0);
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > parameters {
> > > > > > > vector[N] y;
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > model {
> > > > > > > y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > So you can see I've set eta to 1, rho_sq to 0.1 and sigma to 3. I then fit the following simplified version of the stan model in the manual in section 15.3 to one of the (vector) draws from the GP above. This is model 1 in the R file:
> > > > > > > data {
> > > > > > > int<lower=1> N;
> > > > > > > vector[N] x;
> > > > > > > vector[N] y;
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > transformed data {
> > > > > > > vector[N] mu;
> > > > > > > for (i in 1:N) mu[i] <- 0;
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > parameters {
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > real<lower=0> inv_rho_sq;
> > > > > > > real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > transformed parameters {
> > > > > > > real<lower=0> rho_sq;
> > > > > > > rho_sq <- inv(inv_rho_sq);
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > model {
> > > > > > > matrix[N,N] Sigma;
> > > > > > > // off-diagonal elements
> > > > > > > for (i in 1:(N-1)) {
> > > > > > > for (j in (i+1):N) {
> > > > > > > Sigma[i,j] <-  exp(-rho_sq * pow(x[i] - x[j],2));
> > > > > > > Sigma[j,i] <- Sigma[i,j];
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > // diagonal elements
> > > > > > > for (k in 1:N)
> > > > > > > Sigma[k,k] <- 1 + sigma_sq; // + jitter
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > inv_rho_sq ~ cauchy(0,5);
> > > > > > > sigma_sq ~ cauchy(0,5);
> > > > > > > y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > This model works pretty well, however, the inference on rho_sq is patchy relative to the inference on sigma_sq. The mean of the rho_sq posterior jumps around because of the heavy right tail and this is quite sensitive to the dispersion in the priors (compare output of models 1, 2, in the attached file). I tried to get rid of the heavy tail using uniform priors but that does worse inference overall (see output of model 3). The inference breaks totally if I do either of these 2 things: (1) try to have improper uniform priors to do MLE (model 4), or (2) try to put a prior on rho_sq instead of inv_rho_sq (model 5).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Obviously you can see I've dispensed with inference on the eta parameter for now, setting it to its correct value of 1. I did this because at first I thought the instances of poor inference were due to a weak identification issue with eta in there, but this model is not performing any better without it. Fortunately, the inference on sigma_sq is always really good, which is the main goal of my project -- but I do want to know what's going on with rho_sq.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Does anyone know if there's a way to avoid the fat right tail on the rho_sq without the pathologies of the uniform? Should I be using normals here instead - and would that be generally helpful or just for this specific rho_sq? And do we know why the posterior gives up when I put a prior on rho_sq directly, or use an improper uniform prior?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > As I said, I'm attaching an R file that does this all together. I usually save the stan models separately as per the manual's suggestion, but I figured it would be more convenient for you guys to have it in 1 place. I'm also attaching the log file from running this R script on the unix server I have access to at MIT.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I hope this is clear, let me know if I should provide further information or clarification. Thanks in advance for any input or suggestions you have!
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Cheers
> > > > > > > Rachael

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] issues with inference on lengthscale parameter of gaussian process in stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] issues with inference on lengthscale parameter of gaussian process in stan
messages.body_plain:
This is an interesting discussion.

For what it's worth, I tried reparameterising the model slightly, and using slightly tighter priors. As Aki mentioned above, once you increase the signal, the parameter seems to be fairly identifiable.

The issue is that with the posterior for the lengthscale parameter being so skewed, the modal estimate is quite wrong--optimisers beware. The relevant image is attached.

If you've got rstan, reshape, dplyr and ggplot2 installed, this should run out of the bottle:

https://gist.github.com/khakieconomics/c398c4c76b60bfded9c5

JS

On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 11:25:47 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> We disagree that a delta prior is useful and let's the user worry about other parts of the model!  I don't think the lengthscale is ever sufficiently well known for such approximations to not induce significant predictive uncertainty underestimates that affect inference.
>
> On Mar 22, 2016, at 13:24, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> > Mike:
> >
> > I don’t see how you’re really disagreeing with me!  You write, “spending some time to think about the relevant length scales can help you build some really informative priors to clean things up.”  An informative prior is great.  A delta function prior (that is, treating the lengthscale parameter as known) can be a useful approximation and speed up computation, then the researcher can replace this by a strongly informative prior later.  It’s the usual “pick your battles” strategy.  GP with a reasonable fixed lengthscale will do the smoothing that is needed so the researcher can focus on the more important aspects of the model.
> >
> > When we’re looking for a generic lowess replacement, it’s another story, we’d like the model to “learn” the lenghscale, requiring only a minimal amount of prior information.  But for specific applications, more and more I’ve been leaning toward running hier models with fixed hyperparameters, or with strong priors on the hyperparams.
> >
> > A
> >
> >
> > > On Mar 21, 2016, at 5:21 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > I’m going to have to complicate things by disagreeing with Andy and Seth a nontrivial amount.
> > >
> > > As most people have noted, GPs are horrendously non-identified.  This is in fact a fundamental
> > > property of these objects!  It turns out that the functions supported by any two distinct set of
> > > hyperparameters (even those varying by an epsilon amount) are completely different; in other
> > > words you’ll never see the same function sampled from a GP with two different sets of
> > > hyperparameters.
> > >
> > > Hence by taking only a single set of hyperparameters you are ignoring a giant space of functions
> > > that could interpolate between your data just as well as those supported by your distinguished
> > > hyperparameters but in different ways.  This in term manifests as _drastic_ underestimates
> > > of your predictive uncertainty away from the data.
> > >
> > > If you care only about predictive performance near your data then you might be okay, but
> > > if you really want to know what’s going on between your data then you really do have to
> > > marginalize over the hyperparameters.  Empirical Bayes has the same problem of misrepresenting
> > > the posterior uncertainty.  WON’T SOMEBODY THINK OF THE UNCERTAINTY? <insert
> > > Helen Lovejoy>.
> > >
> > > Also, as Seth, Mike, and Aki note, spending some time to think about the relevant length scales
> > > can help you build some really informative priors to clean things up.  As in Seth’s example, if
> > > you can put together some good priors then you might be able to do a full marginalization in
> > > practice.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Mar 21, 2016, at 7:58 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Hi Rachael. Just to clarify what you have in mind--your fake data simulation creates 2000 draws from a GP, but you're interested in the standard case that you're modeling, which is just inference based on a single draw, right? (If you could use all 2000 draws that would certainly help with identification, but I'm guessing that's not the case.)
> > > >
> > > > As Aki says, the noise variance (sd = 3) is overwhelming the signal variance (sd = 1).  But another issue is that with the covariance parameterized as exp(-.1 d^2), the lengthscale is 2.23 in the parameterization I like, which is exp(-.5 d^2 / l^2). But the data you're observing is on a regular grid in the interval [0,1], and thus the lengthscale is way too long to recover.
> > > >
> > > > I switched it to noise variance of 0.1 and lengthscale 0.2 and prior on lengthscale and now it does a fine job recovering the parameters.
> > > >
> > > > Broadly my thinking, which Andrew mentioned, is that informative priors on the hyperparameters make a lot of sense, and fixing those hyperparameters is just a very informative prior which can be reasonable in many cases. (As a practical matter, it can also help with finding bugs!) Another thing that I think is very helpful as you're testing out / debugging models is to estimate the hyperparameters from the data ("empirical Bayes") which as you note has a long history, and not just in frequentist settings. In Stan, I've had success finding learning parameters using optimizing(...), an example of which I also included in the attached.
> > > >
> > > > In terms of scalability in a hierarchical setting, you might also get some ideas from our paper, which has Stan code at the end: http://sethrf.com/files/fast-hierarchical-GPs.pdf
> > > > Seth
> > > >
> > > > On Mon, Mar 21, 2016 at 9:52 AM, Rachael Meager <rachael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Thanks Mike, the x-axis data is already from 0-1 but I will try out the rest of it and see if it helps.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Monday, 21 March 2016 12:58:05 UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > > > > > Not sure this will make much difference, but I like to:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (1) first rescale the x-axis data to range from 0-1
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (2) reparameterize in terms of inv_rho_sq (ie. `Sigma[i,j] <-  exp(-pow(x[i] - x[j],2)/inv_rho_sq)`) so that values toward zero reflect more linear data
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (3) use a cauchy(0,1) prior (inc. using the tan trick, pg 214 manual v2.9.0) so that the peak prior reflects a linear prior, and half of the mass of the prior reflects length scales that are less than the range of the data
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > --
> > > > > > Mike Lawrence
> > > > > > Graduate Student
> > > > > > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > > > > > Dalhousie University
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Mon, Mar 21, 2016 at 1:34 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi, just a quick thought which Seth F and I have been bouncing around recently . . . you could try just setting the length scale parameter to a fixed value.  There are a few reasons for this.  Most obviously it should make computing go faster.  At the same time, in any particular application such as yours, I think there is a lot of prior information so you should be able to choose a reasonable value for this parameter.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > To put it another way:  from a Bayesian perspective, the right thing to do is to use an informative prior.  But in this case the prior info might be much stronger than the data anyway, so why not just treat this parameter as data?  Alternatively, a strong prior (for example, lognormal centered at the prior estimate with a small sd) should also work well.  In that case, just make sure to run Stan with reasonable inits.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > A
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Mar 21, 2016, at 11:38 AM, Rachael Meager <rachael...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > > > > > Hi Folks,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > First, thank you all so much for rstan and for staffing this forum. My research would be approximately 5000 times harder without you and I'm forever grateful .
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Right now, I'm simulating Gaussian Processes in rstan and trying to fit models for inference about the covariance functions. I find that this sometimes produces relatively poor inference on the covariance kernel's lengthscale parameter ("rho_sq"), and am wondering if I'm making some obvious mistake that I just don't have the experience to spot. I've attached my R file and the session log file, including the execution of sessionInfo().
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > To generate data, I'm using the stan simulation model in the manual in section 15.2 (on page 160, in version 2.9.0). First I construct an "x" vector of 100 points on [0,1], then draw from a GP on the space, like this:

> > > > > > > > vector[N] x;
> > > > > > > > vector[N] y;
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > transformed data {
> > > > > > > > vector[N] mu;
> > > > > > > > for (i in 1:N) mu[i] <- 0;
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > parameters {
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > real<lower=0> inv_rho_sq;
> > > > > > > > real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > transformed parameters {
> > > > > > > > real<lower=0> rho_sq;
> > > > > > > > rho_sq <- inv(inv_rho_sq);
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > model {
> > > > > > > > matrix[N,N] Sigma;
> > > > > > > > // off-diagonal elements
> > > > > > > > for (i in 1:(N-1)) {
> > > > > > > > for (j in (i+1):N) {
> > > > > > > > Sigma[i,j] <-  exp(-rho_sq * pow(x[i] - x[j],2));
> > > > > > > > Sigma[j,i] <- Sigma[i,j];
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > // diagonal elements
> > > > > > > > for (k in 1:N)
> > > > > > > > Sigma[k,k] <- 1 + sigma_sq; // + jitter
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > inv_rho_sq ~ cauchy(0,5);
> > > > > > > > sigma_sq ~ cauchy(0,5);
> > > > > > > > y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > This model works pretty well, however, the inference on rho_sq is patchy relative to the inference on sigma_sq. The mean of the rho_sq posterior jumps around because of the heavy right tail and this is quite sensitive to the dispersion in the priors (compare output of models 1, 2, in the attached file). I tried to get rid of the heavy tail using uniform priors but that does worse inference overall (see output of model 3). The inference breaks totally if I do either of these 2 things: (1) try to have improper uniform priors to do MLE (model 4), or (2) try to put a prior on rho_sq instead of inv_rho_sq (model 5).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Obviously you can see I've dispensed with inference on the eta parameter for now, setting it to its correct value of 1. I did this because at first I thought the instances of poor inference were due to a weak identification issue with eta in there, but this model is not performing any better without it. Fortunately, the inference on sigma_sq is always really good, which is the main goal of my project -- but I do want to know what's going on with rho_sq.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Does anyone know if there's a way to avoid the fat right tail on the rho_sq without the pathologies of the uniform? Should I be using normals here instead - and would that be generally helpful or just for this specific rho_sq? And do we know why the posterior gives up when I put a prior on rho_sq directly, or use an improper uniform prior?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > As I said, I'm attaching an R file that does this all together. I usually save the stan models separately as per the manual's suggestion, but I figured it would be more convenient for you guys to have it in 1 place. I'm also attaching the log file from running this R script on the unix server I have access to at MIT.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I hope this is clear, let me know if I should provide further information or clarification. Thanks in advance for any input or suggestions you have!
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Cheers
> > > > > > > > Rachael

> On Mar 22, 2016, at 11:53 AM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> This is an interesting discussion.
>
> For what it's worth, I tried reparameterising the model slightly, and using slightly tighter priors. As Aki mentioned above, once you increase the signal, the parameter seems to be fairly identifiable.
>
> The issue is that with the posterior for the lengthscale parameter being so skewed, the modal estimate is quite wrong--optimisers beware. The relevant image is attached.
>
> If you've got rstan, reshape, dplyr and ggplot2 installed, this should run out of the bottle:
>
> https://gist.github.com/khakieconomics/c398c4c76b60bfded9c5
>
> JS
>
>
>
> On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 11:25:47 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > We disagree that a delta prior is useful and let's the user worry about other parts of the model!  I don't think the lengthscale is ever sufficiently well known for such approximations to not induce significant predictive uncertainty underestimates that affect inference.
> >
> > On Mar 22, 2016, at 13:24, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >
> > > Mike:
> > >
> > > I don’t see how you’re really disagreeing with me!  You write, “spending some time to think about the relevant length scales can help you build some really informative priors to clean things up.”  An informative prior is great.  A delta function prior (that is, treating the lengthscale parameter as known) can be a useful approximation and speed up computation, then the researcher can replace this by a strongly informative prior later.  It’s the usual “pick your battles” strategy.  GP with a reasonable fixed lengthscale will do the smoothing that is needed so the researcher can focus on the more important aspects of the model.
> > >
> > > When we’re looking for a generic lowess replacement, it’s another story, we’d like the model to “learn” the lenghscale, requiring only a minimal amount of prior information.  But for specific applications, more and more I’ve been leaning toward running hier models with fixed hyperparameters, or with strong priors on the hyperparams.
> > >
> > > A
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Mar 21, 2016, at 5:21 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > I’m going to have to complicate things by disagreeing with Andy and Seth a nontrivial amount.
> > > >
> > > > As most people have noted, GPs are horrendously non-identified.  This is in fact a fundamental
> > > > property of these objects!  It turns out that the functions supported by any two distinct set of
> > > > hyperparameters (even those varying by an epsilon amount) are completely different; in other
> > > > words you’ll never see the same function sampled from a GP with two different sets of
> > > > hyperparameters.
> > > >
> > > > Hence by taking only a single set of hyperparameters you are ignoring a giant space of functions
> > > > that could interpolate between your data just as well as those supported by your distinguished
> > > > hyperparameters but in different ways.  This in term manifests as _drastic_ underestimates
> > > > of your predictive uncertainty away from the data.
> > > >
> > > > If you care only about predictive performance near your data then you might be okay, but
> > > > if you really want to know what’s going on between your data then you really do have to
> > > > marginalize over the hyperparameters.  Empirical Bayes has the same problem of misrepresenting
> > > > the posterior uncertainty.  WON’T SOMEBODY THINK OF THE UNCERTAINTY? <insert
> > > > Helen Lovejoy>.
> > > >
> > > > Also, as Seth, Mike, and Aki note, spending some time to think about the relevant length scales
> > > > can help you build some really informative priors to clean things up.  As in Seth’s example, if
> > > > you can put together some good priors then you might be able to do a full marginalization in
> > > > practice.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Mar 21, 2016, at 7:58 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > > Hi Rachael. Just to clarify what you have in mind--your fake data simulation creates 2000 draws from a GP, but you're interested in the standard case that you're modeling, which is just inference based on a single draw, right? (If you could use all 2000 draws that would certainly help with identification, but I'm guessing that's not the case.)
> > > > >
> > > > > As Aki says, the noise variance (sd = 3) is overwhelming the signal variance (sd = 1).  But another issue is that with the covariance parameterized as exp(-.1 d^2), the lengthscale is 2.23 in the parameterization I like, which is exp(-.5 d^2 / l^2). But the data you're observing is on a regular grid in the interval [0,1], and thus the lengthscale is way too long to recover.
> > > > >
> > > > > I switched it to noise variance of 0.1 and lengthscale 0.2 and prior on lengthscale and now it does a fine job recovering the parameters.
> > > > >
> > > > > Broadly my thinking, which Andrew mentioned, is that informative priors on the hyperparameters make a lot of sense, and fixing those hyperparameters is just a very informative prior which can be reasonable in many cases. (As a practical matter, it can also help with finding bugs!) Another thing that I think is very helpful as you're testing out / debugging models is to estimate the hyperparameters from the data ("empirical Bayes") which as you note has a long history, and not just in frequentist settings. In Stan, I've had success finding learning parameters using optimizing(...), an example of which I also included in the attached.
> > > > >
> > > > > In terms of scalability in a hierarchical setting, you might also get some ideas from our paper, which has Stan code at the end: http://sethrf.com/files/fast-hierarchical-GPs.pdf
> > > > > Seth
> > > > >
> > > > > On Mon, Mar 21, 2016 at 9:52 AM, Rachael Meager <rachael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Thanks Mike, the x-axis data is already from 0-1 but I will try out the rest of it and see if it helps.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Monday, 21 March 2016 12:58:05 UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > > > > > > Not sure this will make much difference, but I like to:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > (1) first rescale the x-axis data to range from 0-1
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > (2) reparameterize in terms of inv_rho_sq (ie. `Sigma[i,j] <-  exp(-pow(x[i] - x[j],2)/inv_rho_sq)`) so that values toward zero reflect more linear data
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > (3) use a cauchy(0,1) prior (inc. using the tan trick, pg 214 manual v2.9.0) so that the peak prior reflects a linear prior, and half of the mass of the prior reflects length scales that are less than the range of the data
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > --
> > > > > > > Mike Lawrence
> > > > > > > Graduate Student
> > > > > > > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > > > > > > Dalhousie University
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Mon, Mar 21, 2016 at 1:34 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi, just a quick thought which Seth F and I have been bouncing around recently . . . you could try just setting the length scale parameter to a fixed value.  There are a few reasons for this.  Most obviously it should make computing go faster.  At the same time, in any particular application such as yours, I think there is a lot of prior information so you should be able to choose a reasonable value for this parameter.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > To put it another way:  from a Bayesian perspective, the right thing to do is to use an informative prior.  But in this case the prior info might be much stronger than the data anyway, so why not just treat this parameter as data?  Alternatively, a strong prior (for example, lognormal centered at the prior estimate with a small sd) should also work well.  In that case, just make sure to run Stan with reasonable inits.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > A
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Mar 21, 2016, at 11:38 AM, Rachael Meager <rachael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hi Folks,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > First, thank you all so much for rstan and for staffing this forum. My research would be approximately 5000 times harder without you and I'm forever grateful .
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Right now, I'm simulating Gaussian Processes in rstan and trying to fit models for inference about the covariance functions. I find that this sometimes produces relatively poor inference on the covariance kernel's lengthscale parameter ("rho_sq"), and am wondering if I'm making some obvious mistake that I just don't have the experience to spot. I've attached my R file and the session log file, including the execution of sessionInfo().
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > To generate data, I'm using the stan simulation model in the manual in section 15.2 (on page 160, in version 2.9.0). First I construct an "x" vector of 100 points on [0,1], then draw from a GP on the space, like this:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > data {
> > > > > > > > > int<lower=1> N;
> > > > > > > > > real x[N];
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > transformed data {
> > > > > > > > > vector[N] mu;
> > > > > > > > > cov_matrix[N] Sigma;
> > > > > > > > > for (i in 1:N)
> > > > > > > > > mu[i] <- 0;
> > > > > > > > > for (i in 1:N)
> > > > > > > > > for (j in 1:N)
> > > > > > > > > Sigma[i,j] <- exp(-0.1*pow(x[i] - x[j],2))
> > > > > > > > > + if_else(i==j, 3, 0.0);
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > parameters {
> > > > > > > > > vector[N] y;
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > model {
> > > > > > > > > y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > So you can see I've set eta to 1, rho_sq to 0.1 and sigma to 3. I then fit the following simplified version of the stan model in the manual in section 15.3 to one of the (vector) draws from the GP above. This is model 1 in the R file:
> > > > > > > > > data {
> > > > > > > > > int<lower=1> N;
> > > > > > > > > vector[N] x;
> > > > > > > > > vector[N] y;
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > transformed data {
> > > > > > > > > vector[N] mu;
> > > > > > > > > for (i in 1:N) mu[i] <- 0;
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > parameters {
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > real<lower=0> inv_rho_sq;
> > > > > > > > > real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > transformed parameters {
> > > > > > > > > real<lower=0> rho_sq;
> > > > > > > > > rho_sq <- inv(inv_rho_sq);
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > model {
> > > > > > > > > matrix[N,N] Sigma;
> > > > > > > > > // off-diagonal elements
> > > > > > > > > for (i in 1:(N-1)) {
> > > > > > > > > for (j in (i+1):N) {
> > > > > > > > > Sigma[i,j] <-  exp(-rho_sq * pow(x[i] - x[j],2));
> > > > > > > > > Sigma[j,i] <- Sigma[i,j];
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > // diagonal elements
> > > > > > > > > for (k in 1:N)
> > > > > > > > > Sigma[k,k] <- 1 + sigma_sq; // + jitter
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > inv_rho_sq ~ cauchy(0,5);
> > > > > > > > > sigma_sq ~ cauchy(0,5);
> > > > > > > > > y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > This model works pretty well, however, the inference on rho_sq is patchy relative to the inference on sigma_sq. The mean of the rho_sq posterior jumps around because of the heavy right tail and this is quite sensitive to the dispersion in the priors (compare output of models 1, 2, in the attached file). I tried to get rid of the heavy tail using uniform priors but that does worse inference overall (see output of model 3). The inference breaks totally if I do either of these 2 things: (1) try to have improper uniform priors to do MLE (model 4), or (2) try to put a prior on rho_sq instead of inv_rho_sq (model 5).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Obviously you can see I've dispensed with inference on the eta parameter for now, setting it to its correct value of 1. I did this because at first I thought the instances of poor inference were due to a weak identification issue with eta in there, but this model is not performing any better without it. Fortunately, the inference on sigma_sq is always really good, which is the main goal of my project -- but I do want to know what's going on with rho_sq.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Does anyone know if there's a way to avoid the fat right tail on the rho_sq without the pathologies of the uniform? Should I be using normals here instead - and would that be generally helpful or just for this specific rho_sq? And do we know why the posterior gives up when I put a prior on rho_sq directly, or use an improper uniform prior?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > As I said, I'm attaching an R file that does this all together. I usually save the stan models separately as per the manual's suggestion, but I figured it would be more convenient for you guys to have it in 1 place. I'm also attaching the log file from running this R script on the unix server I have access to at MIT.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I hope this is clear, let me know if I should provide further information or clarification. Thanks in advance for any input or suggestions you have!
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Cheers
> > > > > > > > > Rachael

messages.body_plain:
Hi all! I have a few responses: First, I really understand this situation a lot better now, thank you all. The lengthscale I chose to simulate with just doesn't seem to be strongly identifiable on the domain [0,1] for the reasons Seth outlined. I've tried various priors, including tight normals, and they don't fix the problem.

What's interesting is that my main goal is to do inference on sigma_sq and all these strategies (fixing rho to a given value, tight prior on rho, normal prior on rho) change the inference on rho but don't really change the sigma_sq inference. That's good news but I guess it's confusing because I think it must mean the model can successfully separate out the information about sigma from the information (or lack of it) about rho. Is that right?

Question for the thread: Are there analogously values of sigma_sq we wouldn't be able to identify in a GP setting?

Seth -- thanks for replying and for your explanation of what is happening! It really helped. Yes, I can only use 1 draw from the GP for this problem, you're right that I'm simulating more than I need. I'm curious about your example because you said that the inference in the example you posted was good -- but when I run it, it's still only good on sigma. The true lengthscale is at the 2.5% percentile of the posterior for rho which is not a good situation, in my book. Is that what you get when you run it? I'm attaching the output I got. (PS: your paper on hierarchical GP was/is on my to-read list!)

Michael - thanks for replying! It's true that fixing rho doesn't help us with rho, and maybe it will hurt posterior predictive inference, but if I just want inference on sigma_sq it seems like it should be ok -- no? Or are you saying that our posterior distribution on sigma_sq is inappropriately tight due to the (incorrect) assumption that we know the true rho? That sounds intuitive, but in this very specific case I'm not sure that's true, given that changing rho doesn't seem to change sigma_sq inference very much even in the tails. But perhaps I'm just not looking at the right output carefully enough, and have overlooked something important?

Jim - thanks for replying, the reparameterisation is really neat and obviously I am a fan of anything that produces a graph called "Why we do full bayes".  (Also you helped me realise I made an error before when I conflated bayes with improper priors and MLE -- I was heuristically extrapolating from the models with unimodal symmetric posterior distributions in basic stats, but of course it's not generally true outside that class.)  I'm playing around with your example to see if I can break the inference on rho again despite the reparameterisation, and I'll report back if I find anything interesting.

> On Mar 21, 2016, at 12:34 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Hi, just a quick thought which Seth F and I have been bouncing around recently . . . you could try just setting the length scale parameter to a fixed value.  There are a few reasons for this.  Most obviously it should make computing go faster.

Just wanted to point out this isn't always true.  It will make the
calculation per iteration faster, but unless you choose the right scale,
it may be slower than fitting the right scale.  At least that's what we've found
adding hierarchical priors over fixed priors with a too-broad variance.  For
instance, in IRT models, taking

  theta ~ normal(0, 2.5);

would be slower than

  theta ~ normal(0, sigma);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

when the simulated value for sigma was around 1.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayes Factors via product spaces?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayes Factors via product spaces?
messages.body_plain:
You're always in one model or the other in Stan, too.
It's just that we marginalize out the mixture indicator
parameter.  That should just make computation more efficient.

The key to implementing anything in Stan is to understand
what density you want to fit.  If you can write the model
down in JAGS, that will determine the density you're fitting.
Then we should be able to code it in Stan directly.

- Bob

> On Mar 22, 2016, at 11:52 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Is there any update on this thus far?  I happened to stumble on this post from googling about a stan implementation of the product space method.
>
> Intuitively it seems like one could implement a similar concept in stan.
>
> The key in bugs/jags is that you're always in one model or another.
> When in model 1, you're estimating model 1 with some probability of switching to model 2, where model 2's "priors" are evaluated as the posterior of model 2 (previously estimated). The latter is *only* to make jumping easier. I don't think it's actually required for computing the BF in theory, it just helps with mixing.
>
> Could one do something analogous?
> In stan, one can pit two models against each other as a mixture; (p[1]likelihood[1] + p[2]likelihood[2])*priors.
> I tried this and of course it didn't seem to 'work'; I had an intercept-only model and a full model, and the probability of each was roughly .5 (no change from prior of ~logistic(0,1)).
> Or several chains would converge to suggest p[1] was much higher, although BayesFactor suggests the opposite (this seems highly dependent on initial values).
> I'm using the example from the BayesFactor package (below).
>
> Is it possible to conditionally set priors, or to 'weight' the priors themselves by the probability of each model?
>
>
> library(BayesFactor)
> library(rstan)
> data(attitude)
> ds <- attitude
> ds <- scale(ds)
> options(mc.cores=parallel::detectCores())
> rstan_options(auto_write=TRUE)
>
> bf.stan <- "
> data{
>     int N;
>     int J;
>     matrix[N,J] y;
> }
>
> parameters {
>     vector[6] beta;
>     real intercept[2];
>     real<lower=0> resid[2];
>     real p_logis;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
>     simplex[2] p;
>
>     p[2] <- exp(p_logis)/(1 + exp(p_logis));
>     p[1] <- 1 - p[2];
> }
>
> model {
> real lp_k[2];
> real lp;
> vector[N] yhat[2];
>     beta ~ cauchy(0,1);
>     intercept ~ cauchy(0,1);
>     resid ~ cauchy(0,1);
>     p_logis ~ logistic(0,1);
>
>     for(n in 1:N){
>         yhat[1,n] <- intercept[1];
>         yhat[2,n] <- intercept[2] + y[n,2:7]*beta;
>     }
>     lp_k[1] <- log(p[1]) + normal_log(y'[1],yhat[1],rep_vector(resid[1],N));
>     lp_k[2] <- log(p[2]) + normal_log(y'[1],yhat[2],rep_vector(resid[2],N));
>     lp <- log_sum_exp(lp_k);
>     increment_log_prob(lp);
> }
> "
> stanOut <- stan(model_code=bf.stan,data=list(y=ds,N=30,J=7),iter=10000,chains=8)
>
>
>
>
>
> On Monday, November 3, 2014 at 5:00:19 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I was not able to definitively answer Martin Smira's question
> about whether it would be possible to implement the product-space
> approach to Bayes factor computations with HMC.
>
> This was developed by Carlin and Chib:
>
>   B.P. Carlin, S. Chib
>   Bayesian model choice via Markov chain Monte Carlo methods
>   Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 57 (1995), pp. 473–484
>
> There's also an overview in a (paywalled) psych journal that kicked
> off the discussion (Lee and Wagenmakers are two of the co-authors):
>
>   http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022249611000423
>
> And there's a discussion by Charles Geyer in the umbrella sampling chapter of
> the MCMC Handbook (not one of the free chapters, I'm afraid).
>
> The most explicit reference I saw for how a model like this can be
> coded is in a BUGS vol2 example:
>
>   http://www.medicine.mcgill.ca/epidemiology/joseph/courses/EPIB-682/pines.pdf
>
> We do not have that example working in Stan, nor could I get a version
> working.  From what I can tell, the product-space approach simulates a reversible
> jump MCMC method with Gibbs sampling and pseudo-priors, with some fiddly
> pre-tuning required to adjust the pseudo-priors.  But I'm afraid I don't even
> understand why it'd work in BUGS because the posterior just looks wrong (so there's
> probably something I'm not understanding --- like maybe they only take the parameter
> samples from one of the branches [which clearly won't work in Stan]).
>
> I had problems trying to conceptualize what the model would even look
> like in Stan and was wondering if anyone had any suggestions or an explanation
> of why it wouldn't be possible.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Effect of unused parameters?
messages.subject_clean: Effect of unused parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

In some of my models, I am using a ragged array of sorts.
E.g., I may use:

vector[K] mu[K];
in which I may only actually *use* mu[1,1], mu[2,1:2], mu[3,1:3], and so on.
I place priors only on the mu values I use, and thus not on, e.g., mu[1,2:K].
I then only ever use those mus (and thus, not mu[1,2:K], mu[2:3:K]) in the likelihood where appropriate.

In the output of course, HMC allows the particles to float off indefinitely, so the mean may be huge (and the sd infinite).
I've thought this is 'fine' and just a quirky side effect of having unconstrained and unused parameters.

However, are there implications for convergence and inference for the used variables?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How scalable is Naive Bayes in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How scalable is Naive Bayes in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
To make this more concrete, here's the posterior
for theta

data {
  int<lower=0> M;

  int<lower=1, upper=K> s[M];

  ...

model {
  ...
  theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);

  for (m in 1:M)
    s[m] ~ categorical(theta);

And here's how you can code it directly without
using any parameters:

transformed data {
  vector[K] counts;
  cat_counts <- rep_vector(0, K);

  for (m in 1:M)

    cat_counts[s[m]] <- cat_counts[s[m]] + 1;
}
generated quantities {
  simplex[K] theta;
  theta ~ dirichlet(counts + alpha);

dirichlet(counts + alpha) is the analytic posterior here, so you
can make independent draws of theta in the generated quantities block.

The posteriors for phi all work the same way.

- Bob

> On Mar 21, 2016, at 3:45 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> The Dirichlet is conjugate and you're using labeled data,
> so the posteriors for alpha and beta will also be Dirichlet
> and can be computed directly in the generated quantities block.
>
> An intermediate step would be to collect sufficient stats
> and convert the looped categorical into multinomials.  That
> will be a whole lot faster, but still not as fast as just
> calculating the analytic posterior and drawing a sample from
> that directly.
>
> There's a discussion of doing both of these thing in the language
> manual chapter on optimizing Stan code.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
Yes, but you'll have to do it yourself with the Jacobians.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  ordered[N] xobs;  // make sure these go up in order
  ...

parameters {
  real xtrue_raw[N];
  ...

transformed parameters {
  real xtrue[N];
  for (n in 1:N) {
    xtrue[n - 1] <- x_obs[n] + inv_logit(xtrue_raw[n]);
  }

model {
  // Jacobian adjustment for xtrue_raw -> xtrue transform
  for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(log_inv_logit(xtrue_raw[n])
                       + log1m_inv_logit(x_true_raw[n]));

There's a discussion in the manual chapter on transforms that
shows this is what we do internally for upper and lower bounds.

- Bob

> Thanks for the fast answer, and sorry, I  oversimplified the model  for loop should be:
>
>   for(i in 1:N_obs) {
>       vector[N_choices] effect;
>
>       effect[1:N_choices-1] <- beta *cond[i];
>       effect[N_choices] <- 0;
>       winner[i] ~  categorical_logit(B + effect );
>   }
>
>
>  softmax(B) should indicate the "underlying" probability of the choices, isn't it?

I don't know what that means.  It's the log-odds when the cond variables
are all zero.

> What I want to achieve is to inform the model that the choice 1 is much more likely than the others (regardless of the actual data that I'm seeing).
>
> And yes, I don't want to put a prior on the outcome, I know the prior in this model should be on "A" (which I then feed in B).

I don't see an A any more.  Any prior you want here toward one category
or the other should be built into B.  But if you have the regression
beta * cond[i], then you can't control that directly.

> But I might have not been clear. So I understood that the K-1 parametrization is "better" than the K.

Only in the sense of being well identified without a prior,
which can help with computation.

> So if I stick to the K-1, do I have a way to indicate that softmax(B)[1] should be around .7?  Or that it should be 3-5 times larger than the other softmax(B)[2:]?

B = (A[1], ...A[K-1], 0).

With K outcomes, you can't control the dimensions independently.  You can make
softmax(B)[1] near 0.7 when you know all the other values of B are
near zero, but otherwise, you only know the log odds relative to the
fixed value.

> And how bad is to use the K parametrization?

Not that bad if you have priors.

> And even if I use it I still don't know how to indicate what I want. If I had 2 choices, I know that .9 in log-odds scale should represent 70%. But I'm really lost since I have more choices, and the value of one choice in the transformed scale affects the rest of the choices.

But anyway, you probably don't want all of this hand-tweaked
coaxing of solutions.  Put some reasonable priors on the parameters
and let the data decide what the answer should be.

- Bob
