messages.subject: Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
messages.subject_clean: Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan Team,

I'm a big fan of Stan and Gelman's Bayesian Data Analysis. I really enjoyed Bob Carpenter's and Michael Betancourt's youtube videos. In the RMHMC video I was blown away by how far the maximum likelihood point of the funnel was from where all the mass of the funnel was. It scared me away from point estimates which are all too common in the Systems Biology literature.

Anyway my colleague and I have a system of ODEs that we're using to describe some longitudinal mRNA data. So far my colleague said he's been using particle swarm optimization to find a maximum likelihood estimate. He gets about 200 ML estimates (which are all different by the way because our parameter space is non-convex), he throws out about 50 of the estimates that "don't give qualitatively correct results". On the remaining 150 estimates he takes quantiles to get estimates of the parameters and confidence bounds around those estimates in what turns out to be a very ad-hoc and probably quite misleading Bayesian analysis.

To me the problem is begging us to run HMC to get actual draws from the posterior. These parameters represent knowledge of a human being's blood clotting system so it's actually very elucidating to see what the most probable values are. The problem is that our system is stiff and as I understand Stan does not support non-stiff ODEs as of now. I figure if you're using something like Newton''s method, calculating the gradient of the objective function (which involves finding the change in the solution at every time point) won't be too bad, especially with autodiff. I'm guessing with more fancy Runge-Kutta methods the problem starts to get really sticky. Where is Stan at in terms of supporting non-stiff ODEs?

Also, our problem is definitely multi-modal, but I am hoping that once RMHMC comes out for Stan that won't be so big of a problem. Am I naive in thinking that? When do you all anticipate RMHMC coming out?

Thanks,
Arya

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, extra parameters with no priors can severely mess up adaptation.
But they’re also just ill-defined and _shouldn’t_ fit.  Because HMC samples
so efficiently it immediately identifies these “flat” parameters by running off
to infinity, while other samplers slowly diffuse which can make it difficult to
identify the problem.

So if you have to have ragged parameters then give them reasonable priors.
You’ll make adaptation easier if the priors are centered around zero and have
the same scale as your posterior standard deviations.  normal(0, scale) would
work well.

The performance of HMC scales really well with additional parameters, so
with proper priors you shouldn’t affect performance too much (the biggest
hit will probably be the I/O overhead for having to save the extra parameters)
but in the end having ancillary parameters is just another place where you
could mess something up so it’s always best to remove them if you can.

messages.body_plain:
> Michael - thanks for replying! It's true that fixing rho doesn't help us with rho, and maybe it will hurt posterior predictive inference, but if I just want inference on sigma_sq it seems like it should be ok -- no? Or are you saying that our posterior distribution on sigma_sq is inappropriately tight due to the (incorrect) assumption that we know the true rho? That sounds intuitive, but in this very specific case I'm not sure that's true, given that changing rho doesn't seem to change sigma_sq inference very much even in the tails. But perhaps I'm just not looking at the right output carefully enough, and have overlooked something important?

I wouldn’t be surprised if sigma_sq ends up being reasonably identifiable
with moderately informative priors.  There’s always the possibility that
sigma_sq could get very large (in which case the rest of the GP would
be unconstrained) or get really small (in which case you overfit your
data) but if you’re not seeing either of those cases then you could
have enough data to constrain the natural variation.

If you’re using the kernel

k(x, y) = alpha * exp( - sum_{n} rho_n (x_n - y_n)^2 ) + sigma2 * delta_{xy}

then the biggest problem is usually a nonidentifiabilty between the rho
and the alpha.  So it would make sense that sigma2 is the first parameter
to become identifiable as you add more data.  That said, if you _fix_ rho
to specific values then you might get underestimated variance on sigma2
as you lose the correlation between the varying rho and the residual noise
needed to ensure a reasonable fit.

Ultimately in these systems I don’t trust my intuition, so I calculate and see.
If you can run a full MCMC and sigma2 looks good despite large variance
among the rho and the alpha then it might be okay to fix rho for this application.
(I am hedging enough yet?  :-p)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
messages.body_plain:
CVODE was implemented internally in Stan 2.9, but has only been exposed in
the CmdStan interface.  So if you want to get started you try it there.  We’re
looking at CVODES and other solvers, as well, but that’s still in development.
It would be cool to see if you can get any traction in fitting your model in
CmdStan already.

A prototype of RHMC might be added to the internal code soon (whenever I
get around to it) but it will be limited in its application.  The problem is that
RHMC requires second and third-order derivatives but we haven’t really
tested our higher-order autodiff all that well.  In particular, it’s unlikely that
the higher-order autodiff will play well with the ODE solvers.

In any case, RHMC won’t help too much with multi modality.  For that you’d
need _Adiabatic Monte Carlo_, but that’s still a research project.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
messages.body_plain:
I certainly wouldn't trust the analysis you described, because
the computation has no interpretation (you can't just find different
modes and call that variance).

We have a non-stiff ODE solver in all the Stan interfaces,
and a stiff ODE solver in CmdStan 2.9 (and it should be in the
2.10 release of RStan).

Nobody has a solution for combinatorial multimodality.  The
ability of a single chain to mix will through very limited multimodality
will depend on the trough between the modes and how easy it is to pass
through.  And there are some techniques that'll help there, but none
that are implemented in Stan.

I'm curious what the longitudinal study of mRNA is.  I just
started to do some work on isoform (splice variant) expression.

- Bob

I’m not sure how that manifests as multi modality.  You could certainly have strong
correlations and potentially partial non-identifiabilities, which HMC can tackle, but
I don’t see how that leads to separate modes.  Typically separates modes requires
a mixture hiding somewhere.

scientists or the typical machine learner to a robust statistical analysis, _especially_
in science.

messages.body_plain:
I have a similar problem.

I want to switch on/off nodes based on the user input. So to make a model more or less naive.

It would be nice if I could include parameters and all sampling of them in IF statements. In this way useless parameters would not have to be added into the model.

Is there any way to do this?

Thanks

On Wednesday, March 23, 2016 at 8:23:31 AM UTC+11, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Yes, extra parameters with no priors can severely mess up adaptation.
> But they’re also just ill-defined and _shouldn’t_ fit.  Because HMC samples
> so efficiently it immediately identifies these “flat” parameters by running off
> to infinity, while other samplers slowly diffuse which can make it difficult to
> identify the problem.
>
> So if you have to have ragged parameters then give them reasonable priors.
> You’ll make adaptation easier if the priors are centered around zero and have
> the same scale as your posterior standard deviations.  normal(0, scale) would
> work well.
>
> The performance of HMC scales really well with additional parameters, so
> with proper priors you shouldn’t affect performance too much (the biggest
> hit will probably be the I/O overhead for having to save the extra parameters)
> but in the end having ancillary parameters is just another place where you
> could mess something up so it’s always best to remove them if you can.
>
> On Mar 22, 2016, at 8:36 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Interesting. Could you articulate why this occurs and how it could influence the posterior space?
> > This is valuable for me --- I have one model I constructed to be fairly generalizable depending on user-input, but requires a ragged storage of parameters to do so.
> > This particular model has had some major, major convergence issues, and it occurred to me that the sampling of unused parameters may be one reason -- I was thinking that if anything, it could seriously affect the warmup period, which then affects the actual sampling.
> >
> > On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 3:26:57 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > No, having these extra dimensions will destroy HMC.  You can’t have them kicking around.
> > >
> > > > On Mar 22, 2016, at 4:20 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Interesting. So it doesn't necessarily influence inference, correct? Intuitively, I feared it would, but ultimately it's just adding a constant 'shape' to the surface over which everything is marginalized anyway, right?
> > > >
> > > > Do unconstrained parameters (unused) contribute to divergent transitions?
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 3:11:36 PM UTC-5, James Savage wrote:
> > > > > Hi Stephen -
> > > > >
> > > > > You may want to add priors to the unused parameters--it will run much faster (in a little test I ran, a model with 2 parameters with 1 unidentified ran 300 times slower than a model with a prior on both).
> > > > >
> > > > > Jim
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 3:49:46 PM UTC-4, Stephen Martin wrote:
> > > > > > Hey everyone,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In some of my models, I am using a ragged array of sorts.
> > > > > > E.g., I may use:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > vector[K] mu[K];
> > > > > > in which I may only actually *use* mu[1,1], mu[2,1:2], mu[3,1:3], and so on.
> > > > > > I place priors only on the mu values I use, and thus not on, e.g., mu[1,2:K].
> > > > > > I then only ever use those mus (and thus, not mu[1,2:K], mu[2:3:K]) in the likelihood where appropriate.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In the output of course, HMC allows the particles to float off indefinitely, so the mean may be huge (and the sd infinite).
> > > > > > I've thought this is 'fine' and just a quirky side effect of having unconstrained and unused parameters.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > However, are there implications for convergence and inference for the used variables?

of the parameter vector a function of the input and
populating and depopulating it yourself.   This is much
easier with database-like entries with multiple
parallel arrays, some containing indexes (like you need
for ggplot in R or what melt gives you in reshape);  then
you don't need to compute lengths.

Then you don't need any conditionals.

You mean something like this:

model {
  theta ~ normal(if_else(fit_mean, mu, 0),
                 if_else(fit_sigma, sigma, 1));

flags as Jonah indicated.

As long as you give mu and sigma proper priors it should work,
but it's going to make the models very hard to read.  The
alternative is a lot of cut-and-paste, which is also not ideal.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
messages.body_plain:
I just modified my most needed (and one of the most problematic) models to include priors for unused parameters, and it *worked*.

Bob, if you recall my previous thread about the slow or halted warm-up, you may recall that my trace plots were extremely flat, with several thousand divergent transitions.

Now I have 0 divergent transitions and all chains are converging.

I'm not sure this is stated in the manual anywhere, but given that it turned this model from a trainwreck to a perfectly functioning model implies that perhaps the manual, if it doesn't already, should mention the effects of unrestricted parameters.

That is - parameters that are unrestricted by the data or by priors cause terrible sampling due to, I assume, terrible adaptation among other possible geometric problems.

On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 4:23:31 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Yes, extra parameters with no priors can severely mess up adaptation.
> But they’re also just ill-defined and _shouldn’t_ fit.  Because HMC samples
> so efficiently it immediately identifies these “flat” parameters by running off
> to infinity, while other samplers slowly diffuse which can make it difficult to
> identify the problem.
>
> So if you have to have ragged parameters then give them reasonable priors.
> You’ll make adaptation easier if the priors are centered around zero and have
> the same scale as your posterior standard deviations.  normal(0, scale) would
> work well.
>
> The performance of HMC scales really well with additional parameters, so
> with proper priors you shouldn’t affect performance too much (the biggest
> hit will probably be the I/O overhead for having to save the extra parameters)
> but in the end having ancillary parameters is just another place where you
> could mess something up so it’s always best to remove them if you can.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
messages.body_plain:
The posterior has to be proper or MCMC doesn't make sense.
An unrestricted parameter doesn't have a proper posterior.
This is discussed at length in the chapter on problematic
posteriors in the language manual.  That chapter also discusses
how Gibbs/Metropolis can mask the issue.

- Bob

One difficulty about adding sparse matrices as a new variable type that all the operations work with is that you need to plumb it through.. all the operations.  If you only add true sparse versions of some operations and allow the type to also work with the dense versions of operations you introduce a lot of opportunities for users to do something naive and kill performance or run out of memory.    I'm enthusiastic about adding a sparse data type but it's not a one person part time project.

> On Mar 23, 2016, at 3:47 AM, Rasmus Berg Palm <rasmusb...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I see. You're right. I can solve all this analytically.
>

> What I'm looking for is the posterior predictive p(y|x,theta) (where theta are all the params), which seems to have a closed form solution due to the conjugate priors.

Right --- you just add the observed counts to the prior Dirichlet
parameter to get the posterior's Dirichlet parameter. The
posterior predictive for further multinomial data is then Dirichlet-multinomial:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet-multinomial_distribution

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If they're a separate type, we can limit their use
to a set of functions rather than having them auto-promote
to dense matrices (the way int autopromotes to real in Stan).
But I've also not taken them on due to all the plumbing
through I/O.  Once we get the refactor in place, we'll revisit
it.  Eigen's getting better sparse matrix funcitonality all the
time.

I added a note to add sizes of u, v, and w in the docs:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1709#issuecomment-200467751

- Bob

messages.subject: Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
messages.subject_clean: Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
messages.body_plain:
Given many (10k+) series of observations of different candidates over times 1:t, I want to estimate what value I should expect at t+1 for any candidate.
I will select the 100 candidates with the highest expectation for a future purpose, and so I will need to shrink the expected values for the selected series back towards the mean for all series in order to get an accurate revised expectation for these selected candidates.

I'm thinking to model this in 2 steps using
1) gaussian processes to estimate the initial expectation for time t+1 and its uncertainty; and then subsequently
2) a gaussian mixture model for the distribution of true expectations, connected to the initial expectations from the previous step by the uncertainty from the previous step. This is a conventional hierarchical bayesian model.

My problem lies in estimating the uncertainty for the gaussian processes at t+1, which is crucial to an accurate Bayesian shrinkage in the next step. In particular, I'm sure that the observation model for the candidate series (the noise around the observations) is not gaussian, it's heavily left skewed. What I need is a way of modelling a skewed non-gaussian observation model while maintaining good Bayesian accounting for uncertainty in parameters & hyperparameters.

Flaxman, Gelman et al. in "Fast hierarchical Gaussian processes" using Stan, discuss "Extensions to non-Gaussian observation models", They end with the ominous words "In practice, we have had difficulties using HMC to update both z1, . . . , zn and the hyperparameters simultaneously. A reasonable solution might be to follow the blocked approach of [1, 32], wherein the hyperparameters are sampled with, e.g. HMC and then conditional on these hyperparameters the zi are sampled, with HMC or another algorithm."

This sounds to me like they're saying that it doesn't really work to estimate hyperparameters in Stan when using non-Gaussian models, try GPStuff instead. However, GPstuff doesn't seem to allow for skewed likelihoods (although there is a log transform of observations in one of their examples. GPML, the other main package, has a warped Gaussian likelihood model available which is perfect, but does not appear to do proper Bayesian estimates of uncertainty including the uncertainty deriving from the hyperparameters.

Have I understood this all right?
How much does mis-specification of the observation model effect posterior uncertainty anyway?
Is there a way to get where I need to go using Stan?
If not Stan, where else?

I'm happy to put the work into generating a case study for the Stan site, if someone could guide me in this jungle.

thanks for reading,

Jonathan

drawn?

> > > Yea, I guess this one requires a bit of an explanation. What we are looking at is co-occurences of diagnosis. So imagine three outcome categories: 0, A, B, A+B. So category 1 corresponds to neither A nor B being reported, category 2 to only A observed, and so on. We are looking at all possible combinations over a large number of diagnosis, and the idea is that the base rate of having diagnosis A is approximately the same over all combinations. This may not be true for some combinations, but for the vast majority it is indeed true.

messages.body_plain:
I see. I will read the chapter, however from your answer I'm understanding that unbounded parameters (although with proper priors) are somehow harmful for the model.

Is this correct?

To answer your question

=================================================

I have 7 parameters of which only one is part of the naive model (LDA with phi known), and thus necessary.

  //-------------------------------//
  //   topic probability           //
  //-------------------------------//

  simplex[K] theta[M];   // topic distribution for doc m

  //-------------------------------//
  //   linear regression           //
  //-------------------------------//

  vector<lower=1-0.1, upper=maxPoly+1+0.1>[M] sigma; //activation/disease state
  vector<lower=0>[W] err[K]; //standard deviation of the linear equations

  //-------------------------------//
  //   unknown population          //
  //-------------------------------//

  vector[W] gamma;
  simplex[2] known_unknown[M];

  //-------------------------------//
  //   bias         //
  //-------------------------------//

  vector<lower=0> [num_batches]  bias_magnitude;
  vector[W] perturbation[num_batches];

================================================

Those parameter have these priors:

  //-------------------------------//
  //   topic probability           //
  //-------------------------------//

  for(m in 1:M) theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // topic probability per document

  //-------------------------------//
  //   linear regression           //
  //-------------------------------//

  for(m in 1:M) for(k in 1:K) for(w in 1:W) if(counts[m,w]>0)
    counts_10[m,w] ~ lognormal(phi_hat_stable[m,k,w], err[k,w]); //prior on linear regression mean sigma

  for(k in 1:K) err[k] ~ cauchy(0, 2); //error on gene expression for sigma prediction

  //-------------------------------//
  //   unknown population          //
  //-------------------------------//

  for(m in 1:M) known_unknown[m] ~ dirichlet(k_n_hyper);

  //-------------------------------//
  //   cell isolation bias         //
  //-------------------------------//

  gamma ~ multi_normal(lg_mu, lg_sigma); // prior UN-known population

  for(b in 1: num_batches) perturbation[b] ~ gamma(bias_magnitude[b], 1/bias_magnitude[b]);

================================================

The whole model is attached.

Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all,

just few summary note on my use (just of one day) of "size 0" object as method for conditional models.

1) It is really elegant and usually works

2) for constrained objects like simplex it works for parameter but it does not for transformed parameters with the error

"validate transformed params: <T_PARAM> has size 0, but must have a non-zero size"

in this case I had to declare that simplex as vector, which is not ideal although it is implicitly constrained because it is a result of a softmean transformation.

3) I'm not sure if these topic exists in the manuals, but since plasticity is one of the main advantages of Bayes statistics for many applications, I think it would be worth it to write a documentation for it.

In the future it would be great if a more integrated proper methodology could be integrate into Stan framework.

Stefano Mangiola

Data analyst @
Melbourne University
Hovens lab - Papenfuss lab
Royal Melbourne Hospital - WEHI
+61 (0)450135954

2016-03-24 13:06 GMT+11:00 Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com>:
>
> I decided to just add priors. I've used conditionals for other models before but in this case it's not conditional. It's a variable lower diagonal matrix.  I didn't want to use anything in upper triangle. I needed to just place priors on those values.
> On Mar 23, 2016 9:19 PM, "stefano" <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello Stephen,
> >
> > what solution did you use? Could you please formalize it here with an example?
> >
> > Thanks
> >
> > Stefano Mangiola
> >
> > Data analyst @
> > Melbourne University
> > Hovens lab - Papenfuss lab
> > Royal Melbourne Hospital - WEHI
> > +61 (0)450135954
> >
> > 2016-03-23 16:45 GMT+11:00 Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com>:
> > > I just modified my most needed (and one of the most problematic) models to include priors for unused parameters, and it *worked*.
> > >
> > > Bob, if you recall my previous thread about the slow or halted warm-up, you may recall that my trace plots were extremely flat, with several thousand divergent transitions.
> > >
> > > Now I have 0 divergent transitions and all chains are converging.
> > >
> > > I'm not sure this is stated in the manual anywhere, but given that it turned this model from a trainwreck to a perfectly functioning model implies that perhaps the manual, if it doesn't already, should mention the effects of unrestricted parameters.
> > >
> > > That is - parameters that are unrestricted by the data or by priors cause terrible sampling due to, I assume, terrible adaptation among other possible geometric problems.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 4:23:31 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > Yes, extra parameters with no priors can severely mess up adaptation.
> > > > But they’re also just ill-defined and _shouldn’t_ fit.  Because HMC samples
> > > > so efficiently it immediately identifies these “flat” parameters by running off
> > > > to infinity, while other samplers slowly diffuse which can make it difficult to
> > > > identify the problem.
> > > >
> > > > So if you have to have ragged parameters then give them reasonable priors.
> > > > You’ll make adaptation easier if the priors are centered around zero and have
> > > > the same scale as your posterior standard deviations.  normal(0, scale) would
> > > > work well.
> > > >
> > > > The performance of HMC scales really well with additional parameters, so
> > > > with proper priors you shouldn’t affect performance too much (the biggest
> > > > hit will probably be the I/O overhead for having to save the extra parameters)
> > > > but in the end having ancillary parameters is just another place where you
> > > > could mess something up so it’s always best to remove them if you can.
> > > >
> > > > On Mar 22, 2016, at 8:36 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > > Interesting. Could you articulate why this occurs and how it could influence the posterior space?
> > > > > This is valuable for me --- I have one model I constructed to be fairly generalizable depending on user-input, but requires a ragged storage of parameters to do so.
> > > > > This particular model has had some major, major convergence issues, and it occurred to me that the sampling of unused parameters may be one reason -- I was thinking that if anything, it could seriously affect the warmup period, which then affects the actual sampling.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 3:26:57 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > > > > No, having these extra dimensions will destroy HMC.  You can’t have them kicking around.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Mar 22, 2016, at 4:20 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Interesting. So it doesn't necessarily influence inference, correct? Intuitively, I feared it would, but ultimately it's just adding a constant 'shape' to the surface over which everything is marginalized anyway, right?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Do unconstrained parameters (unused) contribute to divergent transitions?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 3:11:36 PM UTC-5, James Savage wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi Stephen -
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > You may want to add priors to the unused parameters--it will run much faster (in a little test I ran, a model with 2 parameters with 1 unidentified ran 300 times slower than a model with a prior on both).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Jim
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 3:49:46 PM UTC-4, Stephen Martin wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Hey everyone,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > In some of my models, I am using a ragged array of sorts.
> > > > > > > > > E.g., I may use:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > vector[K] mu[K];
> > > > > > > > > in which I may only actually *use* mu[1,1], mu[2,1:2], mu[3,1:3], and so on.
> > > > > > > > > I place priors only on the mu values I use, and thus not on, e.g., mu[1,2:K].
> > > > > > > > > I then only ever use those mus (and thus, not mu[1,2:K], mu[2:3:K]) in the likelihood where appropriate.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > In the output of course, HMC allows the particles to float off indefinitely, so the mean may be huge (and the sd infinite).
> > > > > > > > > I've thought this is 'fine' and just a quirky side effect of having unconstrained and unused parameters.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > However, are there implications for convergence and inference for the used variables?
> > > > > > >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Posterior uncertainty estimation for gaussian processes with non-gaussian observation models
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks for the replies Aki & Seth.

t (the number of values in series) will typically be around 2000 but could in some applications be 10000.
Each series will be a separate process, I'm not thinking one GP behind all the series.
The observation model will vary for each series, but a typical case might look roughly like a skew-normal gaussian with a mean of 5, a mode around -5, virtually nothing below -20, little weight above +20, but a long light tail stretching up to +500.

I'm attracted to seeing the observation model as being a mixture of 2 skew normal gaussians, with the mixing proportion as being the latent variable that evolves over time. This should be flexible enough to match the distributions of observations in any series well, and prior knowledge suggests that's it's not a bad picture for the physical reality underlying.

A comment of Andrew's on another GP thread pointed me towards time series models as a simpler alternative to GPs. Therefore I'm thinking that what I should do is start by implementing a time series approach, estimating the parameters of this skewnormal mixture, the fluctuation of the mixing proportion over time, and the resulting expectation and uncertainty at t+1.

Once I have this working I can see whether there is need to upgrade to using GPs. I'm thinking that because
a) I have many data points,
b) I am interested in a single process that evolves relatively slowly over time, and
c) I only want to do inference relatively near my data
it might not be worth paying the price in time and complexity to upgrade to GP.

Does this seem like a sensible approach, considering what I want and the computational issues using Stan?

Many thanks again!

Jonathan

On Wednesday, March 23, 2016 at 7:41:08 PM UTC, Seth Flaxman wrote:
> Sorry to be ominous. ;)
>
> I'm sure Aki can tell you whether GPstuff has what you're looking for.
> (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1206.5754.pdf lists a number of likelihoods that
> might be useful, including Gaussian scale mixture and Student-t...)
>
> But you might be okay in Stan, as there've been some improvements on
> the backend since we wrote that paper, and many more are slated for
> the future. Plus there's ADVI. Also, see the other discussion started
> by Rachael in which we discuss various compromises / informative
> priors which might help in the short term. Inducing points or random
> fourier Features (which I have an implementation of in Stan that's
> almost ready to share, but have also had issues with learning
> hyperparameters) might also help.
>
> A key question: how large is t? Am I right that you're imagining a
> single GP prior from which all of the series of observations are
> drawn?
>
> Seth
>
> On Wed, Mar 23, 2016 at 2:15 PM, Jonathan Shaw <jonatha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Given many (10k+) series of observations of different candidates over times
> > 1:t, I want to estimate what value I should expect at t+1 for any candidate.
> > I will select the 100 candidates with the highest expectation for a future
> > purpose, and so I will need to shrink the expected values for the selected
> > series back towards the mean for all series in order to get an accurate
> > revised expectation for these selected candidates.
> >
> > I'm thinking to model this in 2 steps using
> > 1) gaussian processes to estimate the initial expectation for time t+1 and
> > its uncertainty; and then subsequently
> > 2) a gaussian mixture model for the distribution of true expectations,
> > connected to the initial expectations from the previous step by the
> > uncertainty from the previous step. This is a conventional hierarchical
> > bayesian model.
> >
> > My problem lies in estimating the uncertainty for the gaussian processes at
> > t+1, which is crucial to an accurate Bayesian shrinkage in the next step. In
> > particular, I'm sure that the observation model for the candidate series
> > (the noise around the observations) is not gaussian, it's heavily left
> > skewed. What I need is a way of modelling a skewed non-gaussian observation
> > model while maintaining good Bayesian accounting for uncertainty in
> > parameters & hyperparameters.
> >
> > Flaxman, Gelman et al. in "Fast hierarchical Gaussian processes" using Stan,
> > discuss "Extensions to non-Gaussian observation models", They end with the
> > ominous words "In practice, we have had difficulties using HMC to update
> > both z1, . . . , zn and the hyperparameters simultaneously. A reasonable
> > solution might be to follow the blocked approach of [1, 32], wherein the
> > hyperparameters are sampled with, e.g. HMC and then conditional on these
> > hyperparameters the zi are sampled, with HMC or another algorithm."
> >
> > This sounds to me like they're saying that it doesn't really work to
> > estimate hyperparameters in Stan when using non-Gaussian models, try GPStuff
> > instead. However, GPstuff doesn't seem to allow for skewed likelihoods
> > (although there is a log transform of observations in one of their examples.
> > GPML, the other main package, has a warped Gaussian likelihood model
> > available which is perfect, but does not appear to do proper Bayesian
> > estimates of uncertainty including the uncertainty deriving from the
> > hyperparameters.
> >
> > Have I understood this all right?
> > How much does mis-specification of the observation model effect posterior
> > uncertainty anyway?
> > Is there a way to get where I need to go using Stan?
> > If not Stan, where else?
> >
> > I'm happy to put the work into generating a case study for the Stan site, if
> > someone could guide me in this jungle.
> >
> > thanks for reading,
> >
> > Jonathan
> >

messages.body_plain:
This all sounds sensible to me, especially given the scale of the
data. You could always take a small subset of the data and see how a
GP fit compares to a time series fit in terms of predicting t+1.

Re: "each series is a separate process." This sounds like "no
pooling." But if your data lends itself to it (do you have groups of
some kind?), you might consider partial pooling (hierarchical
structure) on the parameters you'll be estimating for the time series
model.

Seth

messages.subject: Results difference with different parametrisation: The case of the Anova I random model
messages.subject_clean: Results difference with different parametrisation: The case of the Anova I random model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am writing this question to have a discussion on very different results I obtained using two different Stan parametrisation of the same model. I would have thought that my STAN models provide the same results, but unfortunately no. I am also comparing the results obtained with a similar parametrisation with JAGS (JAGS is not dead, right ? :-) ) and with beta-expectation tolerance intervals obtained analytically, using Robert Mee 1984 paper (Mee R.W., Beta-expectation and beta-content tolerance limits for balanced one-way ANOVA random model. Technometrics. 1984;26:251-254.). Notice I am not taking the results of Mee as granted (there are some approximation), but I know by experience that they are a good approximation of the tolerance intervals.

A little bit of background: the target is to obtain the posterior distribution of the parameters and the beta-expectation tolerance interval using MonteCarlo estimation (which, in this case, are the prediction interval obtained by integrating posterior parameters into the model/likelihood). Under flat prior, I am (well,... I was) confident that the posterior modes must be similar to the maximum likelihood estimators, and the beta-expectation tolerance interval of Mee's paper is the same than the MC-computed one.

Next, the data set is one of these that provides difficulties to maximum likelihood estimator, with a negative variance component for the random effect (and thus, lme() or SAS/PROC MIXED would put the estimate to 0).

Here is the results with the first part of the code (attached), really just translating the ANOVA 1 random model into Stan (Note also I obtained  similar results when running the ANOVA models obtained with brms or rstanarm package, for what's worth. I am running Stan 2.9.0-3 on Mac OS X 10.10.5 and R 3.2.2, but also, similar results have been obtained under Windows 7 (Stan 2.9.0 on R 3.2.2).

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-EnrXqYPw7_A/VvP7VFGz6YI/AAAAAAAAElE/ZefznXhgZzsjvlUuG282nLZ74M5t30kQw/s1600/SDPredInt.png> <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-xEvm_9eqrAU/VvP7NT0EryI/AAAAAAAAEk8/NaWSIo0GWi4nyIpcaEXxMrr-ARAzSAKaA/s1600/SDChains.png> <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-NuaPzn-0xq4/VvP7RmE8B3I/AAAAAAAAElA/mqP8H_2nnQUiKRyvPM-TujH9Ex_dFSYWQ/s1600/SDPostDens.png>

Observation : posterior mode are well achieved. Variability of b0 (the fixed intercept) is way too big. Prediction interval (beta-exp. tolerance interval) is way too large (right figure, red). Actually the HPD on b0 is already larger than the tolerance interval obtained using Mee's paper (blue).

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-S3O42DBjjwY/VvP8XS7LnkI/AAAAAAAAElU/H920-5CCosMx_-A8D4Jdb3m66Si0I5eTQ/s1600/tauPredInt.png> <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-8y7MDydFcMU/VvP7pGc-IgI/AAAAAAAAElI/gXdD93L4xgo9wOUup58WE-7vf6qlbdvmw/s1600/Tauchains.png>  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-02uvofyImRI/VvP7ra7xuCI/AAAAAAAAElM/g9RxfjNXRfAwUG8svpei1YU2wxBcdc7MA/s1600/tauPostDens.png>

Pierre

> On Mar 23, 2016, at 8:24 PM, stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I see. I will read the chapter, however from your answer I'm understanding that unbounded parameters (although with proper priors) are somehow harmful for the model.

> Is this correct?

The problem is improper posteriors, not unbounded parameters.
Too-thick or too-thin tails can also be a problem as can scales
well beyond unit scale (like normal(0, 1e-100) or normal(0, 1e100).
But something like y ~ normal(0, 1) has theoretically unbounded
support, but should sample just fine.

>
> To answer your question
>
> =================================================
>
> I have 7 parameters of which only one is part of the naive model (LDA with phi known), and thus necessary.
>
>   //-------------------------------//
>   //   topic probability           //
>   //-------------------------------//
>
>   simplex[K] theta[M];   // topic distribution for doc m
>
>   //-------------------------------//
>   //   linear regression           //
>   //-------------------------------//
>
>   vector<lower=1-0.1, upper=maxPoly+1+0.1>[M] sigma; //activation/disease state

We recomend against these kinds of interval-constrained priors.
Leave them unbounded and add a reasonable at least weakly
informative prior.

>   vector<lower=0>[W] err[K]; //standard deviation of the linear equations
>
>   //-------------------------------//
>   //   unknown population          //
>   //-------------------------------//
>
>   vector[W] gamma;
>   simplex[2] known_unknown[M];
>
>   //-------------------------------//
>   //   bias         //
>   //-------------------------------//
>
>   vector<lower=0> [num_batches]  bias_magnitude;
>   vector[W] perturbation[num_batches];
>
> ================================================
>
> Those parameter have these priors:
>
>   //-------------------------------//
>   //   topic probability           //
>   //-------------------------------//
>
>   for(m in 1:M) theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // topic probability per document
>
>   //-------------------------------//
>   //   linear regression           //
>   //-------------------------------//
>
>   for(m in 1:M) for(k in 1:K) for(w in 1:W) if(counts[m,w]>0)
>     counts_10[m,w] ~ lognormal(phi_hat_stable[m,k,w], err[k,w]); //prior on linear regression mean sigma
>
>   for(k in 1:K) err[k] ~ cauchy(0, 2); //error on gene expression for sigma prediction
>
>   //-------------------------------//
>   //   unknown population          //
>   //-------------------------------//
>
>   for(m in 1:M) known_unknown[m] ~ dirichlet(k_n_hyper);
>

Great variable name :-)

>   //-------------------------------//
>   //   cell isolation bias         //
>   //-------------------------------//
>
>   gamma ~ multi_normal(lg_mu, lg_sigma); // prior UN-known population
>
>   for(b in 1: num_batches) perturbation[b] ~ gamma(bias_magnitude[b], 1/bias_magnitude[b]);
>
> ================================================
>
> The whole model is attached.

These mixture models are difficult to fit because of multimodality.

messages.subject: Every iteration hits max treedepth
messages.subject_clean: Every iteration hits max treedepth
messages.body_plain:
Hi there

I'm trying to apply a model that I've got working to a different, messier dataset. As such I didn't necessarily expect NUTS to be successful, but what happened surprised me.

For 3 of the 5 chains, every post-warmup sample hit the max treedepth (as well as most pre-warmup samples). My understanding is that this means that the step size is too small, so each iteration doesn't reach the point of u-turning.

I'm trying to get a better understanding of NUTS, so I'd like to know what could have caused such a low step size to be chosen during warmup?

Cheers
Sam

That really helped a lot! The model is running a lot faster now, though it’s still a bit saturated during the warmup-phase. messages.body_plain:
At this point the big advantage for sparsity is the lower memory use.  It lets you manipulate matrices that just don't fit in memory. It does take a lot of sparsity before you get a speed advantage and it depends on whether it's column-oriented or row-oriented sparsity (empty rows are simply not stored/processed so that improves faster).  It's on my plate to do an explicit comparison (and soon since it's come up for rstanarm) but I'm swamped so it'll be a few weeks.

Krzysztof

Thanks, Jonah.  I was specifically asking about the diagnostics that
are available with HMC, optimization and ADVI through CmdStan.
The fact that all four paths (what CmdStan calls "method", i.e.,
sample, optimize, advi, diagnose) all have diagnostic files
makes the terminology tricky.

In CmdStan, there's a separate diagnostics file produced (with unconstrained params
and other quantities I don't understand) for sampling, but it looks like there's
no programmatic way to get that info in R --- it just gets written to file (and
would have to be read back in with a generic R csv reader or something).

Daniel and I have been going through all the output to try to make
sure our writers are comprehensive enough.

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Consolidated-Output-for-Sample,-Optimize,-ADVI,-and-Diagnose

> On Mar 24, 2016, at 5:34 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> The diagnostic files have nothing to do with the “diagnose” method.

I couldn't find any doc on the "diagnostic_file" argument in the CmdStan
manual other than "Auxiliary output file for diagnostic information".
The Stan language manual doesn't appear to have anything unless
it's named something other than "diagnostic".

Daniel and I were trying to figure out what all the output was
and what all the input config is across RStan and CmdStan.

I couldn't find a way to call the "diagnose method" in RStan,
or find a way to get the "diagnostic files" other than as files.
So I was confusingly talking about both kinds of diagnosis.

> In general the diagnostic output files report unconstrained values
> and gradients (and momenta in HMC) to see everything going on
> under the hood.  This is additional information to the samples output
> and not [HEAVY DUPLICATION].

The initial part of the file appears to be an exact duplicate of
the config output in the output.csv files, and several of the columns
appear to be the same (though maybe they're not --- I couldn't find any
doc).  I guess whether that's "heavy" is in the eye of the beholder;
sorry if that was offensive, but I was just trying to mark duplicate
output so we could try to avoid some of the duplication going forward.

I realize there's new info there, too.  It was confusing that
the name of the parameter was the same, but Daniel figured out it was
unconstrained when the values didn't line up with the output file.

There is also a diagnostic file output for ADVI and optimization, though
the one in optimization appears to only dump a dup of the config.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the replies!

I guess I can see the point in not wanting the particularly long tail, which actually makes sense given that I'm using logistic regression, and large variance won't make a difference inside the inv logit. That being said, in my application there will be usually be a large number of groups (30-100) which probably means there's lower risk for the scale to overfit with large values.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] reparametrizing a half-cauchy
messages.body_plain:
Such reparameterizations aren’t so much for increased speed but rather
improved robustness.  Cauchy’s are difficult to sample because the heavy
tails take forever to explore, but an auxiliary parameterization yields much
nicer tails at the expense of the extra parameters.  Whether the expense
is worth it or not depends on how much time you end up spending in the
tails — if you have lots of data then the posterior will have nice tails and
it won’t matter, but if you have sparse data then it could make a significant
difference.

messages.body_plain:
You could also try doing the same thing with the other
varying intercepts ("random effects") as with sex, that
is use only (A - 1) of the A possibilities and set the other
one to 0.  The models aren't identified other than through
priors otherwise.

Also, I'm not sure why you use the same hierarchical scales
sigma and sigma_change everywhere.  Don't you expect the scale
of effects to vary?

Given that you're setting the first cutpoint to 0, you
probably want the rest of them to be positive,
so rather than

  ordered[J-2] tau_raw;

you probably want

  positive_ordered[J - 2] tau;

which ensures all tau[j] > 0.

I just defined tau directly.  We won't need tau_raw, but can
just define the cumulative probabilty terms so that the calls
to Phi aren't repeated:

    vector[J] phi_cumulative;
    phi_cumulative[j] <- Phi(y_hat);  // tau[1] = 0 by construction
    for (j in 2:(J - 1))
      phi_cumulative[j] <- Phi(y_hat - tau[j - 1]);
    phi_cumulative[J] <- 1;

Then I'd use those to define theta:

  theta[1] <- phi_cumulative[1];
  for (j in 2:J)
    theta[j] <- phi_cumulative[j] - phi_cumulative[j - 1];

It'll be much more efficient without the repeated calls to Phi
and there's some savings from not having to write out two versions
of tau.  You could shave a little more off by defining theta[J] directly
and making phi_cumulative size J - 1 in stead of J, but that probably won't
be noticeable.

I'd also suggest writing the linear predictor as

    y_hat
      <- beta
      + sex * female[i]

      + a_state[state[i]]

      + a_party_id[party_id[i]]
      + a_age[age[i]]

      + a_edu[edu[i]]
      + a_race[race[i]]
      + a_wave_sex[wave_sex[i]]
      + a_wave_age[wave_age[i]]
      + a_wave_edu[wave_edu[i]]
      + a_wave_race[wave_race[i]]
      + a_wave_party_id[wave_party_id[i]];

I find that much easier to read than

> y_hat <- beta + sex * female[i]+a_state[state[i]]+
> a_party_id[party_id[i]] + a_age[age[i]]+a_edu[edu[i]] + a_race[race[i]]+
> +a_wave_sex[wave_sex[i]]+a_wave_age[wave_age[i]]+a_wave_edu[wave_edu[i]]+a_wave_race[wave_race[i]]+a_wave_party_id[wave_party_id[i]];

R and BUGS and JAGS make you write + at the end of a line because
they have parsers that treat end-of-line whitespace differently
than other whitespace, but start of line is traditional in code
and in math typesetting.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, March 24, 2016 at 2:34:24 PM UTC+2, Jonathan Shaw wrote:
> t (the number of values in series) will typically be around 2000 but could in some applications be 10000.

10k+ independent models with t=2k-10k means that you need to consider the computational speed of alternative approaches.

> Each series will be a separate process, I'm not thinking one GP behind all the series.
> The observation model will vary for each series, but a typical case might look roughly like a skew-normal gaussian with a mean of 5, a mode around -5, virtually nothing below -20, little weight above +20, but a long light tail stretching up to +500.
>
> I'm attracted to seeing the observation model as being a mixture of 2 skew normal gaussians, with the mixing proportion as being the latent variable that evolves over time. This should be flexible enough to match the distributions of observations in any series well, and prior knowledge suggests that's it's not a bad picture for the physical reality underlying.

Do you want the variance and skewness of the skew normal to evolve in time, too?

>
> A comment of Andrew's on another GP thread pointed me towards time series models as a simpler alternative to GPs.

I'm confused. What do you mean by "time series models"? GPs can be used as time series models, too. There are some time series models which are faster in Stan than basic GP implementation with dense covariance or precision matrix.

> Therefore I'm thinking that what I should do is start by implementing a time series approach, estimating the parameters of this skewnormal mixture, the fluctuation of the mixing proportion over time, and the resulting expectation and uncertainty at t+1.
>
> Once I have this working I can see whether there is need to upgrade to using GPs. I'm thinking that because
> a) I have many data points,
> b) I am interested in a single process that evolves relatively slowly over time, and
> c) I only want to do inference relatively near my data
> it might not be worth paying the price in time and complexity to upgrade to GP.
>
> Does this seem like a sensible approach, considering what I want and the computational issues using Stan?

Benefit of Stan is that it's easy to code the model with skew normal and mixing proportion. I guess that for your data NUTS is going to be slow (which is problem if you need to run it 10K+ times, unless you can use a computer cluster). ADVI might be fast enough, but you need to check its reliability.

With plain skew normal the problem would be easier. INLA is fast (for certain types of dynamic models) for 1D data and has skew normal. GPstuff is fast (for certain types of dynamic models) for 1D data and adding skew normal is easy. I don't know how easy it would be implement mixture of skew normal in INLA. Adding mixture of skew normals (with time varying mixing proportion) in GPstuff or GPy could be one day of work for someone familiar with these software.

Aki

messages.subject: Analogies to Stan's handling of missing data
messages.subject_clean: Analogies to Stan's handling of missing data
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

First off, thanks very much to the developers of Stan.  I've been using it in a great deal.  It solves a number of problems that I would have if I were to use other programs, all in one go.  I'm also really excited to see new features being added (parallelization, WAIC and loo, etc.).

I've got a data set with some missing data.  I've read previous <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/mEGf1RFBlcU> threads <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/g0Iko45_8A8> on this topic, and the documentation in the User's Guide, which have explained how to write the model.  I'm trying to figure out how to write this up for a manuscript, in a way that someone unfamiliar with Stan would understand.  My sense is that Stan is using the parameter estimates for observed data to inform the estimates for missing data in a way that is similar to a specially-made imputation algorithm (in which the imputation model is exactly the same as the analysis model).  Is this accurate?  If so, would the estimates from Stan asymptotically approach estimates from FIML, just as infinite imputations would?

Thanks for your thoughts.

Best wishes,
Katherine

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Analogies to Stans' handling of missing data
messages.body_plain:
Stan's handling of missing data, like that of JAGS and BUGS,
is the standard Bayesian approach, where the missing data are just
treated like other parameters.   So you're defining a joint
density p(y, y_miss, theta) where y is observed data, y_miss
is missing data, and theta are the usual parameters.  Then
you get inference for the posterior p(y_miss, theta | y) in
the usual way.  Nothing special about "missing data" per se.

So it's not like a standalone imputation system (multiple or
otherwise), where you do the imputation, then plug the imputed
values into the "full data" model.  Rather all the inference is
joint.

I don't know what FIML is or what you mean by infinite imputations.

Asymptotpics are tricky here as you have to carefully design what's
growing;  usually the data related to imputing the missing data doesn't
grow, as in when you have missing predictors for an item and you impute
them based on the other predictors (and perhaps the outcome).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan: formatting data for multi-dimensional vectors/row_vectors?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] rstan: formatting data for multi-dimensional vectors/row_vectors?
messages.body_plain:
There's doc in the CmdStan manual, but it probably didn't make
it into R's doc.

It's just a rectangular data structure for the shape.  all of
the following are M x N:

  matrix[M, N]  a;
  vector[N] a[M];
  row_vector[N] a[M];
  real a[M, N];

The array indices are picked up first, then the underlying types.
That's because

  vector[N] a[M];

is declaring a to be an M-array of N-vectors.  So you have to
index into the array to get the vector.

- Bob

messages.subject: Dynamic Tobit model in Stan
messages.subject_clean: Dynamic Tobit model in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I am trying to implement in Stan a generalization of the Tobit model, a dynamic Tobit model with lagged observed variables.
My core idea is that of trying to model the soccer players performances (ratings) over the season through the previous performance (lagged dependent  variable) and a bunch of predictors.  The final aim is to be able - in a rough way - to do some predictions and to test the goodness of the model with cross validation and elppd approach. So far, a simple AR(1) varying-intercept hierarchical model - with as many groups as the different players positions in the field and without predictors except the intercepts - gives good results in terms of fitting and of Rhat. Since for every player a censored value arises whenever the player doesn't play - i.e., when his performance is not observed - i need to move towards a model that is able to deal with it, and the dynamic Tobit seems to be suitable for this objective.

However, the main computational problem - as I outline in the attached pdf file - stems from the fact that there is not a closed form for the likelihood, since this would require an integral with as many dimension as censored times. In the literature (you can find the reference in the pdf file) a simulated likelihood approach is proposed, and I am trying to implement this in Stan.

In the attached Stan file you find the draft of the model. Just for being clearer about my code:

- t are the data, the ratings of the players (values bounded between 1 and 15), collected for N (around 300) players and for L (around 20) games.
- eta_error are the generated truncated normal random variables, epsilon are  Uniform(0,1) random variables
- Phi_factor regard the  contributes for the simulated likelihood, for the observed and for the censored times.
- so far, the eta_error component is not still included in the "oberved likelihood  part", as the general procedure of Chang would suggest.

I launch the Stan model with these settings:

fanta_stan_dyn_tobit<-stan(file="dynamicTobit5.stan",data=fanta_dat_dyn_tobit,
                           iter=1000,
                           init="0",init_r=0,
                           control=list(adapt_delta=0.9, max_treedepth=12),
                           chains=3, cores=3,verbose = FALSE)

As results, with this code I have several divergent transitions after warmup (500 for each chain), terrible mixing, high Rhat and , even with a smaller dataset with  N = 15 and L= 7 the code speeds up slowly.
I suspect that the specification for the scale parameters could be wrong, but from the original paper of Chang-Sheng-Kai it is not straightforward understand how to properly model them (I force them to be between 0 and 1).
I don't know why, but if in lines 60- 61 of the Stan file I set up the truncation with the following:

increment_log_prob(normal_log(eta_error[r, n, l-1], 0, 1));
      increment_log_prob(normal_cdf(trunc_point, 0, 1));

without the "-" (as written in the reference manual and as it seems to me obvious), my inference gets better, with more reasonable results (in some sense close to the simple AR(1) varying intercept model) and with Rhat much more close to 1.1...I don't grab this behaviour, maybe I am doing some mathematical mistakes with the truncation.

So far I tried to:
- change priors, use the "Matt tricks"
- Use sampling statement, with the T[,] for truncations.
- Reparametrize the model.

Anyway, thank you in advance for your patience. I am managing with this problem for a while, feel free to tell me if and what doesn't makes sense.
I appreciate any advice.
Thanks

Leonardo

messages.subject_clean: implementing Stan's HMC sampler in MATLAB (automatic parameter tuning & finite differences)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

since the current version of Stan is not compatible with the models I deal with (see this post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/general/-gaLDaepCwQ>), I decided to implement some of the features of Stan in MATLAB.
In particular, I am now interested in implementing its state-of-the-art HMC sampler, and I have a couple of questions about it (I've been reading Chapter 58 of Stan's reference guide).
For the core algorithm, I can start with Matt Hoffman's MATLAB code <http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~mdhoffma/> for NUTS (which includes the dual-averaging algorithm for choosing the step-size during burn-in). However, I am also considering to implement the general three-stage procedure for automatic parameter tuning used in Stan, which seems pretty robust. Stan's manual (58.2) reports a fairly good description of the procedure, but it omits some implementation details (e.g., how is the diagonal covariance matrix regularized?). Is there a more detailed reference for this? Or, what is the code I should look at?

Not having access to the analytical gradient, in the first instance I will approximate derivatives of the log posterior with finite differences (FD). I appreciate that this will introduce errors and slow down the algorithm due to loss in precision -- and there are pathological cases in which FD will not work -- but I guess that for low-dimensional, non-pathological posteriors it should be fine (or at least better than nothing). Is there any particular problem I should be aware of when using FD for this?
Thanks,
Luigi

messages.subject: Ideas on fitting Dirichlet Process Mixture models in Stan
messages.subject_clean: Ideas on fitting Dirichlet Process Mixture models in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I read all the messages posted in the user group about Dirichlet Process models in Stan and I completely understand that stan uses HMC and hence, is not able to sample discrete parameters yet. I needed to somehow find a way to implement DP and DPM models and I thought of two solutions:

idea 1: I wrote my own DP sampling code in R. I then combined my code with my Stan model in a Gibbs sampling fashion where all parameters are sampled in Stan except beta0. Then given sampled parameters, I use my own code to sample beta0. I put this sampling into a loop from 1 to Num-of-iterations and in each iteration, I use stan with iter = 2, and warmup = 1 and my own code. The code seems working and converges. Would this idea make sense to you?

idea 2: In Stan manual, there is an example of using LDA for topic modeling where authors propose marginalizing over the discrete parameter. We know with Latent Dirichlet Allocation, we can choose a fixed number of mixtures to approximate DP. Therefore, I used the same idea to approximate DP. The issue is my code is super slow. I fixed number of mixture components to 30 and ran the code for 300 subjects (this basically leads to two nesting loops with 30*300 iterations). As the tutorial highlighted for the mixture models, we should avoid vectorizing for this models. Is there any way to make the code faster? What would you think?

Attached are my .stan and my .R code for idea 2 and for the model below:

Y_i =  beta0_i + beta_1 * X[i] + \epsilon
\epsilon ~ Normal(0, var = sigma^2)

--- Priors:
beta0_i ~ G
G ~ DP(\alpha, G0 = N(0, 10))

beta_1 ~ Normal()
sigma^2 ~ flat prior

Thanks very much for your help,
-Sepehr

The problem isn't the discrete parameters, it's that the
DP has different numbers of parameters each iteration.

> I needed to somehow find a way to implement DP and DPM models and I thought of two solutions:
>

I put this sampling into a loop from 1 to Num-of-iterations and in each iteration, I use stan with iter = 2, and warmup = 1 and my own code. The code seems working and converges. You have to balance the number of iterations in Stan with
the autocorrelation time;  too few iterations and you don't
move far enough, too many and you do too much work.

> 	• idea 2: In Stan manual, there is an example of using LDA for topic modeling where authors propose marginalizing over the discrete parameter. We know with Latent Dirichlet Allocation, we can choose a fixed number of mixtures to approximate DP. Therefore, I used the same idea to approximate DP. The issue is my code is super slow. This is a common approach (it's one of the later BUGS example).
There's not a way to make the code faster.
And given that the posterior is so multimodal, you can't use
the usual convergence diagnostics.

You might try something like variational approximation
or even penalized maximum likelihood.

something labeled LDA in the program, or in the math below --- I

latent ability at that time as part of the model?

Or is there a way to only deal with the observed games in
the likelihood, but have the variance somehow depend on time
so that if there's a bigger time between games, there might be
a bigger difference in ability?

Usually forcing parameters into a constrained interval if
they are not physically constrained (like probabilities) is
a bad idea.  It's easy for the real answer to want to be outside
the interval and force all the probability mass against the boundaries
and present both statistical and computational problems.

> I don't know why, but if in lines 60- 61 of the Stan file I set up the truncation with the following:

>

You probably want the CDF on the log scale, normal_cdf_log(...).
If it's truncation below a point, it's just -normal_cdf_log(...) (the
negation being because it's in the denominator and we're working in
the log domain).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] implementing Stan's HMC sampler in MATLAB (automatic parameter tuning & finite differences)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] implementing Stan's HMC sampler in MATLAB (automatic parameter tuning & finite differences)
messages.body_plain:
So, I did some very quick tests with a 15-D correlated Gaussian with unit variance and various degree of correlation (up to rho = 0.99).
I compared NUTS with numerical gradient vs NUTS with exact gradient vs an adaptive slice sampling method that estimates the covariance matrix and subsequent slicing direction using warmup samples (the method I would be otherwise using; so both NUTS and slice sampling have an adaptive component).

Up to rho = 0.9, the numerical gradient does okay at least on this very simple case.
The number of effective samples (Neff) per "gradient evaluation" is comparable between the numerical and analytical gradients (perhaps with a tiny reduction in efficiency of the former, less than 5-10%).
Of course the numerical method takes a much larger number of function evaluations (2*D function evals per gradient evaluation, if using a central difference scheme).
However, performance of the numerical gradient drops for the largest value of rho that I tried (rho = 0.99); there is a difference of almost a factor of 10 in Neff per gradient evaluation between numerical and exact gradient.

For values of rho of 0.9 or less, the comparison of NUTS with numerical gradient with the slice sampler is in strong favour of the slice sampler, which is up to 20 times better in terms of Neff per function evaluation. The advantage of slice sampler becomes astronomical for rho = 0.99.
I tried using HMC (with dual-averaging) and numerical gradient and it seems to perform better than NUTS with numerical gradient (I just picked a unit-length trajectory) -- this suggests that the trajectories in NUTS end up being too long and accumulate too large error.

This was very quick and dirty -- I just wanted to get some ballpark.
Clearly this is not a fair comparison since the adaptive slice sampler can estimate quite easily the shape of the covariance matrix.
NUTS would get a bigger advantage for complex density shapes. However, if the shape of the distribution is particularly complex, NUTS with numerical differentiation would also start to perform poorly.
Things can get better with better differentiation schemes, but they would require more function evaluations.

In conclusion, I think it might not be worth for me to implement HMC/NUTS with naive numerical differentiation.
It seems that any gain might be swamped by the loss in efficiency due to accumulated numerical error and the increased cost in function evaluations to estimate the gradient numerically.
Of course there might be clever solutions to this problem, but I'd rather focus on other methods at this point -- coming back to HMC/NUTS when I can compute an exact gradient.

Best,
Luigi

> For values of rho of 0.9 or less, the comparison of NUTS with numerical gradient with the slice sampler is in strong favour of the slice sampler, which is up to 20 times better in terms of Neff per function evaluation. The advantage of slice sampler becomes astronomical for rho = 0.99.
> I tried using HMC (with dual-averaging) and numerical gradient and it seems to perform better than NUTS with numerical gradient (I just picked a unit-length trajectory) -- this suggests that the trajectories in NUTS end up being too long and accumulate too large error.
>
> This was very quick and dirty -- I just wanted to get some ballpark.
> Clearly this is not a fair comparison since the adaptive slice sampler can estimate quite easily the shape of the covariance matrix.
> NUTS would get a bigger advantage for complex density shapes. However, if the shape of the distribution is particularly complex, NUTS with numerical differentiation would also start to perform poorly.
> Things can get better with better differentiation schemes, but they would require more function evaluations.
>
> In conclusion, I think it might not be worth for me to implement HMC/NUTS with naive numerical differentiation.
> It seems that any gain might be swamped by the loss in efficiency due to accumulated numerical error and the increased cost in function evaluations to estimate the gradient numerically.
> Of course there might be clever solutions to this problem, but I'd rather focus on other methods at this point -- coming back to HMC/NUTS when I can compute an exact gradient.
>
> Best,

messages.body_plain:
I haven't run your code but a few things immediately stand out. First are mu and theta really constrained to be positive? From what you said you're trying to model I would think mu and theta are unconstrained. Also in the model block you're putting a prior on 1/tau_square, with tau_square declared as a parameter. If you do it this way you need to adjust for the Jacobian of the transformation. If you really want to put the prior on the precision (1/tau_square) then you can avoid this issue by declaring that to be the parameter and putting the prior directly on that and you won't need a jacobian adjustment (you'll just have to use sqrt(1/precision) in the model). But it would probably be preferable to parameterize in terms of the standard deviation and put a prior on that (so you don't have to take square roots or reciprocals).

Hope that helps,

Jonah

>
> The problem isn't the discrete parameters, it's that the
> DP has different numbers of parameters each iteration.

That's true. But I guess number of components (parameters) by itself is a parameter and is discrete. If could sample that parameter, implementing DP would be very easy.

>
> > I needed to somehow find a way to implement DP and DPM models and I thought of two solutions:
> >
> >
> >         • idea 1: I wrote my own DP sampling code in R. I then combined my code with my Stan model in a Gibbs sampling fashion where all parameters are sampled in Stan except beta0. Then given sampled parameters, I use my own code to sample beta0. I put this sampling into a loop from 1 to Num-of-iterations and in each iteration, I use stan with iter = 2, and warmup = 1 and my own code. The code seems working and converges. Would this idea make sense to you?
>
> You have to balance the number of iterations in Stan with
> the autocorrelation time;  too few iterations and you don't
> move far enough, too many and you do too much work.

That's awesome. In my results I saw some big autocorrelation is some parameters and I knew I wanted to increase number of iterations in the Stan model, however, I was reluctant as I thought I might undermine the Markov Chain theory by having more iterations on some parameters. I'll definitely give it a shot. Thanks for the idea.

>
> >         • idea 2: In Stan manual, there is an example of using LDA for topic modeling where authors propose marginalizing over the discrete parameter. We know with Latent Dirichlet Allocation, we can choose a fixed number of mixtures to approximate DP. Therefore, I used the same idea to approximate DP. The issue is my code is super slow. I fixed number of mixture components to 30 and ran the code for 300 subjects (this basically leads to two nesting loops with 30*300 iterations). As the tutorial highlighted for the mixture models, we should avoid vectorizing for this models. Is there any way to make the code faster? What would you think?
>
> This is a common approach (it's one of the later BUGS example).
> There's not a way to make the code faster.
> And given that the posterior is so multimodal, you can't use
> the usual convergence diagnostics.
>
> You might try something like variational approximation
> or even penalized maximum likelihood.
>
> I'm afraid I didn't follow the combination of regression and
> something labeled LDA in the program, or in the math below --- I
> don't see how the betas connect to anything.
>
> Are you trying to do a DP mixture of regressions?

This was a simple example that I wrote to show my corresponding stan code. You may consider subjects with random intercepts (intercepts are subject-specific) as in Linear Mixed effects models. Instead of putting a specific prior on these subject-specific intercepts (usually normal dist in LME models), I wanted to relax the distribution assumption. Therefore, I put a G prior where G itself has a Dirichlet Process prior. And yes, the result is basically putting a mixture of normal distributions where they are mixed over mean.

> - Bob
>
>
> > Attached are my .stan and my .R code for idea 2 and for the model below:
> >
> > Y_i =  beta0_i + beta_1 * X[i] + \epsilon
> > \epsilon ~ Normal(0, var = sigma^2)
> >
> > --- Priors:
> > beta0_i ~ G
> > G ~ DP(\alpha, G0 = N(0, 10))
> >
> > beta_1 ~ Normal()
> > sigma^2 ~ flat prior
> >
> > Thanks very much for your help,

> > I read all the messages posted in the user group about Dirichlet Process models in Stan and I completely understand that stan uses HMC and hence, is not able to sample discrete parameters yet.
>
> The problem isn't the discrete parameters, it's that the
> DP has different numbers of parameters each iteration.
>
> That's true. But I guess number of components (parameters) by itself is a parameter and is discrete. If could sample that parameter, implementing DP would be very easy.

The number of components isn't directly a parameter, but it's close.
But even the conjugate Gibbs samplers for these have problems with
modality.  And Gibbs can be very slow to mix.

>
>
> > I needed to somehow find a way to implement DP and DPM models and I thought of two solutions:
> >
> >
> >         • idea 1: I wrote my own DP sampling code in R. I then combined my code with my Stan model in a Gibbs sampling fashion where all parameters are sampled in Stan except beta0. Then given sampled parameters, I use my own code to sample beta0. I put this sampling into a loop from 1 to Num-of-iterations and in each iteration, I use stan with iter = 2, and warmup = 1 and my own code. The code seems working and converges. Would this idea make sense to you?
>
> You have to balance the number of iterations in Stan with
> the autocorrelation time;  too few iterations and you don't
> move far enough, too many and you do too much work.
>
> That's awesome. In my results I saw some big autocorrelation is some parameters and I knew I wanted to increase number of iterations in the Stan model, however, I was reluctant as I thought I might undermine the Markov Chain theory by having more iterations on some parameters. I'll definitely give it a shot. Thanks for the idea.

You just have to be careful with detailed balance.  But as long as
the parameters are being treated the same way each time, that's usually
easy.  You can do all sorts of tricks with Gibbs like sampling some parameters
more frequently than others and still get the right answer asymptotically.

>
>
> >         • idea 2: In Stan manual, there is an example of using LDA for topic modeling where authors propose marginalizing over the discrete parameter. We know with Latent Dirichlet Allocation, we can choose a fixed number of mixtures to approximate DP. Therefore, I used the same idea to approximate DP. The issue is my code is super slow. I fixed number of mixture components to 30 and ran the code for 300 subjects (this basically leads to two nesting loops with 30*300 iterations). As the tutorial highlighted for the mixture models, we should avoid vectorizing for this models. Is there any way to make the code faster? What would you think?
>
> This is a common approach (it's one of the later BUGS example).
> There's not a way to make the code faster.
> And given that the posterior is so multimodal, you can't use
> the usual convergence diagnostics.
>
> You might try something like variational approximation
> or even penalized maximum likelihood.
>
> I'm afraid I didn't follow the combination of regression and
> something labeled LDA in the program, or in the math below --- I
> don't see how the betas connect to anything.
>
> Are you trying to do a DP mixture of regressions?
>
> This was a simple example that I wrote to show my corresponding stan code. You may consider subjects with random intercepts (intercepts are subject-specific) as in Linear Mixed effects models. Instead of putting a specific prior on these subject-specific intercepts (usually normal dist in LME models), I wanted to relax the distribution assumption. Therefore, I put a G prior where G itself has a Dirichlet Process prior. And yes, the result is basically putting a mixture of normal distributions where they are mixed over mean.

I see.

To get back to your earlier question, there's also the mixture of
mixtures.  That'll let you fit up to a max number of components, but will
"select" the right number of components for you.  There's a nice arXiv
paper I saw on this recently (referenced from Christian Robert's blog):

http://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.06241v1.pdf

- Bob
